entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders-london.txt" target="_blank">Agentic coding: A roundtable with industry leaders (London) - Speakers: Arnaud Giuliani (CPTO \& Co-founder @ Kotzilla), Christos Gkekas (Software Engineer), Iury Souza (Senior Engineer, SumUp), Maia Grotepass (Staff Engineer Android, Qonto), Slobodan Manojlović (VP, Lead Software Engineer), Tristan Hamilton (Technical Lead, HubSpot), Jose Alcérreca (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iQ0R0EfOBiw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-a-roundtable-with-industry-leaders-london ## About the talk As new tools rapidly reshape modern software engineering, this panel will explore how companies and developers are leveraging agentic coding, automated agents, and specialized developer tooling in their daily workflows. We aim to highlight practical applications, discuss measurable productivity improvements, and candidly address the challenges engineering teams face when integrating these tools at scale. ## Summary - Code generation shifts development bottlenecks across the pipeline. Once teams accelerate code reviews, new constraints emerge around live experiments and safe production releases. - Specialized agent teams can replace single general assistants across complex domains. Teams build distinct agents for areas such as performance or logging, coordinating them through routers or shared pools. - Autonomous pull requests require guardrails and clear human accountability. Some workflows auto-submit routine fixes for tech debt, but each PR points back to a designated owner and relies on strict automated checks. - Harness engineering needs centralized shared tooling alongside room for experimentation. Teams maintain core infrastructure for shared concerns such as logs and crashes while pruning inactive skills through automated scripts. - Local developer hardware is strained by concurrent agent-driven builds. Engineers encounter exhausted memory and slow machines when agents trigger multiple Gradle builds simultaneously. ## Topics agentic-coding, ai-tooling, code-review, harness-engineering, entries.summary: This document introduces the transcript of an industry roundtable from Android Dev Summit in London discussing agentic coding, exploring how automated tools reshape development workflows, productivity, and maintenance.

entries.title: Keep the screen on
entries.summary: Added documentation for the new `keepScreenOn` modifier in Jetpack Compose (available in Compose UI 1.9.0 and higher). This allows developers to easily keep the screen on conditionally—such as during video playback—by applying the modifier to a composable, avoiding the need to manually manage WindowManager flags.

entries.title: Range between devices
entries.summary: The ranging documentation has been updated to include Android 17 (API level 37) features, such as Wi-Fi Proximity Detection, the Downlink-TDoA Tag (DT-Tag) device role for UWB sessions, and antenna mode configuration. It also documents Android 16 QPR2 additions like technology filtering for OOB configs, updates background location permission requirements for UWB DL-TDoA, and refines the Kotlin and Java code snippets for managing ranging sessions and callbacks.

entries.title: Common shared element use cases
entries.summary: Updated the shared element documentation for animating text font size changes in Jetpack Compose. The code snippet now correctly references the fully qualified `SharedTransitionScope.ResizeMode.scaleToBounds()` instead of the shorthand `ScaleToBounds()`, ensuring developers use the accurate API syntax.

entries.title: Customize shared element transition
entries.summary: Updated the documentation for Jetpack Compose shared element transitions to reflect API naming and signature changes. Specifically, `ScaleToBounds` was updated to the `scaleToBounds()` function call, and the parameter order and signature for `Modifier.renderInSharedTransitionScopeOverlay()` were corrected to match the latest library version.

entries.title: Navigation with shared elements
entries.summary: Updated the documentation for Jetpack Compose navigation shared elements to reference stable library versions and correct API links. Specifically, the minimum required version for `navigation-compose` to support predictive back with shared elements was updated from the alpha release (`2.8.0-alpha02`) to the stable `2.8.0` release, and the reference link for the `composable` builder was updated to point to the correct package summary.

entries.title: Hero benchmarks

This change ensures the documentation accurately reflects the current capabilities and availability of spatial tracking modes.

entries.title: Set up the Jetpack XR SDK
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack XR SDK dependency versions in the setup documentation for both Groovy and Kotlin build files. entries.title: Appstate Statestore
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack AppState StateStore library documentation to release version 1.0.0-alpha02 across all artifacts. This update provides developers with the latest bug fixes and improvements by bumping the dependency versions in the guide and adding the release notes entry for November 04, 2026.

entries.title: Appstate Transform
entries.summary: Released version 1.0.0-alpha02 of the androidx.appstate.transform library, updating all multiplatform dependencies and declaring the new version notes for developers.

entries.title: Biometric
entries.summary: The Biometric library has been updated to version 1.4.0-beta01, transitioning the 1.4 release from alpha to beta. This update includes both `androidx.biometric:biometric:1.4.0-beta01` and `androidx.biometric:biometric-compose:1.4.0-beta01`, signaling increased stability and moving closer to a final release for developers implementing biometric authentication and Compose-based authentication UI.

entries.title: Camera Feature Combination Query
entries.summary: The Camera Feature Combination Query library has been updated to version 1.7.0-rc02, bumping the release candidate version and updating dependency snippets for both the base and play-services artifacts.

entries.title: camera viewfinder
entries.summary: Updated the camera-viewfinder library artifacts (viewfinder-compose, viewfinder-core, and viewfinder-view) to version 1.7.0-rc02. This release includes the latest bug fixes and improvements leading up to the stable 1.7 release, and updates the corresponding dependency snippets and release notes.

entries.title: CameraX
entries.summary: Android CameraX libraries have been updated to version 1.7.0-rc02, which includes important bug fixes for an UnsupportedOperationException on API 30 when using SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW and a native thread leak when unbinding VideoCapture. Developers should update their dependency versions to 1.7.0-rc02 to benefit from these fixes and stability improvements.

entries.title: Compose Animation
entries.summary: The documentation has been updated to reflect the release of Jetpack Compose Animation version 1.13.0-rc01, moving the release candidate into the RC phase and updating the latest update timestamp.

entries.title: Compose Foundation
entries.summary: Jetpack Compose Foundation version 1.13.0-rc01 has been released. This update introduces a notable API behavior change for `Modifier.border`, which now consistently uses the outline size during rendering, accompanied by a temporary feature flag (`ComposeFoundationFlags.isBorderMatchesOutlineBoundsFixEnabled`) to revert the behavior if necessary.

entries.title: Compose Material
entries.summary: Jetpack Compose Material library updated to include the release of version 1.13.0-rc01, transitioning the library closer to a stable release by promoting it to a Release Candidate and removing the previous beta version from the latest updates table.

entries.title: Compose Material 3
entries.summary: Jetpack Compose Material3 version 1.5.0-rc01 has been released, updating the library dependencies and introducing important bug fixes. Key improvements include resolving a hardcoded pressed shape in `ToggleButton`, fixing value updates on tap when `RangeSlider` thumbs overlap, addressing precision loss in discrete `Slider` components, and fixing scroll interference issues when dragging a `RangeSlider` inside horizontally scrollable containers.

entries.title: Compose Remote Foundation
entries.summary: Released version 1.0.0-alpha06 of `androidx.compose.remote.foundation:foundation`, which updates the dependency versions and introduces API changes. Specifically, it renames `remoteBitmap` to `bitmap` on `RemoteBasicImage` and adjusts `style` to be the final parameter on `RemoteBasicText` to align better with Compose Foundation standards.

entries.title: remote compose
entries.summary: Updated Remote Compose dependencies to version 1.0.0-alpha23 and documented release changes, including renaming Action to RemoteAction, decoupling RemoteColor from Compose UI Color, reordering shape outline parameters, deprecating rememberMutableRemote* factories, and fixing a bug in chained drawWithContent modifiers.

entries.title: Compose Runtime
entries.summary: The Compose Runtime documentation has been updated to reflect the release of version 1.13.0-rc01 on November 04, 2026. This release candidate promotes the 1.13.0 version branch and includes an update to the androidx.tracing:tracing-wire dependency to version 2.0.5.

entries.title: Compose UI
entries.summary: The Compose UI documentation has been updated to reflect the release of version 1.13.0-rc01 on November 04, 2026. This promotion from beta indicates that version 1.13 is nearing a stable release, allowing developers to test the release candidate for final stability verification.

entries.title: Compose
entries.summary: Updated Jetpack Compose library versions across multiple artifact groups (animation, foundation, material, material3, runtime, and UI) to the new 1.13.0-rc01 release candidate (and 1.5.0-rc01 for Material3), signaling progress toward upcoming stable releases.

entries.title: Coordinatorlayout
entries.summary: Added release notes for CoordinatorLayout version 1.4.0-alpha01, which updates the minimum SDK requirement to API 23, bumps compileSdk to API 36.1, introduces a new `CoordinatorLayout.Behavior#onRequestChildRectangleOnScreen` overload with request source information, removes obsolete API 21 annotations, and includes minor text formatting updates.

entries.title: Core
entries.summary: Released `androidx.core:core-telecom:1.1.0`, introducing seamless migration controls via `backwardsCompatSdkLevel`, promoting Call Extensions to stable with new remote mic-mute capabilities, adding per-child call log exclusions and network-slicing opt-outs, and significantly hardening cross-SDK audio routing, call-setup performance, and deadlock prevention.

entries.title: Enterprise
entries.summary: Added release notes for Version 1.2.0-alpha01 of the enterprise-feedback library. This update raises the minimum SDK requirement from API 21 to API 23, introduces JSpecify nullness annotations, merges public and experimental API files, and fixes a potential ClassCastException or NullPointerException in KeyedAppStatesService.

entries.title: Exifinterface
entries.summary: Exifinterface version 1.5.0-beta01 has been released, moving the library to beta stage and updating the release table accordingly. This update matters for developers tracking the progress of the Exifinterface library toward a stable 1.5.0 release.

entries.title: Glance Adaptive
entries.summary: Updated the Glance Adaptive library documentation to reflect the release of version 1.0.0-alpha04 across adaptive-appwidget, adaptive-core, and adaptive-wear artifacts. This release introduces the new `GlanceAdaptiveWidgetReceiver` base class for Glance Adaptive widgets and adds an integer resource for declaring widget categories, along with dependency updates and minor feedback link fixes.

entries.title: Glance Wear
entries.summary: Glance Wear version 1.0.0-alpha22 has been released, introducing several meaningful API updates and behavioral improvements. Key additions include a new `WearWidgetContentTooLargeException` to handle oversized widget content with actionable guidance, new configuration helpers such as `WearWidgetConfigExtras` and `GlanceWearProfiles.createWearWidgetsProfile`, and expanded touch modifier support (`onTouchDown`, `onTouchUp`, `onTouchCancel`) across all compatible Wear OS devices for better press feedback.

entries.title: Heifwriter
entries.summary: Androidx.heifwriter has been updated to version 1.2.0-rc02, advancing the release candidate and updating the dependency implementation instructions for developers integrating the library.

entries.title: ink
entries.summary: Android Jetpack Ink libraries have been updated to version 1.1.0-alpha11. This release introduces experimental APIs for animated paint textures and phase offsets for animated stroke textures, adds Stroke shape (PartitionedMesh) serialization for improved performance and saving partially erased strokes, and includes bug fixes for concurrent inputs and barrel twist compatibility.

entries.title: input
entries.summary: Androidx.input:input-motionprediction version 1.0.1 has been released, introducing support for stylus AXIS_RZ in the motion event predictor. Developers should update their dependency declarations to version 1.0.1 to incorporate this bug fix and reduce input latency.

entries.title: navigation3
entries.summary: The Navigation 3 library has been updated with the release of version 1.3.0-alpha04 and stable version 1.2.1. Version 1.3.0-alpha04 fixes an issue where shared NavEntries failed to render if popped and pushed again before completion, while version 1.2.1 downgrades the compileSdk requirement from 37 to 36 to align with Compose 1.10 dependencies.

entries.title: Test Backup
entries.summary: AndroidX Test Backup version 1.0.0-alpha04 has been released, introducing new features such as Preferences DataStore testing support, cross-device restore options, automatic test failure device log collection, and several API refinements and removals.

entries.title: Test Uiautomator
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack UIAutomator documentation to reflect the release of version 2.4.1. This release updates the dependency versions and includes important bug fixes for ShellServer to prevent random port selection collisions and startup failures.

entries.title: Wear Remote Compose Material 3
entries.summary: Released Wear Compose Remote Material 3 version 1.0.0-alpha15, introducing significant API alignments with Wear Compose Material 3 (such as parameter updates across buttons, cards, and indicators, adopting RemoteAction for callbacks, and adding a required defaultFontFamily to RemoteTypography) alongside numerous bug fixes for clipping, animations, and default color pairings.

entries.title: Wear Compose
entries.summary: Android released Wear Compose version 1.8.0-alpha03, introducing several API updates including material3-ripple integration, inset focus rings support, `LocalTimeSource` for testing `TimeText`, and `Modifier.suppressStatusBar()` while removing the unreleased `StatusBarSuppression()` composable. Key bug fixes include reduced GPU memory usage for idle `Dialogs`, state preservation fixes for `TransformingLazyColumn`, and gesture improvements for `OneHandedGestureDefaults.scrollDownToNextItem`.

entries.title: Wear
entries.summary: The `androidx.wear:wear-remote-interactions` library has been updated to version 1.3.0-rc01, transitioning from beta01 without any functional code changes. This brings the library closer to a stable 1.3.0 release.

entries.title: Web
entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces the initial 1.0.0-alpha01 release of the AndroidX Web library (`androidx.web:web` and `androidx.web:web-compose`), bringing new APIs like `WebContent` and `WebContentView` to manage persistent web engine session states across UI views and activities.

entries.title: Webkit
entries.summary: AndroidX Webkit version 1.19.0-alpha01 has been released, introducing significant API updates including an Executor overload for WebView startup, new immutable state classes (`NavigationState` and `PageState`) for `NavigationListener`, support for wildcard URLs in `Profile#addQuicHints`, and the deprecation of Attribution Reporting APIs.

entries.title: AndroidX releases
entries.summary: This update to the AndroidX versions documentation reflects a series of library progressions across Jetpack components for November 4, 2026. Notably, several core Jetpack Compose libraries (Animation, Foundation, Material, Material3, Runtime, and UI) advanced from beta to release candidate (1.13.0-rc01), signaling approaching stable releases. Additionally, Camera and its related viewfinder/feature combination modules moved to 1.7.0-rc02, Biometric progressed to 1.4.0-beta01, AppFunctions advanced to 1.0.0-rc01, and CoordinatorLayout introduced a new 1.4.0-alpha01 release. These updates matter as they indicate the stabilization phase for major UI and framework components, helping developers prepare for upcoming stable versions.

entries.title: Recent Release Notes

This update includes release candidates and alpha versions for key libraries such as Appfunctions (1.0.0-rc01), Compose (1.13.0-rc01), Material 3 (1.5.0-rc01), Biometric (1.4.0-beta01), and various camera, navigation, and wear components, helping developers track the latest stable and pre-release androidx dependencies.

entries.title: Alpha Releases
entries.summary: Added a new release entry for November 04, 2026, documenting alpha version updates for various AndroidX libraries, including updates to Compose Remote, Coordinatorlayout, Navigation3, Wear Compose, and Webkit.

entries.title: Beta Releases

entries.title: RC Releases
entries.summary: Added release candidate entries for November 04, 2026, including updates to Appfunctions 1.0.0-rc01, various Camera and Compose libraries, Heifwriter, and Wear Remote Interactions. This update tracks the latest stable candidates leading up to upcoming AndroidX library releases.

entries.title: Stable Releases
entries.summary: Added release entries for November 04, 2026, documenting updates to Core-telecom (1.1.0), Input-motionprediction (1.0.1), Navigation3 (1.2.1), and Test Uiautomator (2.4.1). This helps developers track the latest stable library versions available for production use.

entries.title: Kotlin Multiplatform
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack Multiplatform library release versions and dates in the documentation. Specifically, Compose Runtime advanced to release candidate 1.13.0-rc01, and Navigation3 updated to versions 1.2.1 and 1.3.0-alpha04, keeping developers informed on the latest KMP-ready library milestones.

entries.title: Android latest updates
entries.summary: Jetpack library versions have been updated to reflect recent pre-release milestones. Compose core and animation libraries advanced to version 1.13.0-rc01 (and Material3 to 1.5.0-rc01), CameraX artifacts advanced to version 1.7.0-rc02, and Wear remote interactions progressed to version 1.3.0-rc01.

entries.title: Control the camera
entries.summary: Added migration resources to the deprecated Camera1 documentation, directing developers to the official Camera1-to-CameraX migration guide and the corresponding GitHub agentic skill to facilitate updating legacy camera implementations.

entries.title: Take photos

entries.title: SDK Platform Tools release notes

Additionally, it introduces the new `libadbusb` USB backend for Linux and macOS to improve device connection reliability, and fixes several critical server crashes on macOS.

entries.title: Google Maps for Android Automotive Intents

entries.title: Navigation 3

entries.title: Preview your UI in Compose for Wear OS

entries.title: Coordinate your UI with the system status bar

entries.title: Get started with widgets

These updates bump the Compose remote libraries and tooling previews to alpha23, Glance wear libraries to alpha22, and Remote Material3 to alpha15, ensuring developers use the latest APIs and bug fixes.

entries.title: Features and APIs
entries.summary: The Android 17 features documentation for `ProfilingManager` was updated to reflect API refinements. Specifically, the response type for `TRIGGER_TYPE_KILL_EXCESSIVE_CPU_USAGE` was updated from a call stack sample to a background system trace snapshot, documentation links for profile retrieval were split into dedicated upload and analysis guides, and the code example for registering anomaly triggers was improved with null safety, proper list initialization, and correct error-checking logic.

entries.title: Android Developers
entries.summary: Updated the App Functions implementation references to replace the deprecated `@AppFunction` annotation with `@AppFunctionDeclaration` across code examples. This ensures developers use the correct current API annotation when declaring app functions that are described by KDoc.

entries.title: Migrating to the AppFunctionServiceEntryPoint API
entries.summary: Updated the annotation from `@AppFunction` to `@AppFunctionDeclaration` in the AppFunctions service entry point migration documentation. This change reflects API updates for declaring app functions correctly.

entries.title: Android Developers

This matters because it cleans up deprecated or redundant gesture-specific AlertDialog usage examples from the reference guide.

entries.title: Overview of AppFunctions
entries.summary: The documentation was updated to reflect an API change, renaming the `@AppFunction` annotation to `@AppFunctionDeclaration` across all code examples. This is important for developers to use the correct, up-to-date annotations when defining app functions for AI integration.

entries.title: Add the AppFunctions API to your app
entries.summary: Updated the App Functions documentation to reflect an API renaming, changing the `@AppFunction` annotation to `@AppFunctionDeclaration` in code examples. This matters for developers as it ensures their implementation matches the correct, updated SDK naming conventions.

entries.title: Connect your app to the Android intelligence system
entries.summary: Removed the Agent-to-UI (A2UI) documentation section from the intelligence system overview, streamlining the content to focus solely on the Computer Control API. This change matters as it temporarily removes reference to the Jetpack Compose A2UI renderer feature from this specific documentation page.

entries.title: Compare Compose and View metrics
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack Compose migration metrics documentation to remove outdated references to version 1.0, replaced internal Skia dashboard links with the public Hero benchmarks guide for tracking performance against Views, and added the Hero benchmarks link to the recommended reading section.

entries.title: Migration strategy
entries.summary: Added references to the new 'Hero benchmarks' documentation across the additional resources and recommended sections. This matters because it provides developers with direct access to real-world performance comparisons regarding startup and scrolling between Jetpack Compose and traditional Views to help guide their migration strategy.

entries.title: Jetpack Compose Performance
entries.summary: Updated the Jetpack Compose performance documentation to specify that Compose 1.9.0 and later achieves 0% jank on Pixel 6, matching the performance of the traditional Views system for scrolling.

entries.title: Follow best practices
entries.summary: The Jetpack Compose performance best practices documentation was updated to include a link to new empirical Hero benchmark data demonstrating scrolling and startup performance when using R8 and Baseline Profiles. Additionally, a reference link for `computedStateOf` was corrected to point to the appropriate performance documentation.

entries.title: Hero benchmarks
entries.summary: Updated the hero benchmark documentation to reflect the hardware migration from the Pixel 3a to the Pixel 6 (running Android 17 / API 37) starting with Compose 1.12. It adds a new summary table comparing Compose 1.12, Compose 1.11.4, and the Views baseline, updates startup metrics to show Compose 1.12 performing on par with Views for initial display (TTID) and about 2% slower for full display (TTFD), refines scroll jank descriptions for the Pixel 6, and expands instructions for running benchmarks locally.

entries.title: Use the Jetpack Picture-in-Picture Library
entries.summary: Updated the initialization of `BasicPictureInPicture` and `VideoPlaybackPictureInPicture` in the Jetpack Picture-in-Picture documentation to include a single-thread executor parameter (`Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()`). This change ensures proper threading configuration for PiP implementations, making the code examples more accurate and robust for developers.

entries.title: Game Stats
entries.summary: Removed the temporary testing disclaimer and the milestones table regarding the September 2026 rollout of Game Stats on the You tab, while also updating the corresponding image caption to generally refer to the gamer profile.

entries.title: Integrate Game Stats
entries.summary: The testing and verification instructions for Game Stats have been significantly streamlined. Detailed steps involving internal test tracks, specific UI navigation methods (like the 'Track your playtime' section), and troubleshooting notes were removed in favor of a concise, simplified process focused on signing into the Play Store and viewing stats directly via the gamer profile.

entries.title: Integrate continue watching using REST API
entries.summary: Updated the Engage REST API documentation to correct the API endpoint name from `clearClusters` to `clearCluster` and added documentation for the account-level URL endpoint that does not require a profile ID.

entries.title: Support 16 KB page sizes
entries.summary: This update significantly expands the documentation on verifying 16 KB ELF segment alignment and RELRO security flags for shared libraries. It adds guidance on using the Android Studio APK Analyzer as a recommended verification method, provides updated multi-platform command-line instructions (including Windows PowerShell support), and clarifies the compliance conditions and potential segmentation fault risks associated with `GNU_RELRO` and writable `LOAD` segments.

entries.title: Local network permission
entries.summary: The documentation has been updated to reflect the transition of the local network permission from an opt-in feature in Android 16 to full enforcement starting in Android 17 (API level 37) using the new `ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK` runtime permission. The Android 16 opt-in configuration is now deprecated, and developers are directed to follow the Android 17 enforcement guidelines.

entries.title: Benchmark your app
entries.summary: Added references to the new Jetpack Compose Hero benchmarks documentation under both 'Additional resources' and 'Recommended for you' sections. This matters because it directs developers to a real-world Macrobenchmark case study comparing Compose and Views performance using the Pokedex app.

entries.title: Write a Macrobenchmark
entries.summary: Added references and links to the new Hero benchmarks case study in the Samples and Recommended for you sections. This matters because it provides developers with real-world examples of using Macrobenchmark to measure startup and scroll performance across Jetpack Compose and Views.

entries.title: Analyze profiles with AI
entries.summary: Added documentation explaining how to use AI coding agents with the Perfetto AI skill to automate root-cause analysis for `ProfilingManager` performance profiles, system traces, and Java heap dumps.

entries.title: Analyze traces in bulk
entries.summary: The bulk-trace-analysis.md documentation has been updated to improve clarity, streamline explanations of PerfettoSQL query design, and polish the interpretation of violin plot results for high and low-latency traces.

entries.title: Debug commands for local profiling
entries.summary: Updated the `ProfilingManager` debug-mode documentation to include comprehensive local testing instructions. The updates detail how to handle Android version-specific behaviors (Android 15 vs Android 16) for pulling unredacted/redacted profiles, force-enabling background traces for trigger testing, using the `cmd profiling_service` tool for verbose logging, triggering on-demand collections, simulating triggers, and inspecting overall service state via `dumpsys`.

entries.title: Case study: Debug an ANR
entries.summary: Updated the ANR debugging documentation to include Kotlin code snippets alongside Java, detailed instructions on how to automate ANR investigations using an AI agent with Perfetto AI skills, and refined explanations of trace analysis steps to help developers identify thread blocking issues.

entries.title: Case study: Debug an OOM crash
entries.summary: This new documentation page provides a comprehensive guide on how to use `ProfilingManager` to capture, deobfuscate, and analyze Java heap dumps following an `OutOfMemoryError` crash in Android apps.

entries.title: Overview
entries.summary: Updated the ProfilingManager documentation to reflect new capabilities across Android 15 and Android 16, including support for app-driven and trigger-based profile collections, Java heap dumps, heap profiles, and stack sampling. The guide now includes comprehensive sections on profile retrieval, analysis via Perfetto and AI agents, debugging case studies, and instructions for integrating ProfilingManager using AI coding agents.

entries.title: Query profiles with PerfettoSQL
entries.summary: Streamlined the documentation for querying `ProfilingManager` profiles using PerfettoSQL. The updates condense introductory explanations, improve query syntax (such as updating function creation to use `CREATE OR REPLACE PERFETTO FUNCTION`), refine descriptions for sample queries covering slice duplication, jank, memory aggregation, and cold startup latency, and align jank queries to match generalized `GLOB` patterns.

entries.title: Visualize profiles in the Perfetto UI
entries.summary: Expanded the documentation for 'ProfilingManager' to cover visualization of Java heap dumps alongside system traces in the Perfetto UI. The updates explain how to use the Heapdump Explorer, detail the differences between 'ProfilingManager' heap dumps and standard HPROF dumps (including what metadata is collected versus what sensitive data is omitted for privacy), and add guidance on advanced next steps like PerfettoSQL querying and AI analysis.

entries.title: Trigger-based profiling
entries.summary: Updated the `ProfilingManager` trigger-based capture documentation for Android 16 (API level 36) and higher. The revision introduces a comprehensive categorization of trigger types (background trace-based, new capture-based, and variable anomaly triggers), details the persistence lifecycle of registered triggers across app restarts and reboots, adds guidelines on unregistering triggers, and updates code snippets and explanations for setting up and handling trigger callbacks.

entries.title: Retrieve and upload profiles
entries.summary: Updated the ProfilingManager upload worker documentation with comprehensive details on file locations, naming conventions, automatic cleanup behavior, and best practices for compressing profile files before uploading them via WorkManager.

entries.title: Rate limiting and collection behavior
entries.summary: Updated documentation for `ProfilingManager` to include detailed data retention policies for undelivered profiles (up to 7 days for queued results and 5 days for local storage cleanup), clarified how process and system rate limits operate over rolling time windows, and added best practices for managing profile volume in production using population segmentation and remote configuration.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/actionable-strategies-for-reducing-your-apps-bitmap-memory-footprint.txt" target="_blank">Actionable strategies for reducing your app's Bitmap memory footprint - Speakers: Fung Lam (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KD_55WdEYj0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/actionable-strategies-for-reducing-your-apps-bitmap-memory-footprint ## About the talk Managing Bitmap memory is critical for mitigating Out-Of-Memory (OOM) risks in visually rich Android apps. While developers know to reduce image sizes, achieving long-term app stability comes from mastering two other key pillars: Reuse and Recycle. This session delivers a practical playbook for optimizing memory performance using modern tools, open-source libraries like Glide and Coil, and system-level APIs. In this session, you will learn how to diagnose real-world memory regressions using Android Vitals, implement advanced caching (Reuse) patterns with Glide and Coil, and proactively release memory (Recycle) using the onTrimMemory callback. ## Summary - Google Play is introducing memory performance thresholds enforced in February 2027. Exceeding the 90th percentile limit directly impacts your app's health assessment and can reduce visibility on the Play Store. - Bitmaps expand by dimensions and color depth when decoded, making them the largest memory consumers in most apps. Just a few full-resolution images can take hundreds of megabytes. - Downsample images and decode only visible regions to reduce memory consumption. Request matching image dimensions via CDN or use APIs like \`BitmapRegionDecoder\` rather than loading oversized full-resolution images. - Multiple image loaders multiply default memory heap cache usage and duplicate stored Bitmaps. Standardize on one loader or set explicit memory budgets across existing loaders. - Release image memory when your app moves to the background by handling \`onTrimMemory\`. Stop background polling and animations in \`onStop\` to prevent background memory growth. ## Resources - \[Android memory documentation\](https://developer.android.com/memory) ## Topics entries.summary: This document introduces strategies for reducing an Android app's bitmap memory footprint to prevent out-of-memory errors and meet Google Play's upcoming memory performance thresholds. It outlines best practices for downsampling images, consolidating image loaders, and proactively releasing memory.

entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring the Android Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript on agentic coding with industry leaders. This addition provides developers with direct access to expert discussions and insights on AI-driven development workflows.

We aim to highlight practical applications, discuss measurable productivity improvements and candidly address the challenges engineering teams face when integrating AI at scale. Moderated by Ben Trengrove, Google Developer Relations Engineer ## Summary - AI tools accelerate code writing and PR creation, but teams face friction in downstream stages like code review and business approvals. - Code reviews are shifting from manual line-by-line checks toward agent-assisted verification and intent reviews. - CI infrastructure faces severe compute scaling challenges from rising code volumes, prompting investments in remote build execution and caching with Bazel. - Enterprises manage AI token costs with usage limits and automated model routing. ## Topics entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-workflows-with-small-models.txt" target="_blank">Agentic coding workflows with small models - Speakers: Ian Ballantyne (Technical Member of Staff, Google DeepMind), Jose Alcérreca (Developer Relations Engineer), Zoe Lopez-Latorre (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sBWgIjWU6PI - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/agentic-coding-workflows-with-small-models ## About the talk While large frontier models dominate the headlines, small language models (SLMs) like Gemma 4 offer low-latency, cost-effective, and fully offline intelligence to augment daily developer workflows. This talk explores practical patterns for integrating small models into Android development, from smart task routing to cost optimization, using Gemma 4 as our primary hands-on case study to demonstrate real-world use cases and how to configure developer tools and agentic workflows. ## Summary - Small language models offer zero marginal cost and offline access on local hardware. Frontier models cost 20 to 200 times more for the same workloads. - Quantization-aware training cuts memory footprints by 75% with less loss than post-training compression. Speculative decoding then speeds up predictable coding tasks up to 3x. - Evaluating small models requires testing the full stack rather than relying on Python leaderboards. Android Bench provides 100 PR-sized tasks reflecting actual Android development. - Android Bench tests show Gemma 4 solves over half of tasks with its full context window enabled. Long-horizon tasks remain out of reach. - Multi-model orchestration combines frontier and small models through techniques like task cascading and automatic routing. This preserves reliability while reducing token costs. ## Resources - \[Are we there yet? (AWTY) framework\](https://goo.gle/awty) - \[Android Bench\](https://developer.android.com/bench) ## Topics small-language-models, agentic-workflows, benchmarking, gemma, android-studio, evaluations entries.summary: This new documentation page explores the integration of small language models, such as Gemma 4, into Android development workflows for low-latency, cost-effective, and offline intelligence. It outlines practical implementation patterns, memory optimization strategies like quantization-aware training, and multi-model orchestration techniques.

This practical, example-driven session shows you how to level up your agentic engineering using Claude Code and the Android CLI. We will walk through a complete workflow to automate complex development tasks and ship features faster. You will learn to: - Optimize the token efficiency of your harness using Android CLI, Skills, Hooks and MCP. - Offload and parallelize long-running tasks to subagents. - Set up continuous verification loops that stop early termination and run until tests pass. ## Summary - Android CLI gives coding agents shell access to Android tools such as emulators and Firebase Crashlytics. It sits in your shell space and works across agents. - Keep agent conversations to around 150,000 tokens to prevent context rot. Slice work into scoped issues and run Gradle in quiet mode to avoid long logs. - Keep \`AGENTS.md\` under 250 lines and reserve it for permanent rules such as architecture constraints. Letting an agent edit this file degrades performance and raises costs. - Deterministic hooks and context-specific skills manage agent actions better than sprawling files. Install only vetted skills or start with the base Android CLI skill. - Verification loops stop developers from acting as manual QA testers. Tier checks to run fast unit tests first and slow emulator runs last. ## Resources - \[Android CLI installation\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Agent modification study\](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.11988) - \[Android Bench\](https://developer.android.com/bench) ## Topics claude-code, android-cli, agentic-engineering, benchmarking, performance ## Transcript ### This session breaks down the compliance pathways for all developers, from large studios to hobbyists. We will outline the key requirements for publishing on Google Play and third-party app stores. The talk will feature a live demo of the new Limited Distribution accounts, showing how students and hobbyists can easily and safely share apps. By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand the 3 main developer verification paths. See the new Limited Distribution account flow live. Identify your specific next steps for compliance. ## Summary - Android developer verification links distributed apps to accountable legal entities to curb financial fraud and burner malware networks. Regional enforcement began across four markets before global enforcement expands next year. - Developers can register through Google Play Console or a dedicated Android Developer Console. Students and hobbyists can register packages for free to share across up to 50 associated devices. - The Android Developer Console API enables third-party stores and developers to programmatically automate app registrations and resolve package conflicts. The Android Developer Status API checks whether package names are registered. - Experienced users can sideload unregistered apps by enabling Advanced Flow in developer options. This path enforces a device reboot and a 24-hour countdown to disrupt social engineering scams. ## Resources - \[Developer Console Documentation\](https://developer.android.com/console) ## Topics sharing apps on Android with their friends, family, classmates, and colleagues. \[09:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=577s) Using this flow is 100% free. \[09:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=579s) There's no annual fee, no D-U-N-S number, and no business registration paperwork. \[09:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=583s) All you need is a Google account. \[09:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=585s) Registering a package for use in limited distribution is simple. \[09:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=588s) All you need to do is go to the Android Developer Console and register a valid package name, such as Camera Magic, and give it a friendly name. \[09:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=596s) Once you've entered your package name, you finish registering by adding a public SHA-256 key generated during build step, and doing this will bind that package and build name to your account, registering it as yours. \[10:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=609s) Once you've registered your package successfully, you can share it with someone else by adding their device as an associate of your developer account. \[10:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=616s) You do this by creating a new associated device in the developer console, assigning it a friendly name, and then generating a QR code and link that you can share with the owner of this new device. \[10:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=625s) When they open the link, they will be prompted to answer whether or not you are a developer that they know and trust and whether or not they want to allow their apps to be installed on your device. \[10:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=634s) Once a user has consented, they will receive their own generated code to send back to you and once you enter that code, their device will be allowed to install apps associated with your developer account. ### Advanced flow for power users \[10:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=645s) In addition to limited distribution as an alternative for developers, we also have the Advanced Flow as an option for power users who want to continue installing unregistered packages at their own discretion. \[10:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=658s) We built the Advanced Flow to allow experienced users to install unregistered apps when they choose to accept the risk, while keeping critical guardrails in place against social engineering scams for everyday users. \[11:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=669s) In real world financial fraud and call forwarding scams, criminals rely on urgency, fear, and high pressure phone coercion to force victims into side loading malicious payloads. \[11:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=680s) By requiring a device reboot and an unskippable 24-hour countdown, Advanced Flow disrupts this pressure, giving potential victims the time and space to make an informed decision about what they're being asked to do. \[11:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=692s) To enable this option, you'll begin by putting your device into developer mode by going to Settings, About phone, and tapping the build number 7 times. \[11:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=699s) If you're watching this and you weren't already a developer, congratulations on your new role. \[11:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=704s) Thank you for laughing. \[11:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=706s) Now that the device is in developer mode, we can access the Advanced Flow option by going to System, Developer options, and toggling allow apps from unverified developers. \[11:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=716s) Once you've toggled this option, you may need to enter your PIN and then you'll have to acknowledge the warning indicating that if somebody is telling you to do this, it's likely a scam. \[12:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=726s) Next, you restart the device to initiate the 24-hour security delay. \[12:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=730s) This step is critical in helping victims of scams get an opportunity to de-escalate from urgency tactics employed by scammers, and then get help in shutting down this attempt to exploit them. \[12:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=742s) During the 24-hour window, Settings displays an active countdown timer of the time remaining before you can use the Advanced Flow. \[12:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=749s) Once the 24 hours is up, the user can select whether to disable verification temporarily for 7 days or to keep it off permanently. \[12:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=759s) One last time, the user has to acknowledge the risk inherent with removing this default safety precaution before tapping Done to complete the device configuration for Advanced Flow. \[12:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=770s) From that point forward, users are able to install unregistered apps. \[12:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=773s) This gives power users the unrestricted control over apps that they want to install that they expect, while keeping everyday users safe. ### Rollout roadmap and key milestones \[13:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=783s) Now let's review our rollout timeline for developer verification. \[13:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=786s) Phase 1 began in March 2026 with the introduction of the Android Developer Console. \[13:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=791s) And then Phase 2 started 5 months later when developer tooling became more generally available. \[13:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=796s) Phase 3 was our most recent critical milestone, September 30th, 2026. \[13:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=800s) On this date, regional enforcement began across the 4 regional rollout markets we mentioned before: Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. \[13:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=807s) In these markets now, 7 major partner stores enforce verified developer requirements. \[13:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=812s) Phase 4 will look to expand this user protection requirement thoughtfully and incrementally next year in 2027. \[13:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=819s) And lastly, it's important to note that if you're based in China, but you distribute to these enforced regions, you must also register the apps that are going to be distributed as well. \[13:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=827s) I'll pass this back to Naheed to close us out and give a recap on what you need to do. ### Action checklist and resources \[13:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=831s) All right. \[13:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=834s) All right. \[13:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=835s) So, thanks, Rob. \[13:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=836s) So, to recap the most critical steps, so for developers who distribute on Play, audit your apps on the Play Console today and make sure that your apps are registered and claimed, the specifically the ones that you distribute outside of Play. \[14:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=851s) Secondly, for apps you exclusively distribute outside of Play, create your Android Developer Console account, this link. \[14:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=859s) And then for students and hobbyists, you can create your free account and distribute up to 50 devices. \[14:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=866s) Thank you all so much for joining us today. \[14:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=868s) We are thrilled to partner with you and making Android a safer and a secure ecosystem for billions of users worldwide. \[14:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=877s) There's a QR code on the next slide where you can access the developer documentation. \[14:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=881s) We can't wait to see you what you build next. \[14:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=884s) Have a wonderful Android Dev Summit. \[14:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UL31gug0oS4\&t=886s) Thank you.</a>

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/app-security-in-the-agentic-era.txt" target="_blank">App security in the agentic era - Speakers: Kristen O'Leary (Senior Developer Relations Engineer), Sabs (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/app-security-in-the-agentic-era ## About the talk This presentation explores the strategic shift from viewing AI as a generic coding assistant to leveraging it as a context-aware, automated security peer reviewer integrated directly into the Android development lifecycle. We discuss how specialized AI agents, connected to the Android toolchain via skills, can help improve app security. By bridging the gap between raw LLM capabilities and deep project context, this approach empowers development teams to maintain high-velocity feature delivery without compromising rigorous security and policy standards. ## Summary - Generic AI agents miss key context during audits, but Android security skills provide researcher-backed guidance. They check intent security and enforce permissions using project-specific build configurations. - The Play policy skill runs static analysis to catch compliance issues before submission. It can cross-reference code analysis against existing Play Store declarations. - The Play Integrity API evaluates app and device integrity at runtime. The Protected with Play dashboard unites integrity and distribution monitoring in one place. - Targeted APIs allow apps to protect user privacy without requesting broad permissions. Examples include the SMS Retriever API and the alpha Location Button library. ## Skills - \[Android CLI and Android skills\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Resources - \[Google Bug Hunters key stats\](https://bughunters.google.com/about/key-stats) - \[Play Integrity API\](https://goo.gle/play-integrity-api) - \[Advanced Protection Mode\](https://goo.gle/aapm) - \[Location Button\](https://goo.gle/location-button) - \[SMS Retriever API\](https://goo.gle/sms-retriever-api) ## Topics app-security, ai-agents, play-integrity-api, permissions, location-button, advanced-protection-mode ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=5s) Hi, I'm Kristen. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=7s) Hi, and I am Sabs. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=8s) And we're here to talk to you about today about security in the agentic era. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=14s) In the past year, we gave up over $2 million in rewards for the Android Bug Hunters program, and over 200k for mobile. \[00:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=23s) In today's agentic era, app security is constantly evolving. \[00:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=28s) So, let's talk about the tools to help us solve these problems quickly and effectively. \[00:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=34s) To improve how agents perform for Android security, the answer isn't a better prompt. \[00:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=38s) It's tools and workflows to help agents understand our toolchains and API to help keep your app safe. \[00:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=47s) So, it's 4:30 p.m. \[00:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=49s) On a Thursday. \[00:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=59s) So, whether you're on a small team, wearing every hat, or on a large one, where security checks hit as you are cutting the release, the reality is the same. \[01:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=68s) We are product engineers, shipping high-quality features fast, and we're not necessarily security researchers. \[01:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=76s) So, what's the natural instinct? \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=78s) So, we hand that warning to an agentic tool, and ask the agent for a fix. ### Context limitations of AI agent security audits \[01:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=85s) But agentic tool, working without your project context, has three blind spots. \[01:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=91s) It may not know your app is built from dynamic feature modules or multi-APK bundles. \[01:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=97s) It sees a file, not a shipped artifact. \[01:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=100s) It may not know, be able to trace the data flow from your Kotlin UI down to your KMP shared logic into the native C++ JNI calls. \[01:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=110s) It sees only one layer. \[01:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=113s) Last, but not least, it may not have awareness of your minimum SDK or your Gradle build flavors. \[02:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=122s) So, we pointed an agent the app, and asked for a security audit. \[02:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=128s) Six findings came back. \[02:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=130s) And here's the thing. \[02:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=132s) Every single one of them they're is not wrong. \[02:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=135s) They're defensible, but only one of them is the bug we actually started with. \[02:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=141s) The rest is a mix of good practice, things to investigate further, speculation, and things that may not even apply. \[03:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=188s) That's a genuine security task, and on a multi-module app, it's a large one. \[03:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=206s) It may read modules that export nothing at all. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=209s) It may re-derive from first principle what makes an intent redirect exploitable. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=214s) It may follow paths that were never reachable. \[03:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=217s) You're paying for exploration, not analysis. \[03:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=220s) A skill is what supplies the missing strategy. \[03:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=224s) Android security skills, for example, provide your agent with instructions that follow current guidance, the same sequence of steps a security researcher would actually follow, and the agent stops guessing. \[03:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=235s) It doesn't rediscover the rules because the rules were provided by the skill. ### Android security skills for agents \[04:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=241s) Currently, we have launched two security skills: Intent Security and Permissions. \[04:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=246s) Intent security is about what other apps can make your app do. \[04:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=251s) Your app holds permissions, a sign-in session that they don't. \[04:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=255s) So, every exported component and every pending intent you hand out is a potential way for someone to act through you. \[04:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=263s) The skill helps safeguard against this. \[04:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=266s) The permissions skill helps close the gap between a permission that is declared and one that is actually enforced. \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=274s) It can help you write the appropriate permissions check. \[04:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=278s) It helps identify if a provider with a wild card path grants the whole database instead of one directory. \[04:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=285s) It catches over-asking permissions too. \[04:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=288s) For example, requesting a broad access where the photo picker would do. \[04:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=293s) Use it with the Android CLI, and then ask, "Audit for intent security." \[04:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=297s) No config. \[04:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=298s) No rule tuning. \[05:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=300s) So, the output isn't a wall of warnings. here's the fix. \[05:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=307s) And here's the pro tip. \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=309s) Use the Android CLI makes it easy to find and install. \`\`\`shell android skills list android skills add android-intent-security android skills add android-permissions-security \`\`\` \[05:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=314s) And because the skill know exactly what to look for in your project, it sees your app the way it actually ships. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=350s) That's the warning we opened with, but now with a suggested fix and added reasoning. ### Google Play policy insights skill \[05:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=356s) So, the previous skills catch security bugs. \[05:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=358s) Now let's talk about another \[06:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=379s) If you're publishing an existing Play Store app, it can also cross-reference that static code analysis with Play Store declarations. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=386s) Running this skill can help you catch potential Play policy issues before, not after, app submission, and helps speed up your submission process. \[06:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=393s) The workflow is similar to the other skills we've been discussing: import it, and then ask, "Audit this app for Google Play policy compliance before I submit it." \[06:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=401s) You'll see a screenshot of an example report on the right, and the Android CLI commands to install it below. \`\`\`shell android skills list android skills add play-policy-insights \`\`\` ### Runtime defense with the Play Integrity API \[06:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=411s) So, everything we've talked about so far happens before you ship: auditing intents, checking permissions, validating compliance. \[06:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=417s) That's build time security, and it's essential. \[07:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=420s) But there's a whole class of threats that only exists once your APK is out in the world, running on devices you may not control. \[07:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=426s) The Play Integrity API answers three questions at run time that your own code cannot answer about itself: Is this a genuine, unmodified build of your app? \[07:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=435s) Is this running on an Android device that's genuine? return verdicts on app integrity, device integrity, and more. \[07:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=447s) And in addition to making it faster and easier to publish your app safer, we're also making it easier to secure your app's revenue and reputation. \[07:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=454s) So, defend your business against fraud and abuse. monetization defenses all in one place. \[07:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=466s) We're also reducing warm up latency for the Play Integrity API so you can use these checks during apps safe, but how about your users? ### SMS OTP protection APIs \[08:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=486s) Let's first take a look at SMS OTP Protection. \[08:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=532s) The system shows a single, one-time prompt. \[08:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=535s) The user taps allow or deny, and if they allow, you get that single message. \[08:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=539s) Still no need for a broad SMS permission. ### One-time access with the location button \[09:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=544s) Some apps may need precise location only one time to complete tasks. \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=549s) The existing only one-time permission has high user friction, so sometimes developers will ask for broader precise permission instead. \[09:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=557s) So, the Location Button is a tool that provides a low friction way to grant the app one-time precise location access. \[09:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eof3mvB-yY\&t=563s) It's an Android UI
