entries.title: Architecting Spatial Content on Android XR with Unity
entries.summary: This new documentation page provides the video and interactive transcript for the Android Dev Summit talk on architecting spatial content on Android XR using Unity, enabling developers to build immersive XR experiences.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/architecting-spatial-content-on-android-xr-with-unity.txt" target="_blank">Architecting Spatial Content on Android XR with Unity - Speakers: Levana Chen (Software Engineer), Jennifer Stanton (Senior Software Engineer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/architecting-spatial-content-on-android-xr-with-unity ## About the talk Discover how to anchor and persist 3D experiences in the real world using Unity and Android XR. This session covers the Spatial Entities framework, Cloud Anchors, and Geospatial APIs, demonstrating how to build context-aware apps that remember physical placements and sync multi-user spatial data across sessions. We will examine the architecture behind spatial entities, understand how to anchor digital assets to physical objects, surfaces, and geographic locations. You will walk away with practical Unity workflows for mapping spaces, persisting content across sessions, and creating shared, location-aware AR/XR experiences. ## Summary - AR Foundation provides a unified scripting API across XR platforms using OpenXR extensions. It lets you represent and query real-world features such as planes and meshes. - Persistent anchors stabilize digital content across sessions and device restarts. You can persist them with \`TrySaveAnchorAsync\` and reload them using serialized GUIDs. - The Spatial Entities framework replaces trackable extensions to provide cross-platform support and better performance for tracking items like bounding boxes and markers. - Manager components should be disabled until Android XR permissions are granted. This avoids subsystem initialization failures caused by restricted access to sensitive environment data. - The Geospatial API uses Google Cloud ARCore services and VPS to position content at real-world outdoor locations. ## Resources - \[Unity Roadmap\](https://unity.com/roadmap) - \[AR Foundation Samples\](https://github.com/unity-technologies/arfoundation-samples) - \[Android XR with Unity Documentation\](https://d.android.com/develop/xr/unity) ## Topics android-xr, unity, ar-foundation, openxr, spatial-entities, anchors, geospatial-api ## Transcript ### Introduction and AR Foundation overview \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=6s) All right. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=6s) Welcome, everyone. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=8s) This is Architecting Spatial Content on Android XR with Unity. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=13s) My name is Jennifer Stanton. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=14s) I work at Unity as a senior software engineer. \[00:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=18s) I work on the XR Features team, specifically on AR Foundation and the related packages that bring augmented and mixed reality to Unity. \[00:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=26s) So, I'm Levana Chen from Google's XR Game Engines team. \[00:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=30s) Our teams focused on delivering plugins and the packages that to bring enhanced XR functionality and the seamless game engine integrations. \[00:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=41s) One of the biggest challenges we hear from you is that supporting multiple XR platforms with the same codebase is a lot of work. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=48s) AR Foundation is Unity's high-level extended reality API layer. \[00:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=53s) You can target multiple XR platforms without major code rewrites, having to manage multiple codebases, and it gives you one scripting API for AR features on any platform. \[01:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=66s) This allows you to focus on creating your app, game, or experience, and Unity takes care of the platform details for you. \[01:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=73s) One way that AR Foundation accomplishes this is through OpenXR extensions. \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=78s) These are a set of open, industry standard APIs defined by the Khronos Group. \[01:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=84s) OpenXR has created Spatial Entities as well. \[01:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=87s) It's a framework for digital content to represent and interact with the physical world. \[01:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=92s) Spatial Entities provide a unified model for representing real-world elements as digital objects. \[01:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=99s) I'm excited to share with you some of the latest info on AR Foundation so that you can begin to create your journey begin your journey to create experiences for XR. \[01:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=109s) Next, I'll go over AR Foundation's capabilities so your digital content can interact with the real world. \[01:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=115s) Then I'll go over project setup, including packages and other dependencies, so you can implement this in your projects. \[02:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=122s) And then I will wrap things up by going through some feature unique to Android XR. ### Key AR Foundation features \[02:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=129s) So, some of the ways that AR Foundation represents the real world digitally are planes. \[02:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=135s) And these are flat surfaces in the physical environment, such as floors, walls, ceilings, and even tables and couches. \[02:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=147s) Meshes are 3D structures representing the geometry of the physical world. \[02:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=152s) And then we also have ways of interacting with the real world, ray casts. \[02:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=156s) Those determine where a ray intersects with digital content. \[02:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=160s) Think of it as a laser pointer, and you get information about where that laser pointer is shining. \[02:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=166s) We also have anchors, which help stabilize and relocate a point in space. \[02:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=172s) I will be going deeper into anchors later in this presentation. \[02:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=176s) So, all four of these are considered AR Foundation Features. \[03:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=181s) There are also a handful more features as well that are not mentioned in this slide. \[03:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=188s) Planes and anchors, specifically, are considered trackables since they extend the ARTrackable class, and their managers track updates from the run time. \[03:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=199s) So, let's go into planes. \[03:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=202s) Planes, we have the ARPlane component, which provides real-time identification of flat surfaces. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=209s) They have semantic labels that you can query so you know if your plane is a floor, a table, a wall, and so on. \[03:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=216s) Planes also have dynamic boundaries, so, as the user moves through the real world and can see more of the surfaces, the plane boundaries will dynamically expand, merge, and refine in real time. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=228s) We can also attach a mesh collider to the plane to handle physics. \[03:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=233s) Here you can see an example of plane detection. \[03:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=236s) This is AR Foundation samples ray cast scene running on an Android XR device. \[04:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=242s) It detects real-time, dynamic, 2D polygons. \[04:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=245s) You can build an app that has this functionality by following our project setup guide or by using one of our samples or templates. \[04:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=255s) Next, we have meshes. \[04:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=256s) Meshes are an AR feature that provide 3D meshes of the environment. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=261s) We can attach a mesh collider to these generated meshes, and this allows your digital content to interact with real-world objects. \[04:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=268s) Meshes allow for convincing object occlusion. \[04:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=271s) So, a virtual object can appear to be behind a physical object. \[04:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=276s) If your digital object can move in space, you can use the same geometry to find a path that avoids real-world objects. \[04:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=285s) Next, we have ray casting. \[04:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=287s) Ray casting projects virtual rays into your 3D scene to look for intersections without you having to worry about the complex math. \[04:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=295s) The project A projected ray could potentially intersect with multiple 3D objects in your environment. \[05:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=302s) You can configure the ray cast to only hit certain types of digital content. \[05:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=306s) For example, you could configure it to not hit planes and only intersect with meshes. ### Packages and dependencies setup \[05:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=313s) Now, let's take a look at the relevant packages. \[05:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=316s) These packages all work together to communicate with each other and create a full XR experience. \[05:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=322s) As mentioned, AR Foundation handles features like planes and anchors. \[05:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=327s) The OpenXR plug-in handles native APIs on various XR platforms, so you would want to use this package if your device uses OpenXR. \[05:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=337s) The OpenXR plug-in can optionally be paired with OpenXR Spatial Entities package to access Spatial Entities extensions specifically, and more on that later. \[05:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=348s) If you know that you'll be targeting Android XR devices specifically, like the XR headsets and wired XR glasses, the Unity OpenXR Android XR package is needed for that. \[06:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=360s) And because all of this follows the plug-in pattern, the impact to your code should remain minimal. \[06:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=366s) Not all features are available in all AR Foundation packages. \[06:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=370s) For example, if you look at this chart, meshing is not currently available in the Unity OpenXR Spatial Entities package. \[06:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=380s) XR Plug-in Management allows you to manage which OpenXR features are selected in your project. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=386s) So if you're in the Unity editor, you would go to Edit, Project Settings, and then XR Plug-in Management would be over on the left sidebar. \[06:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=396s) And here you can find OpenXR features and feature groups, so you can select and deselect which features and feature groups that you want to include in your build. \[06:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=407s) For example, in this screenshot, we're looking at all of the ones that come with the Android XR OpenXR package. \[06:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=413s) And then you can mix and match these with spatial entities, for example, if you wanted to. \[06:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=419s) So, here is the Package Manager window. \[07:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=423s) I've highlighted some of the packages that you might see in a typical XR project setup. \[07:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=428s) As you can see, we have AR Foundation, which has been mentioned. \[07:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=432s) We also have the OpenXR plug-in. \[07:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=435s) We have the Android XR package. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=438s) I've also highlighted some others from other platforms because you can certainly make a project that compiles to multiple platforms. \[07:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=449s) And then we also have on the bottom right some other packages as well. \[07:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=454s) Composition Layers, those work with OpenXR devices; Core Utils, very useful for anything XR related; and then XR Hands and XR Interaction Toolkit to get your input, which is pretty essential. \[07:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=468s) So next we have project validation. \[07:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=472s) So, again, this is part of XR Plug-in Management. \[07:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=475s) Project validation can detect duplicate features, as well as other issues in your project that you need to fix to get it running. \[08:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=484s) But in this screenshot, I've highlighted the duplicate features. \[08:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=487s) So, what this is basically saying is two of the same features, such as I think we have anchors, maybe planes and raycasts here. \[08:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=497s) The user has selected to include duplicates of these features from multiple packages, and it's just prompting the user to select one or the other. ### Local anchors and persistence \[08:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=506s) So, that brings us to local anchors and persistence. \[08:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=512s) Anchors ensure that digital content stays at desired locations in the environment regardless of changes to the AR session's tracking state. \[08:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=521s) AR platforms automatically update the poses of anchors over time to ensure that they remain in a consistent position, and anchors the best way to make sure that your content remains in place if you walk away from your anchor and then back towards it. \[08:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=536s) And what about when the user closes their app and restarts it later and comes back to it in a separate session? \[09:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=543s) Persistent anchors enable you to save anchors in an AR session and then load them in subsequent sessions. \[09:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=550s) They survive app life cycles and device restarts. \[09:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=553s) Pictured here is our persistent anchors sample in the AR Foundation Samples project. \[09:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=559s) The sample scene has a menu that has all of the supported functionality on that platform, such as saving and loading anchors. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=567s) And so that brings us to the life cycle of persistent anchors. \[09:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=572s) First you would create an anchor locally, so it's not saved anywhere yet, not saved to persistent storage, just a local anchor. \[09:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=581s) And then you would persist it to storage. \[09:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=584s) After that, you can restart the app, and then you can load it from storage. \[09:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=589s) Some platforms including Android XR also support erasing or un-persisting anchors. \[09:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bz_01jWmNZc\&t=596s) Spatial Entities provider supports automatically loading all saved anchors so that you don't have to manually request each anchor by its entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/balancing-ultra-low-latency-and-cloud-economics-in-virtual-voice-agents.txt" target="_blank">Balancing ultra-low latency and cloud economics in virtual voice agents - Speakers: Devin Reimer (CEO) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/balancing-ultra-low-latency-and-cloud-economics-in-virtual-voice-agents ## About the talk Bringing conversational AI into immersive experiences opens up huge possibilities, yet there's a constant friction between low response latency and sustainable cloud costs. In this session, Devin Reimer (Founder \& CEO of AstroBeam) breaks down how the team behind Stellar Cafe achieved industry-leading voice interaction response times (1.15s--1.4s) while keeping the business model commercially sustainable. Explore the hybrid architecture behind these low latency pipelines, focusing on intelligent orchestration between on-device models and optimized cloud inference to cut expensive API calls without degrading dialogue. You'll walk away with a practical blueprint covering Time-to-First-Token optimization across Speech-to-Text and streaming Text-to-Speech pipelines, parallel safety guardrails that bypass latency overhead, and unit economics per active user session. ## Summary - End-to-end latency around 1.5 seconds lets conversational voice agents feel comfortable to users without slowness complaints. Consistency matters even more than peak speed so conversations never feel broken. - Parallelizing speech pipelines cuts response times and stays 3 to 5 times cheaper than speech-to-speech models. Running safety checks concurrently alongside initial text-to-speech chunks adds zero latency. - Agent intelligence demands low transcription error rates and expressive speech. Crucially, models must also remain easy to build with so developers avoid brittle engineering overhead. - Cloud economics must be modeled up front by comparing per-user server costs against expected revenue. Stellar Cafe achieved viable margins at about $1.20 per hour per user with flat pricing. - Open-weight models avoid the frequent sunsets and rising fees typical of closed models. Self-hosting them provides predictable costs and protects production schedules from forced migrations. ## Resources - \[Devin Reimer on Bluesky\](https://devinreimer.bsky.social) - \[AstroBeam website\](https://astrobeam.com) - \[Devin Reimer on LinkedIn\](https://linkedin.com/in/devinreimer) ## Topics voice-agents, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, large-language-models, low-latency, cloud-economics, game-development ## Transcript ### Introduction to voice agents and core challenges \*\*Devin Reimer\*\* \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=5s) Welcome to Balancing Ultra-Low Latency and Cloud Economics in virtual voice agents. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=13s) So, I'm Devin Reimer. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=14s) I'm the founder and CEO of AstroBeam. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=16s) Previously, I was the CEO and co-founder of Owlchemy Labs, probably most known for Job Simulator. \[00:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FQt2V0VafaE\&t=23s) So, at AstroBeam, we are focused on building real-time AI in games. entries.summary: This document outlines Devin Reimer's talk on balancing ultra-low latency, intelligence, and cloud economics when building virtual voice agents for interactive games and Android XR applications. It details architectural strategies—such as parallelized speech pipelines and open-weight models—to achieve sustainable user unit economics without compromising response times.

In this session, discover how Firebase AI Logic empowers developers to deploy secure, budget-conscious AI experiences at scale. We will cover from security foundations and Firebase App Check, cost management, dynamic model routing to leveraging the multimodal capabilities. ## Summary - Firebase AI Logic routes requests from client SDKs directly to Gemini APIs without a custom back end. Server prompt templates store prompts in the cloud to avoid app updates. - Firebase App Check protects resources against abuse by ensuring requests originate from your app. It integrates attestation providers like Play Integrity and reCAPTCHA Enterprise before you enforce checks. - Gemini Nano 4 executes on-device inference to lower latency and safeguard user privacy. Firebase AI Logic manages fallback routing to the cloud when needed. - Spend caps and Firebase AI Logic triggers keep cloud costs predictable. Firebase automatically pauses your AI service at 100% spend, and triggers let you run custom functions before or after generation. - Gemini Live API powers bidirectional conversational audio and video streaming. The client SDK manages the underlying WebSocket connections and streaming protocols. ## Topics firebase-ai-logic, gemini-nano, firebase-app-check, on-device-ai, cost-optimization, gemini-live-api ## entries.summary: This document introduces Firebase AI Logic and Gemini Nano integration for Android, providing a serverless approach to securely route client SDK requests to Gemini APIs while protecting resources with Firebase App Check and server-managed prompt templates.

entries.title: Build world anchored experiences for wired XR glasses
entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces a Dev Summit talk detailing how to build world-anchored experiences for XREAL Aura wired XR glasses. It provides developers with essential guidance and an interactive transcript for creating immersive augmented reality applications.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/build-world-anchored-experiences-for-xreal-aura-wired-xr-glasses.txt" target="_blank">Build world anchored experiences for wired XR glasses - Speakers: Yasmine Quintana Evjen (Senior Product Manager), Dereck Bridie (Developer Relations Engineer), Paul Hoover (Senior Interaction Designer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/build-world-anchored-experiences-for-xreal-aura-wired-xr-glasses ## About the talk Go beyond screen-space and anchor your apps in the real world with Android XR. This session teaches you how to build geospatially aware Android XR experiences using Jetpack Compose Glimmer and ARCore's Geospatial API. We will start by covering how to get a device's geospatial pose with ARCore. Then, you'll see how Glimmer's minimal UI components can be anchored to real-world locations via the Visual Positioning System (VPS). We'll combine these to build a simple, location-aware spatial experience. ## Summary - Android XR brings digital experiences into physical environments across a spectrum of devices, from intelligent eyewear to wired XR glasses. Existing 2D Android-compatible apps work on XR headsets and wired XR glasses with minimal modifications. - Jetpack Compose Glimmer provides components and styles tailored for optical see-through displays. Built-in helper functions adjust brand colors to glasses-safe shades to maintain visibility and contrast across lighting conditions. - The Glimmer library adds new components such as pagers and button groups. A depth API helps separate stacked elements on see-through displays where black is transparent. - Subspace composables place interfaces in 3D space and can follow ARCore anchors via a follow target, such as a tracked QR code. - The Geospatial API in ARCore combines Street View data and GPS measurements to position devices accurately in supported areas. You can attach Glimmer components to real-world geospatial anchors using coordinates from Places API queries. ## Resources - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Glimmer guide\](https://goo.gle/glimmer-guide) - \[Geospatial API documentation\](https://goo.gle/xr-geospatial) - \[Android XR developer resources\](https://goo.gle/xr-dev) - \[Android XR experiments\](https://goo.gle/xr-experiments) - \[Android XR codelabs\](https://goo.gle/xr-codelabs) - \[Android XR developer documentation\](https://developer.android.com/xr) ## Topics android-xr, supported rooftops, which means that the altitude value will be determined relative to the rooftop at the building at that location. \[18:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1119s) So, you can also rotate the anchor using a quaternion, which specifies like the rotational values of the anchor. \[18:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1126s) But we'll actually use the defaults in this example because we'll be making the UI rotate to face the user. \[18:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1133s) And then, we'll attach the Glimmer UI from before to this anchor, and that really gives you the building blocks for a spatially-anchored experience. \`\`\`kotlin when (anchorResult) { is AnchorCreateSuccess -\> Subspace(FollowTarget.anchor(anchorResult.anchor)) { SpatialPanel(SubspaceModifier.rotateToLookAtUser()) { PlaceIndicator(place) } } else -\> Log.e("Demo", "Failed to create anchor $anchorResult") } \`\`\` \[19:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1140s) So, we believe that the Geospatial API can enable great wayfinding experiences, and designing with Glimmer will help create glanceable user experiences made especially for your see-through displays. \[19:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1152s) For more information on the Geospatial API, visit the recently updated developer.android.com/xr. \[19:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1158s) And I'll hand it back to Yasmine to finish us off. ### Conclusion and developer resources \[19:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1167s) In this session, we went over a few capabilities of Android XR: ARCore for Jetpack XR and Jetpack Compose Glimmer. \[19:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1175s) We're enthusiastic about what new features Android XR will bring to wired XR glasses. \[19:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1183s) Developers are already building for Android XR, and we hope to see your creative work on the Google Play Store. \[19:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1189s) To help you get started, please check out our developer documentation, be inspired by our XR experiments, and jump into it with the codelabs. \[20:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1200s) We have a ton of great XR sessions, demos, and workshops planned for all of you. \[20:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1205s) So, please tune in and learn about building for Android XR across immersive and augmented experiences. \[20:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1215s) On behalf of the Android XR team, thank you all so much for being here, and we hope you enjoy the rest of your time here at the Android Developer Summit. \[20:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4NGBZnfnD6o\&t=1223s) So, thank you.</a>
entries.summary: This document introduces Android XR development techniques for building world-anchored, spatial experiences on wired XR glasses like the XREAL AURA using Jetpack Compose Glimmer and ARCore's Geospatial API.

entries.title: Building a Formula E co-driver on Android with ML Kit and Gemini Nano
entries.summary: This new documentation page provides the talk session video and interactive transcript from the Android Dev Summit regarding building a Formula E co-driver using ML Kit and Gemini Nano. It matters because it offers developers practical insights into integrating on-device machine learning and generative AI capabilities into Android applications.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-a-formula-e-co-driver-on-android-with-ml-kit-and-gemini-nano.txt" target="_blank">Building a Formula E co-driver on Android with ML Kit and Gemini Nano - Speakers: Alastair Breeze (Staff Software Engineer - Google Cloud's Office of the CTO), Oli Thompson (Junior Data Scientist, Formula E) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nV63eqjPeEI - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-a-formula-e-co-driver-on-android-with-ml-kit-and-gemini-nano ## About the talk A racing car is a demanding environment of high speed, heat, and telemetry constraints. How can an on-device agent help process real-time vehicle data for sports and engineering applications? This technical session explores an experimental hybrid architecture combining edge hardware and cloud agents. We'll walk through a research proof-of-concept using a Raspberry Pi to stream CAN bus telemetry, a Pixel phone running an on-device conversational agent powered by ML Kit and Gemini Nano, and an agent-to-agent (A2A) Cloud connection for post-race workflows. ## Summary - Formula E race environments challenge edge AI with extreme heat and low latency requirements. A Pixel phone hosted an agent to answer drivers traveling over 200 km/h. - Android hosts the edge architecture using Agent Developer Kit and Gemini Nano through ML Kit. Edge agents can converse directly with cloud agents over the A2A protocol. - Vehicle integration routes live CAN bus telemetry through a Raspberry Pi to publish downsampled 10 Hz data over MQTT. The Android agent combines this data with driver voice input to evaluate queries and speak back. - Track testing at Goodwood proved the phone handled severe heat without issues. Last-minute debugging resolved Bluetooth connections to the driver helmet before the car drove up the hill. ## Topics gemini-nano, ml-kit, on-device-ai, ai-agents, formula-e ## Transcript ### entries.title: Building audio-first experiences for intelligent eyewear with Gemini Nano 4
entries.summary: Added a new developer summit talk page documenting how to build audio-first experiences for intelligent eyewear using Gemini Nano. This provides developers with essential resources and session transcripts for integrating advanced on-device AI into wearable tech.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-audio-first-experiences-for-intelligent-eyewear-with-gemini-nano-4.txt" target="_blank">Building audio-first experiences for intelligent eyewear with Gemini Nano 4 - Speakers: Amy Zeppenfeld (Developer Relations Engineer \| Android XR), Alice Zheng (Senior Product Manager) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-audio-first-experiences-for-intelligent-eyewear-with-gemini-nano-4 ## About the talk Discover how to build robust, hands-free audio experiences powered by on-device AI. We'll cover everything you need: setting up your glasses activity, capturing mic and camera feeds, and using voice along with other audio cues as your ultimate UI. Through an exciting real-world showcase of the open-source XR Language Teacher built in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, learn to orchestrate Gemini Nano 4 (built on Gemma 4 and optimized for Android devices), and ML Kit, and leverage the LiteRT runtime to build fast XR experiences that hear, see, and speak naturally. ## Summary - The Jetpack Projected library (alpha) bridges Android phones to intelligent eyewear. Adding a projected activity to your existing app projects content to display or audio-only glasses. - ML Kit introduces alpha on-device speech libraries for audio-first interactions on select devices. It offers Text to Speech with 8 voices across 21 locales and Speech Recognition with a Gemini Nano advanced mode on Pixel 10. - Gemini Nano 4 processes camera frames and transcribed questions together in one pass. It powers offline experiences by chaining on-device speech models locally on supported flagship phones. - A two-pass design prioritizes real-time audio latency on smart glasses. Pass 1 streams spoken text using inline XML tags for mid-sentence locale switching, while Pass 2 extracts structured data in the background. - The open-source XR Language Teacher implementation ships in the Google AI Edge Gallery app. Developers can adapt its code for other multimodal assistant use cases. ## Resources - \[Android XR Developer Documentation\](https://goo.gle/xr-dev) - \[Android XR SDK and Developer Resources\](https://developer.android.com/xr) - \[ML Kit APIs Documentation\](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit) - \[Google AI Edge Offerings and Gallery App\](https://developers.google.com/edge) - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Topics intelligent-eyewear, android-xr, gemini-nano, on-device-ai, ml-kit, speech-recognition, running locally on the phone. \[20:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1207s) So on supported flagship Android devices, you can get optimized performance by using the ML Kit APIs directly. \[20:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1214s) The Android system will take care of the model delivery for you, so there's nothing for you to bundle in your app. \[20:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1220s) So to put all this together, the microphone goes into speech recognition, and the camera frame and the transcript together goes into the Gemini Nano 4, and Gemini Nano 4 writes out into the speech synthesis and then comes out from the speaker. \[20:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1234s) Three models, chained, all running locally on your phone. \[20:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1239s) And here are a few reasons why Gemini Nano 4 is particularly suited for this problem. \[20:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1244s) First, it sees and reads in one pass. \[20:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1248s) Through ML Kit, Gemini Nano 4 handles text and images natively, so you're not using a detector, then a classifier, then a translator. \[20:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1256s) It is one model that look at the camera frame and the question together. \[21:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1261s) And second is its extensive language support. \[21:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1264s) Gemini Nano 4 was trained on over 140 languages. \[21:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1268s) And also, for language tutor, translation on its own is not enough. \[21:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1272s) You want idioms, you want formal versus casual registers, you also want example sentence a real person would say. \[21:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1279s) And lastly, it is steerable enough to have a personality. \[21:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1283s) Practicing pronunciation out loud could be intimidating. \[21:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1287s) And this model follows a system prompt well, so user can pick their own teacher persona. \[21:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1292s) And maybe a patient and encouraging one could make people more willing to try. \[21:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1298s) And here's one more thing I like to highlight about the design. \[21:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1302s) While the conversation is happening in the glasses mode, the app is quietly writing vocabulary cards in the background. \[21:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1309s) The word, the translation, the example sentence, and the photo from the moment you ask your question. \[21:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1315s) The user doesn't need to manually tap anything. \[21:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1317s) They're just walking and talking. \[21:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1319s) And then later that day, everything are just waiting for them on their phone, which is exactly what I wanted when I was in Tokyo. \[22:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1326s) So audio first does not have to mean audio only. \[22:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1330s) Glasses is a right surface for curiosity, and your phone is a right surface for the reflection afterwards. \[22:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1336s) Let the hands-free moment leave something behind. \[22:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1340s) Now, let's zoom in on a few practical tips for building real-time experiences with Gemini Nano 4 and ML Kit that we learned from building this demo. ### Prioritizing real-time latency with two-pass design \[22:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1350s) Tip 1, prioritize real-time latency with a two-pass design. \[22:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1355s) On audio glasses, when you ask, "What is that?" \[22:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1359s) Every moment of silence is noticeable. \[22:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1362s) In the example of XR Language Teacher, we need two things for each turn of the user interaction from the model: an immediate spoken answer, and also a structured vocabulary card to save to the app. \[22:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1373s) If we ask the model for two things together in a single pass, then every token spent on that background data generation will delay the first spoken sentence. \[23:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1383s) So instead, we separate what the user needs right now from what the app needs a few seconds later. \[23:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1390s) So we split each turn into two passes. \[23:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1393s) In Pass 1, we stream the camera frame and the question for the spoken reply alone, triggering text-to-speech as soon as the first sentence completes. \[23:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1402s) And because that TPU or NPU finish generating that short reply long before the text-to-speech finishes speaking out loud, we actually get a multi-second window where the user still listening, and the chip is already sitting idle. \[23:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1415s) And since Pass 1 already identified the object in its text reply, Pass 2 doesn't even need the image input. \[23:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1422s) We just pass Pass 1's reply back into that idle chip to extract and save the structured card before the teacher even finishes talking. \[23:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1433s) Now, let's zoom in to Pass 1, which wi-- brings me to the second tip. \[23:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1437s) Use lightweight XML tags when streaming. \[24:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1441s) Because Pass 1 streams directly to text-to-speech, you don't want heavy JSON object to hold up your first spoken word. \[24:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1449s) Instead, you want plain text that can speak immediately with lightweight, on-- inline tags whenever the app needs to take action mid-stream. \[24:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1457s) So let me show you the problem that led us here. \[24:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1460s) Remember that wooden cup-and-ball toy on the market stall I mentioned? \[24:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1465s) In Japanese, it's called "kendama". \[24:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1468s) Early on, the model recognized it from the camera frame and returned the right answer, "That's kendama, a wooden toy." \[24:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1476s) So we handed that complete sentence into the English text-to-speech session, and here is what came out. \[24:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1482s) That's ken-mi, a wooden toy. \[24:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1485s) That doesn't sound quite right. \[24:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1487s) Instead, that sentence should actually sound... \[24:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1490s) That's kendama, a wooden toy. \[24:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1494s) So why did that happen? \[24:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1496s) Kendama is written with hiragana, "ken", and the kanji character, "dama". \[25:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1501s) And the English text-to-speech engine handles the phonetic hiragana like "ken" just fine, but completely falls apart when it hits the kanji part and turning dama into something that sounds like me. \[25:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1514s) And this happens actually across many different languages in different ways if you don't switch locale. \[25:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1519s) For example, in Spanish, you might hear... \[25:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1521s) Suh-BOH-luh... \[25:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1523s) When you're actually expecting... \[25:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1524s) Cebolla. \[25:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1528s) And similarly, in French, you might hear... \[25:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1531s) PAIN oh chock-uh-lat... \[25:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1533s) When you are actually expecting... \[25:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1534s) Pain au chocolat. \[25:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1536s) Yes, a TTS session is usually designed for a single locale at a time, but a language teacher need to code-switch in every single sentence. \[25:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1546s) So, in pass 1, we ask the model to wrap every target language word or phrase inside the target XML tag as it streams. \[25:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1554s) And as chunks arrives, our client split on target, route each span to the matching Text To Speech locale, which could be Japanese, Spanish, French, or whatever language you're learning, and then play them back seamlessly, switching accent mid-sentence, so word like kendama comes out right. \[26:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1571s) So, the take away here is the model already knows which vocabulary belongs to which language, which words belongs to which language, and having it tag target spans inline while streaming, it's far cleaner than post-processing this whole thing yourself afterwards. \[26:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1587s) And here's pass 1 in code. \`\`\`kotlin // 1. Pass 1 System + Turn Prompt (XrLanguageTeacherPersona.kt) // System: "Always start immediately with ... (strictly 1 to 3 sentences total). // Inside , wrap every Japanese word AND every complete Japanese example sentence // inside ... tags (never output )." val pass1TurnPrompt = """ The student is looking at the camera view and asked: "$question". Answer in English teaching Japanese inside ...: if they refer to 'this'/'that' or point to an object, ground it to the focal item in the camera frame; if they ask for a phrase or greeting, teach that phrase. """.trimIndent() // 2. Stream multimodal dialogue (ImagePart + TextPart) and split tags to TTS val generativeModel = Generation.getClient() val pass1Request = generateContentRequest(ImagePart(frame), TextPart(pass1TurnPrompt)) { temperature = 1.0f; topK = 1; maxOutputTokens = 1024 } generativeModel.generateContentStream(pass1Request).collect { chunk -\> val delta = chunk.candidates.firstOrNull()?.text.orEmpty() streamReplyAndSplitTargetTagsToTts(delta) // Speaks 1st complete sentence immediately } // Streams: "That's けん玉 --- a wooden toy. けん玉をください。" \`\`\` \[26:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1589s) At the top, we use the prompt to instruct the model to reply in one to three sentence inside the reply tags and then wrap every Japanese word or example sentence inside the target tags. \[26:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1600s) Then we pass the camera \`ImagePart\` and the prompt \`TextPart\` into ML Kit's \`generateContentStream\`, splitting target spans into Text To Speech as each sentence arrives. \[26:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1613s) And that brings me to pass 2 and our third tip. \[26:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1617s) While using lightweight XML tags are great for a live audio stream, use structured output, which are built to return a clean, typed object when saving data to your app. \[27:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1628s) Because our XR Language Teacher is conversational, users can also ask follow-up questions where no new word is taught. \[27:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1636s) And when a word is taught, the database needs clean dictionary fields to create the vocabulary cards. \[27:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1643s) So instead of writing brittle regular expressions to parse pass one's transcript, we let pass 2 extract type-safe object in the background. \[27:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1653s) And to enforce the schema in pass 2, we use ML Kit's structured output API, which under the hood is using constrained decoding. \`\`\`kotlin import com.google.mlkit.genai.prompt.Generation import com.google.mlkit.genai.prompt.generateTypedContentRequest import com.google.mlkit.genai.schema.annotations.Generable import com.google.mlkit.genai.schema.annotations.Guide // Pass 2 schema (XrLanguageTeacherGenerableSchemas.kt): @Generable(description = "Vocabulary flashcard for the taught word or short phrase") data class GenerableVocabCard( @Guide(description = TeacherResponseSchema.WORD_FIELD_DESCRIPTION) val word: String, @Guide(description = "Native-language meaning or translation") val meaning: String, @Guide(description = "Target-language example sentence") val example: String, @Guide(description = "Native-language translation of the example sentence") val example_translation: String, ) @Generable(description = "Optional vocabulary card extracted from a teacher reply") data class GenerableOptionalVocabCardWrapper( @Guide(description = "Vocabulary flashcard if a vocabulary term was taught, or null otherwise") val card: GenerableVocabCard? ) \`\`\` \[27:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1662s) You simply annotate a data class with \`@Generable\` and each field with \`@Guide\`, just like our vocabulary card class example here. \[27:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1670s) And by wrapping the nullable card field, pass 2 returns a populated card when a new word was taught, or null on purely conversational turns. \[28:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1680s) And here is pass 2 in code. \`\`\`kotlin // 1. Pass 1 Streamed Output -\> Pass 2 Extraction Prompt (no image needed!) val replyWithTargetTags = "That's けん玉 --- a wooden toy. けん玉をください。" val pass2Prompt = """ If the teacher reply below teaches or introduces a specific Japanese vocabulary item, extract only its core focal dictionary term into "card" with keys "word", "meaning", "example", and "example_translation". If purely conversational with no focal term taught, set "card" to null: $replyWithTargetTags """.trimIndent() // 2. Extract @Generable card on idle NPU while TTS audio plays val pass2Request = generateContentRequest(TextPart(pass2Prompt)) { temperature = 1.0f; topK = 1; maxOutputTokens = 256 } val typedRequest = generateTypedContentRequest(pass2Request, GenerableOptionalVocabCardWrapper::class) val card: GenerableVocabCard? = generativeModel.generateContent(typedRequest).candidates.firstOrNull()?.response?.card // Extracts: {"word": "けん玉", "meaning": "a wooden toy", "example": "けん玉をください。", ...} \`\`\` \[28:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1682s) At the top, we take pass 1's streamed reply text, no image needed, and build our extraction prompt. \[28:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1689s) Then, while the user is still listening to Text To Speech, we pass the prompt and our wrapper class into \`generateTypedContentRequest\` and extract a clean, tag-free vocabulary card, or null if no word was taught. \[28:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1704s) All right. \[28:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1705s) We covered a lot of things. \[28:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1706s) It is a reasonable thought to have at this moment, "Great, another thing that looks lovely on stage that I will never touch." \[28:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1713s) Not this one! \[28:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1714s) XR Language Teacher ships in the Google AI Edge Gallery app alongside other on-device AI experiences. \[28:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1720s) You can download it today, put it on your own phone, and point at any anything you want to learn how to say it in a different language today. \[28:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1728s) And if you want to know how it's built, this entire implementation is open source on GitHub. \[28:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1734s) And don't worry if not all of your users have audio or display glasses or supported flagship Android devices already. \[29:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1742s) Our code base also shows you examples of how this same experience can be adapted for a mobile-only experience. \[29:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1749s) And if you want to reach other platforms too, the Google AI Edge Gallery app code also shows you how to build this feature using the Google LiteRT runtime and MediaPipe Tasks APIs. \[29:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1759s) Or if you want to bring other open source on-device audio or language models, you can also see how to do that from the code. ### Adapting to other use cases with AI agents \[29:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1768s) So we open sourced XR Language Teacher to make your prototyping easier. \[29:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1772s) Point your agent of choice at our GitHub repo to turn this live, on-device, AI-powered experience into something else. \[29:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1780s) It could be a museum guide, maybe a cooking assistant looking at your counter, a repair walkthrough, accessibility narrator, a field inspection tool. \[29:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1790s) The model, the runtime, the open-source implementation, and the tooling are all available now so that you can get ready for the upcoming intelligent eyewear launch this fall. \[29:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1798s) We'd love to see what you make with it. \[30:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1802s) To wrap up, today, we showed powerful examples of what's possible with AI models running seamlessly on-device. \[30:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1809s) And here are a few ways to get started. \[30:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1812s) First, grab the resources on the screen. \[30:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1814s) Download the AI Edge Gallery app to try out the demo and check out the reference code on GitHub. \[30:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1819s) And scan the QR codes to access Android XR SDK, ML Kit APIs, and Google AI Edge offerings. \[30:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1827s) Second, start experimenting right on the phone today. \[30:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1832s) There are a lot of things that we covered that can already be built with a mobile first experience already. \[30:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1838s) And third, look at the mobile app you are already shipping and ask yourself, what core features would be better hands-free? \[30:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1845s) Adding a Projected Activity to your existing APK is all it takes to bring that experience to glasses, too. \[30:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1852s) Thank you so much for joining us today. \[30:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1854s) We can't wait to see what incredible audio-first experiences you build on Android and for intelligent eyewear. \[31:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW3mg0iyi_w\&t=1860s) Thank you.</a>

entries.title: Building reliable text editing experiences in Compose
entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring the Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript for building reliable text editing experiences in Jetpack Compose. This helps developers easily access video resources and transcripts related to advanced text input handling.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-reliable-text-editing-experiences-in-compose.txt" target="_blank">Building reliable text editing experiences in Compose - Speakers: Anastasia Soboleva (Software engineer), Haoyu Zhang (Senior Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-reliable-text-editing-experiences-in-compose ## About the talk The journey to reliable text editing in Compose culminated in the complete rewrite of BasicTextField. This shift to a buffer-driven architecture eliminated IME race conditions once and for all. This session unpacks why legacy input syncing had to go and how TextFieldState keeps keyboard updates in sync. From there, take a deep dive into formatted editing to explore the mechanics of TrackedRange, the performance costs of edit blocks, and the real-world catches behind style boundaries, before taking an early peek at Markdown rendering. ## Summary - The \`TextFieldState\` API overload replaces the callback-based overloads in Compose. It updates synchronously with user typing, eliminating timing issues with software keyboards and unnecessary recompositions. - Input and output transformations let you manipulate text using \`TextFieldBuffer\`. You can intercept edits before committing them or format display text without manually computing offset mappings. - Hoisting \`TextFieldState\` depends on your architecture needs. You can keep it locally in a composable or store it directly in a \`ViewModel\` for business logic access. - Compose 1.12 adds formatted text editing APIs to \`TextFieldBuffer\`. You can apply styles with customizable \`ExpandPolicy\` options, and existing style ranges update automatically as users edit. - A new markup text library for Jetpack Compose is currently in development. It supports formats like Markdown with incremental parsing and rendering for live editing and streaming. ## Resources - \[Migration guide to TextFieldState\](https://goo.gle/migrate_to_state_textfield) ## Topics jetpack-compose, textfieldstate, text-editing, basictextfield, formatted-text, input-transformation ## Transcript ### Introduction to text editing in Compose \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=5s) Hi, everyone! \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=6s) Thank you for joining our talk. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=8s) My name is Anastasia, and with me is my colleague Haoyu. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=11s) And we are going to show you today how to build reliable text-editing experience. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=16s) Whether you are building a simple login screen, a search as you \[17:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1072s) So the first is \`ExpandPolicy.InsideOnly\`. \`\`\`kotlin val state = TextFieldState("The fox") state.edit { addStyle( \[17:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1075s) In this mode, inserting text at the boundary will not expand the style ranges. doesn't expand either. \[18:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1097s) So here's a demo showing how it works in an editor. \[18:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1102s) So next is \`ExpandPolicy.AtStart\`. \`\`\`kotlin val state = TextFieldState("The fox") state.edit { addStyle( SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), start = 4, end = 7, policy = ExpandPolicy.AtStart ) insert(4, "quick ") \`\`\` \[18:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1104s) As the name suggest, inserting text at the start of the range expand the style range. \[18:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1109s) So when we insert text right before the style range expands to cover the newly inserted text. \[18:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1116s) So here's another demo showing how it works. \[18:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1120s) Third is \`ExpandPolicy.AtEnd\`. \`\`\`kotlin val state = TextFieldState("The fox") state.edit { addStyle( SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), start = 4, end = 7, policy = ExpandPolicy.AtEnd ) insert(length, " jumps") \`\`\` \[18:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1122s) So we're inserting text at the end of the range expand the style range. \[18:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1127s) So this is also the most common, setting for the editors. \[18:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1133s) So here's a demo showing how it works. \[18:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1136s) So finally, it's \`ExpandPolicy.AtBoth\`, which expand the style when the text is inserted at the start of the range and at the end of the range. \`\`\`kotlin val state = TextFieldState("The fox") state.edit { addStyle( SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), start = 4, end = 7, policy = ExpandPolicy.AtBoth ) insert(4, "quick ") insert(length, " jumps") } \`\`\` \[19:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1147s) So another demo for this. \[19:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1151s) We covered all the styling-applying APIs so far. \[19:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1154s) In addition to that, we also introduced new query APIs like \`getSpanStyles\`, \`getParagraphStyles\` to fetch the styles currently applied in a given range. \`\`\`kotlin // Outside edits. ReadOnly API in TextFieldState. val textFieldState.styles: TextFieldTextStyles fun TextFieldTextStyles.getSpanStyle(range: TextRange): List\> // Inside edits, returned TrackedRange fun TextFieldBuffer.getSpanStyles(range: TextRange): List\> \`\`\` \[19:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1165s) Here are two versions of the query APIs. \[19:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1168s) On the \`TextFieldState\`, the style query APIs are read-only. \[19:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1172s) They return a list of immutable \`AnnotatedString.Range\` objects. \[19:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1176s) And but in the TextFieldBuffer, \`getSpanStyles\` returned a list of newly introduced \`TrackedRange\` objects, which I will introduce later. \[19:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1185s) So all style queries are order aware. \[19:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1188s) They return the style ranges exactly the order when the style is applied. \[19:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1192s) So this allows you to apply, just like AnnotatedString, to apply another style on top of an existing style to overwrite the earlier ones. \[20:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1203s) So next is \`TrackedRange\` API. \`\`\`kotlin var TrackedRange\<\*\>.textRange: TextRange var TrackedRange\<\*\>.expandPolicy: ExpandPolicy var TrackedRange.spanStyle: SpanStyle var TrackedRange.paragraphStyle: ParagraphStyle val TrackedRange\<\*\>.isValid: Boolean fun removeStyle(trackedRange: TrackedRange\<\*\>): Boolean \`\`\` \[20:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1204s) \`TrackedRange\` objects are returned by \`addStyle\` or \`getSpanStyles\` APIs in TextFieldBuffer. \[20:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1210s) Think of it as a live handle of the style range in the buffer. \[20:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1215s) You can use it to update the text range, \`ExpandPolicy\` or the style itself in the place. \[20:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1221s) It also has an \`isValid\` property to check if the style range is still in the TextFieldBuffer. \[20:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1227s) This is because style can be removed if the-- if it's collapsed during the editing, or it gets removed deliberately by the \`removeStyle\`. \[20:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1239s) So next let's see how those APIs come together in a real-world use cases. ### Building a WYSIWYG editor \[20:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1245s) The first use case is build What You See Is What You Get, WYSIWYG Editor. \[20:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1249s) In this example, we implemented the bold button feature. \[20:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1253s) Clicking the bold button toggles the bold style on the selected text. \[20:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1258s) So next, let's look at the code. \[21:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1261s) So when the user taps the bold button, we first call \`getSpanStyles\` on a selection to find all the overlapping styles. \`\`\`kotlin fun TextFieldBuffer.toggleBoldSelection() { if (selection.collapsed) return val boldSpans = getSpanStyles(selection) if (!isFullyBold(boldSpans, selection)) { addStyle( SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), selection, ExpandPolicy.AtEnd ) } else { unboldSelection(boldSpans.first()) } } \`\`\` \[21:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1268s) And then we check if the entire selection is already bold or not. \[21:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1272s) Here, the selected word is not bold. \[21:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1275s) Since it's not bold, we \`addStyle\` to the selected range. \[21:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1278s) We pass \`ExpandPolicy.AtEnd\`, so that user can continue typing the bold right after this word. \[21:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1286s) Now, let's look what happens if the selected range is already bold. \`\`\`kotlin fun TextFieldBuffer.unboldSelection( boldSpan: TrackedRange ) { val hasBoldBefore = boldSpan.start \< selection.min val hasBoldAfter = boldSpan.end \> selection.max when { hasBoldBefore -\> boldSpan.range = TextRange(range.start, selection.min) hasBoldAfter -\> boldSpan.range = TextRange(selection.max, range.end) hasBoldBefore \&\& hasBoldAfter -\> { val oldEnd = boldSpan.end boldSpan.range = TextRange(boldSpan.start, selection.min) addStyle( boldSpan.spanStyle, start = selection.max, end = oldEnd ) } else -\> removeStyle(range) } } \`\`\` \[21:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1290s) In that case, we need to clear the bold style from the selected range. \[21:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1294s) Here, the user-selected the word is inside the longer bold phrase. \[21:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1298s) Because the bold style extends before the selection, we need to update the style range, leaving the selected word unbolded. \[21:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1306s) To do this, we can use a \`TrackedRange\` API. \[21:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1310s) And for this specific case, instead of deleting this style and recreating it, we can just adjust the bold span range in-place to end before the selection at index 10. \[22:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1323s) Of course, this is a highly simplified implementation. \[22:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1327s) For a full demo, you can check our Compose samples repository. \[22:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1332s) And next, let's look at a pattern-based styling. \[22:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1336s) In this demo, when user types Markdown asterisks around a word, the editor automatically converts it into bold text as they type. \[22:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1347s) Now, let's see how it's implemented using \`InputTransformation\`. \`\`\`kotlin object MarkdownBoldTransformation : InputTransformation { val regex = Regex("""\*\*(.\*?)\*\*""") override fun TextFieldBuffer.transformInput() { val matches = regex.findAll(asCharSequence()).toList() for (match in matches) { val range = match.range val content = match.groupValues\[1\] replace(range.first, range.last + 1, content) addStyle( SpanStyle(fontWeight = FontWeight.Bold), start = range.first, end = range.first + content.length, policy = ExpandPolicy.atEnd ) } } } \`\`\` \[22:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1351s) In our transforming input filter, we find all the matching patterns over the button. \[22:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1358s) And for each match, we extract the content inside the double asterisks. \[22:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1362s) In this example, it's the word "fox". \[22:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1366s) And next, we remove the asterisks and replace the matching pattern with its content. \[22:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1373s) And finally, we call \`addStyle\` to the bold to apply the bold style to the content text. \[22:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1379s) Just remember, \`InputTransformation\` will submit to the final text field state. \[23:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1385s) This means the bold style is applied to the state persistently. \[23:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1391s) And finally, let's look at the search highlighting example. \[23:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1394s) So in this example, when user types a search query, matching words in the text fields is are highlighted, without modifying the text field state. \[23:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1406s) Now, let's look how it's implemented in the \`OutputTransformation\`. \[23:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1408s) When highlighting a search word, you should never mutate the text state. \[23:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1415s) And \`OutputTransformation\` is a perfect place to implement this use case. \[23:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1420s) So let's check the actual implementation. \[23:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1422s) We first search the highlighting words and find all the matches. \`\`\`kotlin class SearchHighlightTransformation( val query: MutableState ) : OutputTransformation { override fun TextFieldBuffer.transformOutput() { val search = query.value if (search.isEmpty()) return val text = asCharSequence().toString() var index = text.indexOf(search) while (index != -1) { addStyle( SpanStyle( background = Color.Yellow, color = Color.Black ), start = index, end = index + search.length ) index = text.indexOf(search, index + search.length) } } } \`\`\` \[23:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1427s) And note that the query is a mutable state. \[23:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1429s) This is because the \`OutputTransformation\` is snapshot-aware. \[23:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1434s) When this mutable states gets updated, the \`OutputTransformation\` is reapplied automatically. \[24:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1441s) And then when we loops through every matches and call \`addStyle\` to draw the yellow highlights over the match range. \[24:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1448s) Again, \`OutputTransformation\` only change the visual text, and the original text states are untouched. \[24:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1456s) Okay, that's all the use cases we have. \[24:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1460s) Just to remind you, all the APIs showed before are available starting from Compose 1.12. ### Upcoming markup text library \[24:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1467s) And to wrap up, I want to share a sneak peek of the new project we're currently working on. \[24:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1472s) It's a markup text library for Jetpack Compose, which support rich text formats like Markdown. \[24:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1481s) One of the most exciting capabilities we're supporting is incremental parsing and incremental rendering. \[24:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1488s) So it's very suitable for live editing or the Markdown streaming. \[24:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1491s) If here's a record of our working prototype in action, and you can see those fading areas are the updating parts in the UI. \[25:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1502s) If this is something you are interested, or you have some use case in your app, please feel free to reach out to us. \[25:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1DvjkRYGs2g\&t=1510s) And thank you, everyone.</a>
entries.summary: This document summarizes a Dev Summit talk detailing the architectural shift to `TextFieldState` and `BasicTextField` in Jetpack Compose, which eliminates IME race conditions and improves text editing performance. It covers new APIs for input/output transformation, formatted text editing, and state hoisting.

entries.title: Building type-safe deep links with Jetpack Navigation3
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk video and interactive transcript regarding building type-safe deep links with Jetpack Navigation 3, helping developers adopt safer navigation patterns.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-type-safe-deep-links-with-jetpack-navigation3.txt" target="_blank">Building type-safe deep links with Jetpack Navigation3 - Speakers: Clara Fok (Software Engineer), Ian Lake (Engineering Manager) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/building-type-safe-deep-links-with-jetpack-navigation3 ## About the talk Managing deep links across modular Android apps can easily lead to broken routes and runtime surprises.This session unpacks Jetpack Navigation3's new type-safe deep linking architecture for Compose to help you build a robust and scalable routing system. We'll explore how to implement out-of-the-box deep link matching APIs, write custom serializers for complex type-safe arguments, and construct dynamic hierarchical back stacks that keep user navigation predictable. ## Summary - Navigation 3 deep link APIs turn incoming deep link requests into navigation keys to determine your initial back stack. The KMP-compatible \`DeepLinkRequest\` class encapsulates the input, including an Android Intent constructor. - A \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` uses Kotlin Serialization to match URI patterns and deserialize arguments into type-safe \`NavKey\` properties. Primitive types work automatically, failing matches if values cannot be parsed. - Developers can extend \`DeepLinkSerializer\` or override \`matchArguments\` to handle complex deep link strings. Subclassing \`UriDeepLinkMatcher\` lets you preprocess raw URI placeholders before Kotlin Serialization runs. - Calling \`withBackStack\` on matchers creates synthetic back stacks lazily for the best match. This ensures proper system back behavior without computing unnecessary back stacks for every other valid match. ## Resources - \[Nav3 recipes repository\](https://goo.gle/nav3-recipes) - \[Now in Android sample app\](https://github.com/android/nowinandroid) ## Topics jetpack-navigation-3, deep-links, kotlin-serialization, kotlin-multiplatform, android-architecture ## Transcript ###
