\[14:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=854s) We wanted just for the best match. \[14:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=857s) So, if we want custom logic for each matcher, but we don't want to create a synthetic back stack eagerly for each match, what do we do? \[14:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=866s) So after a few false starts, we found an approach that balances both requirements. \[14:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=871s) No matter what kind of matcher you have, you can augment that specific matcher by calling a \`withBackStack\` to lazily construct the back stack with the given \`MatchResult\`. \`\`\`kotlin val homeMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher(...).withBackStack { matchResult -\> listOf(Home, matchResult.key) } val sessionMatcher = UriDeepLinkMatcher(...).withBackStack { matchResult -\> listOf(Home, SessionList, matchResult.key) } val backStackMatchers: List\> = listOf( homeMatcher, sessionMatcher ) val matchResults = backStackMatchers.mapNotNull { matcher.match(request) } val bestMatch: BackStackMatchResult? = matchResults.maxOrNull() val backStack = bestMatch?.backStack ?: listOf(Home) \`\`\` \[14:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=882s) So, if we have multiple matchers, each one would have its own \`withBackStack\` call to build the appropriate back stack for that specific \`NavKey\`. \[14:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=891s) You'll get the cleanest code if every matcher you call uses the \`withBackStack\`, which will give you a list of back stack matchers. \[14:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=899s) And when you do find the best match, the match result you get back is a \`BackStackMatchResult\`. \[15:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=904s) This is a sub-class of \`MatchResult\` that adds a new property called \`backStack\`, which is the whole back stack generated by your \`withBackStack\` lambda. \[15:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=914s) This layering approach allowed us to decouple the logic inside the matchers from whatever custom logic you want to use inside your \`withBackStack\` lambda. ### Lightning round, summary, and resources \[15:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=924s) Now, this is a lightning talk, so unfortunately, we're just about out of time, but maybe we can go through a few of the other features that we have in navigation three that you'll find in our nav three recipes. \[15:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=936s) Okay. \[15:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=937s) So, you can add filters to any matcher to short-circuit the matching logic and quickly exclude the matcher based on action, MIME type, or your own custom filters. \[15:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=946s) And this happens before going through any URI parsing or custom serialization, Kotlin Serialization. \[15:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=952s) We also offer a \`StaticKeyDeepLinkMatcher\`, specifically for cases where you don't need to do any parsing to get your \`NavKey\`, but you still want to apply filters. \`\`\`kotlin @Serializable object ImagesKey: NavKey // custom filter val mimeTypeFilter = DeepLinkMatcher.mimeTypeFilter("image/jpg") val matcher = StaticKeyDeepLinkMatcher(ImagesKey, listOf(mimeTypeFilter)) \`\`\` \[16:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=961s) This is perfect for handling action- or MIME-type-only deep links, such as a photo-editing app that can handle opening JPEG images. \[16:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=970s) And speaking of action and MIME type, you can attach any custom \`RequestExtras\` to your \`DeepLinkRequest\`, which your custom filters and \`DeepLinkRequest\` subclasses can use as part of their logic. \[16:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=980s) This lets you mix in AB testing frameworks or external signals. \[16:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=984s) And we also have a whole type-safe APIs for the extras. \`\`\`kotlin val extras = requestExtras { put(SectionExtrasKey, "A") } \`\`\` \[16:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=988s) Oh, and just about all this logic is in Nav3's common KMP code, so all your matchers and back stack logic can be shared across platforms. \[16:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=997s) So, if you want to take a more leisurely look through how Navigation 3 supports deep links, check out our Nav3 recipes. \[16:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=1006s) Yes, and we've also integrated our deep link APIs into our DI recipes, as well as our hero app, NowInAndroid. \[16:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=1014s) Thanks for coming to our lightning talk, and happy navigating. \[16:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cgmY14gf4zg\&t=1016s) Thank you.</a>
entries.summary: This document introduces Jetpack Navigation 3's type-safe deep linking architecture for Compose, detailing how Kotlin Serialization, `DeepLinkRequest`, and `UriDeepLinkMatcher` enable robust, scalable, and multiplatform-compatible routing.

entries.title: Declarative, agent-ready Android builds with Lightbuild
entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring an embedded talk session and interactive transcript about declarative, agent-ready Android builds using Lightbuild from the Android Dev Summit.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/declarative-agent-ready-android-builds-with-lightbuild.txt" target="_blank">Declarative, agent-ready Android builds with Lightbuild - Speakers: Scott Myers (Developer Relations Engineer), Juan Sebastian Oviedo (Senior Product Manager) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/declarative-agent-ready-android-builds-with-lightbuild ## About the talk As Android apps grow and AI coding assistants become essential, using executable code to configure your build can create bottlenecks with slow sync times, fragile logic, and added complexity. Enter Lightbuild: Google's declarative, config-driven interface to the build engine, designed for modern Android development. In this session, we'll explore Lightbuild's new approach to managing builds and how to use it to build a demo app. Learn how decoupling build config from execution delivers faster project opens with lightning-fast sync in Android Studio, while offering a predictable schema for safer, more reliable AI editing. We'll also cover Lightbuild's agent-friendly CLI tools for creating reproducible builds across local machines, teams, and CI/CD pipelines ## Summary - Lightbuild is an experimental build system preview for Android apps that replaces executable scripts with purely declarative data files. It uses Gradle as its execution engine under the hood. - Declarative YAML configuration models project structure as a deterministic, static graph. This allows AI agents to inspect topology and safely modify modules or dependencies using a structured schema. - Fast IDE sync bypasses script evaluation by precomputing dependencies into checked-in \`resolved.deps\` files. These files can also serve as lock files during CI/CD builds. - Every project separates code into library modules while keeping application modules as empty shells. This structure accelerates builds and allows distinct application modules to represent flavors such as demo and prod. - A standalone CLI includes commands such as \`query\` and \`resolve\` that can output JSON for agentic workflows. Lightbuild is currently available in Android Studio Canary for experimental use. ## Resources - \[Lightbuild documentation\](https://goo.gle/lightbuild) ## Topics android-builds, lightbuild, android-studio, declarative-build, ai-agents ## Transcript ### Introduction to Lightbuild \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=6s) Hello, everyone. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=7s) My name is Juan Sebastian Oviedo. \[00:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=9s) I am a product manager in the Android Developer Experience team. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=13s) I'm here with Scott, and today we are excited to share with you an early look at Lightbuild, a new experimental build experience for Android apps. \[00:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=22s) I'll go over the context for this project, the philosophy behind it, and why we believe that now is the right time to rethink how Android projects are configured. \[00:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=32s) I'll also go over how this new approach sets us up for the future of Android app development. \[00:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=40s) Let's start with some context on how things work today. \[00:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=44s) Gradle and imperative build scripts give developers the ability to programmatically define almost anything about their builds. \[00:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=51s) You can, for example, have a logic that dynamically computes version codes based on Git history, or define a custom task that transforms assets. \`\`\`kts // build.gradle.kts android { compileSdk = 37 buildTypes { debug { // Custom logic in build script val commit = providers.exec { commandLine("git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD") }.standardOutput.asText.get() .trim() versionNameSuffix = "-$commit" } } } \`\`\` \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=61s) Alongside Gradle, there's AGP or the Android Gradle Plugin, which takes Gradle's general-purpose engine and adapts it to the Android toolchain. \[01:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=72s) Together, Gradle and AGP form a dynamic system that powers the build configuration experience for millions of production apps today. \[01:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=83s) Due to this flexibility, our development tools operate within a specific architectural life cycle. \[01:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=90s) When you open a project, you switch branches or you edit a build file, the IDE needs to have a clear map, a clear understanding of your project configuration, so it can power features like code completion and code navigation. \[01:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=104s) Because build files are written in an imperative, Turing-complete language, the only general way for the IDE to know what the configuration is for it to run the build scripts. \[01:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=116s) During IDE sync, the build system goes through a configuration phase. \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=120s) It evaluates your build scripts, it executes plugin logic, and it constructs the project model. \[02:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=126s) This aligns Android Studio's view of your project with your actual project configuration. \[02:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=134s) As developers, the thing you care about most is delivering a great Android app and getting it to your users. \[02:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=140s) However, managing build scripts, keeping AGP up to date, and keeping the project in sync with the IDE takes time and effort. \[02:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=150s) There are several initiatives across both Google and the broader ecosystem working to improve the developer experience in this area. \[02:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=158s) Initiatives like Declarative Gradle and the Kotlin toolchain aim to replace executable build scripts with declarative build configuration. \[02:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=168s) In Android Studio, we have the AGP Upgrade Assistant, which guides you through the changes needed to go from one version of AGP to another. \[02:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=177s) We also provide an upgrade skill that agents can install and follow to upgrade AGP. \[03:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=184s) Additionally, we are investing in areas like phased sync and resilient sync, so that developers have a better experience when syncing and importing their projects. \[03:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=195s) Each of these efforts targets a piece of the puzzle so that developers can spend more time creating their apps and less time building their projects, managing their build files, and syncing their projects. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=209s) Alongside this efforts, we asked ourselves a broader question. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=214s) What if we reimagined the way projects are configured from the ground up? \[03:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=219s) When we look at the way modern Android apps are architected today, we see a major shift toward heavy modularization. \[03:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=227s) Large code bases often have dozens, or even hundreds of modules: UI modules, feature modules, domain modules, and data modules. \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=237s) And while the root application might occasionally need custom packaging, the vast majority of those library modules follow a standardized repeatable pattern. \[04:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=247s) They don't actually need to have arbitrary executable code in their build files. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=252s) All they need is a clear way to state their structure and their dependencies. ### Core pillars of Lightbuild \[04:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=260s) That observation led us to create Lightbuild. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=261s) Lightbuild rests on two pillars. \[04:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=266s) First, it uses a declarative syntax for configuration, providing for a clear separation between build configuration and logic. \[04:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=274s) And second, it delivers a fast IDE sync experience through ahead-of-time dependency resolution. \[04:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=281s) I'll go over each of these pillars in detail so you can see how they impact your daily workflow. \[04:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=287s) Let's start with the pillar of declarative build configuration. \[04:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=292s) Take a look at the file on the left side of the screen. \[04:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=295s) This represents the configuration for a module today. \`\`\`kts // build.gradle.kts plugins { alias(libs.plugins.android.library) alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose) } val gitCommit = providers.exec { commandLine("git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD") }.standardOutput.asText.get().trim() android { namespace = "com.example.app" compileSdk = 37 defaultConfig { minSdk = 24 buildConfigField("String", "GIT_COMMIT", "\\"$gitCommit\\"") } buildFeatures { compose = true buildConfig = true } } dependencies { implementation(platform(libs.androidx.compose.bom)) implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui) implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui.graphics) ... \`\`\` \[04:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=299s) Because this file is executable code, it can have local variable definitions, calls to custom helper functions or convention plugins, conditional statements and in-line task definitions. \[05:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=312s) In order for the IDE to know what this configuration resolves to, it actually needs to run the script. \[05:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=318s) Now take a look at the file on the right side of the screen. \[05:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=322s) This is the Lightbuild configuration for a similar module. \`\`\`yaml # lightbuild.yaml group: "com.example" version: "1.0.0" platform: android type: library android: namespace: "com.example.app" compileSdk: version: release: apiLevel: 37 minSdk: version: release: apiLevel: 24 dependencies: maven: - androidx.core:core-ktx:1.10.1 - androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-ktx:2.6.1 - androidx.activity:activity-compose:1.8.0 \`\`\` \[05:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=325s) This file is purely declarative data. \[05:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=329s) There are no local variable definitions, no calls to custom helper functions and no conditional statements or inline task definitions. \[05:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=337s) It clearly states the type of the module, its SDK targets and its dependencies. \[05:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=344s) If a new engineer joins your team and they open this file, they will have no custom build idioms to decipher, and every Lightbuild module in every Lightbuild project uses the same immediately readable language. \[05:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=359s) While the separation between configuration and logic is great for human readability, it's even more transformative for agent-assisted workflows. \[06:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=370s) As developers adopt agents as part of their workflow, those agents need to be able to read and modify build configuration. \[06:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=377s) However, they don't have a way to predict the side effects of a configuration change other than by actually building the project. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=386s) Adding a single line to a configuration file could conflict with a dynamically computed variable elsewhere in the project or with a convention plugin. \[06:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=395s) In Lightbuild, your project's configuration is a deterministic, static data graph. \[06:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=401s) This means that agents can inspect that graph, understand the module topology and modify it using a known schema. \[06:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=410s) An agent can see the list of modules, the list of dependencies and their versions, update dependencies or even add a brand-new feature module simply by reading and writing structured data. \[07:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=421s) It makes your project's configuration a first-class citizen for agent-assisted workflows. \[07:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=429s) Another detail that I want to highlight at this point is the fact that Lightbuild is not a plug-in to a build system, but it is an interface to the build engine. \[07:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=439s) The version of Lightbuild, the preview that we're releasing today uses Gradle under the hood as its execution engine. \[07:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=446s) However, the architectural approach that we followed with Lightbuild makes it so that Android Studio, the IDE, sees and treats the project as a Lightbuild project. \[07:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=457s) Now let's go over the second pillar, which is all about developer productivity and flow: fast IDE sync. \[07:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=465s) Even as developers adopt agents as part of their workflow, Android Studio remains an essential tool for interactive tasks, for example, to review Compose UI previews or to step through code in the debugger as part of investigating an issue, or to analyze a performance with the profiler. \[08:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=483s) Because your project's configuration is a deterministic, static data graph, the IDE doesn't need to go through a script evaluation phase or to execute plugin code to understand your project. \[08:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=495s) Whether you open a project, edit a build file or switch branches, the IDE can process that information quickly and get you right to your tools. \[08:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=506s) One of the reasons this speed and reliability are possible is the way Lightbuild handles dependencies. \[08:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=513s) Normally, when you declare a dependency, the build system needs to go through a tree of transitive dependencies to gather version information and to resolve conflicts. \[08:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=524s) In Lightbuild, whenever your dependencies change, the tool automatically computes the transitive dependency information and writes it to a \`resolved.deps\` file inside of each module directory. \[08:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=538s) This makes it so that when the project is opened again in the future or it gets rebuilt, neither the IDE nor the build tool need to recompute that transitive dependency information. \[09:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=550s) We recommend checking these files into source control so that when you send changes to your teammates for review, they can, two things, they can see if there were any changes to the transitive dependency information, plus their machines will not need to recompute that transitive dependency information. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=567s) Additionally, by checking this information into source control, you make it so that you, your teammates, and your CI/CD pipelines can build with the same dependency versions every time. \[09:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=583s) We are thrilled to announce that Lightbuild is available as an early preview in Android Studio Canary and also through standalone CLI tools. \[09:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=592s) Please keep in mind that this version of Lightbuild is experimental, so it doesn't have all of the features that you need to build and maintain a production application. \[10:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=601s) Please continue to use AGP and Gradle for your production applications while trying out Lightbuild in demo and experimental projects. \[10:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=610s) You can get started today by going to goo.gle/lightbuild, and we look forward to getting your feedback so you can help us shape the product as it evolves. \[10:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=621s) Now, I'll pass the presentation over to Scott so he can show you Lightbuild in action. ### Getting started with Lightbuild in Android Studio \[10:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=627s) Thank you, Juan. \[10:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=629s) My name is Scott Myers. \[10:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=630s) I'm an Android Developer Relations Engineer, and we've been working on Lightbuild for a while and we're excited to show you how you can actually get your hands on it today and play with it. \[10:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=639s) So, the first thing you'll want to do is go to the link that Juan mentioned, goo.gle/lightbuild or just do a search for Lightbuild. \[10:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=646s) And it should take you to this documentation page that'll have all the steps you need to get started, including installing a Canary version of Android Studio, cause remember this is still in preview, it's not yet in the stable version of Android Studio. \[10:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=657s) And also, there's a Lightbuild CLI that you can install to get the full benefits of the agentic experience with Lightbuild. \[11:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=664s) So, once you have that set up, like I have here on my machine, I've got the latest Android Studio Canary running. \[11:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=671s) And now I'm going to step through actually creating a demo Lightbuild project and show you how you can do it, today, even. \[11:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=679s) So, first, I'll go to the New Project wizard. \[11:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=682s) I'll choose, the Empty Activity, hit Next. \[11:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=686s) And now you'll see that this is the normal, project detail screen, but at the bottom here, there's a new option. \[11:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=693s) Under build configuration language, you can choose Lightbuild. \[11:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=697s) And it'll remind you that this is experimental before you hit Finish. \[11:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0mYQtt2RfoQ\&t=702s) And you'll see that right away, our project is synced with the IDE and up and running, ready for us to work with. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/decoding-play-policy-ama.txt" target="_blank">Decoding Play Policy AMA - Speakers: Paul Hua (Trust \& Safety Google Play), Bohdan Kosenko (Trust \& Safety Google Play), Jan Kleinert (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OaZ-_hTaZIA - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/decoding-play-policy-ama ## About the talk An open and honest panel about Play policies to keep your app compliant and quickly published. ## Summary - Reviewers need working credentials to test gated areas such as subscriptions and paywalls. Add credentials in Play Console under Sign-in details, and ensure they bypass two-factor authentication or captchas. - App declarations in Play Console must match the manifests of active bundles across all tracks. Deactivate obsolete version codes so abandoned testing builds do not trigger policy rejections. - App developers are responsible for content produced by third-party generative AI and user data handled by SDKs. Use mechanisms to filter AI output and check the Google Play SDK Index. - Appeals let you communicate with real reviewers after rejections or request extra time to fix policy warnings. Do not resubmit an unchanged app, as repetitive rejections can trigger removals or suspensions. - The advance notice form in Play Console allows developers to submit proof of permission before publishing. Providing authorization documentation upfront protects your submission against impersonation policy rejections. ## Resources - \[Developer Policy Center\](https://goo.gle/play-policy-center) - \[Policy Bytes playlist\](https://goo.gle/policy-bytes-playlist) - \[Play policy insights in Android Studio\](https://d.android.com/studio/publish/insights) - \[Android entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/delivering-seamless-sign-in-and-digital-credentials-on-android.txt" target="_blank">Delivering seamless sign in and digital credentials on Android - Speakers: Chiping Yeh (Developer Relations Engineer), Tom Colvin (CTO, Apptaura) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/delivering-seamless-sign-in-and-digital-credentials-on-android ## About the talk As the industry moves away from passwords and physical wallets, delivering a modern user journey demands both seamless authentication and trusted identity verification. While passkeys establish secure one tap logins, switching devices remains one of the largest drop off points in user engagement. Learn how to reduce migration friction using the Restore Credentials API to meet the new Google Play Zero Tap Sign In standard. This session explores how a single integration with Android Credential Manager unifies passkeys, silent device restoration, and Digital Credentials, allowing you to verify identity attributes directly from the device and build an effortless, secure onboarding flow. ## Summary - Jetpack Credential Manager provides a unified API for passkeys and passwords. It handles the authentication interface and cryptographic operations without developers needing to write UI code. - Conditional Create lets apps upgrade password users to passkeys silently in the background after a successful password autofill. This opportunistically generates and stores a passkey without interrupting the user. - Google Play will require zero-tap sign-in by April 2027 to maintain full publishing capabilities. Apps can meet this requirement by generating a restore key using the Restore Credentials API. - The Digital Credentials API coordinates exchanges between credential holders and verifiers. Holders retain sharing control, while credential payloads stay end-to-end encrypted and inaccessible to Google. - Email and phone number verification replace one-time passwords and magic links with verified digital credentials. Users give consent directly in the Credential Manager bottom sheet without leaving your app. ## Skills - \[Restore Credentials skill\](https://goo.gle/restore-credentials-skill) ## Resources - \[Android passkey demo code\](https://goo.gle/android-passkey-demo) - \[Android identity code samples\](https://goo.gle/android-identity-samples) - \[Zero-tap restoration guide and policy\](https://goo.gle/zero-tap-restoration) - \[Digital Credentials sample app\](https://goo.gle/digital-credentials-sample) ## Topics android, credential-manager, passkeys, restore-credentials, digital-credentials, authentication ## Transcript ### Introduction and passkey overview \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=5s) Hello, everyone. of authentication and digital identity. \[00:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=15s) So, I'm Tom Colvin. \[00:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=15s) I'm CTO of Apptaura, and I'm a GDE on Android, and I'm joined by Chiping Yeh, who is a senior Android Developer Relations Engineer at Google. \[00:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=26s) The venerable password is dead. \[00:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=30s) Or, at least, it should be. \[00:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=32s) I'm going to talk to \[27:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1656s) This user has multiple SIM cards, and chooses one to share with the app. \[27:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1661s) Once the user confirms their choice, the exchange happens all in the background. \[27:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1666s) Then, you just see the next screen with the retrieved phone number populated. \[27:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1672s) The user never had to leave the app, and only had to select and confirm the phone number to share to progress through the flow smoothly, all in a few taps. \[28:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1684s) Just let this finish so you can see the completion one more time. \[28:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1690s) And so you see the phone number on that final screen. ### Resources and conclusion \[28:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1696s) And that's it. \[28:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1697s) We've covered a lot of ground today. \[28:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1699s) We first explored using Credential Manager to improve your passkey implementation, and move to a passwordless world. \[28:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1705s) Please see our resources on Credential Manager and passkeys here to get to learn more and get access to our sample apps. \[28:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1714s) Next, we covered the upcoming zero-tap sign-in requirement for your apps that makes it seamless for your users to sign in when setting up a new device. \[28:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1722s) This will be mandated in the Play Store by April 2027, so please note this on your calendars. \[28:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1731s) Finally, we covered how digital credentials work, and some of their most useful features on Android. \[28:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1736s) Please see our resources on digital credentials here for a deeper dive into the content and access to our samples. \[29:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1744s) Everything we've shared today is live and ready for you to build with. \[29:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1750s) The future of identity on Android is here, and more exciting than ever. \[29:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1755s) Thank you for your time, and I know it's lunchtime, so please enjoy the food outside. \[29:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1759s) And don't be afraid to come up to me or to Tom with questions about passkeys or digital credentials. \[29:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YqdfIR7NUl0\&t=1765s) Cheers.</a>
entries.summary: This document introduces strategies and APIs for delivering seamless authentication and digital credentials on Android, highlighting Jetpack Credential Manager, passkeys, and the Restore Credentials API.

entries.title: Elevate immersive experiences with 3D Engines in Jetpack Compose for XR
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript focusing on how to integrate 3D engines with Jetpack Compose for XR to create immersive experiences.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-immersive-experiences-with-3d-engines-in-jetpack-compose-for-xr.txt" target="_blank">Elevate immersive experiences with 3D Engines in Jetpack Compose for XR - Speakers: Luke Hopkins (Android XR Developer Relations Engineer), Joshua Lorett (Android Staff Engineer), Rodrigo Sanchez (Software Developer - Beyond Sports) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-immersive-experiences-with-3d-engines-in-jetpack-compose-for-xr ## About the talk Learn how to integrate 3D game engines (Godot \& Unity) with Jetpack Compose into a single codebase for mobile and Android XR. We'll explore embedding 3D scenes into spatial containers, setting up Kotlin-to-engine communication ---featuring an exclusive look into how the NBA built their live basketball experience on Android XR. ## Summary - The OpenXR Spatial Containers extension allows 3D engines to share space with native Android UI. Instead of taking over the skybox, real-time engines run inside a managed 3D volume alongside Jetpack XR spatial panels. - Developers can embed real-time engines directly into Jetpack Compose applications as AAR libraries. This approach lets native Android handle business logic and UI while the engine renders 3D components. - Embedding Godot requires an AAR dependency and an AAPT build rule to keep hidden assets. A \`GodotPlugin\` subclass then handles bidirectional communication with Kotlin. - Compose UI loops must stay decoupled from continuous engine tick loops. Blindly forwarding engine updates triggers constant recomposition and causes UI lag. - The NBA app integrates Unity as an embedded library in a separate process using AIDL for inter-process communication, protecting the host app from crashes. ## Resources - \[Android XR developer documentation\](https://developer.android.com/develop/xr) ## Topics android-xr, jetpack-compose, spatial-containers, openxr, godot, unity ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android XR \[00:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=4s) Hello, everyone. \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=5s) My name is Luke Hopkins. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=7s) I'm a developer relations engineer here on the Android XR team. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=11s) In today's talk, we're going to be talking about how you can embed game engines, such as Godot and Unity, into your Android project. \[00:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=18s) Later on, I'll be joined by Josh and Rodrigo from NBA and Beyond Sports, who will discuss how they've been implementing Unity as a library into their NBA application. \[00:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=28s) In this session, we're going to dive I'm going to dive into how to integrate Godot into your Jetpack Compose application as well, and then Josh and Rodrigo will go through their NBA application. \[00:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=39s) Android XR is an extension of the Android ecosystem, expanding upon a wide range of form factors to bring experiences you know and love into a new dimension. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=48s) We've made it intuitive to bring your existing XR and Android apps into this new space, and we're leveraging existing Android technologies that you're already building with today. \[00:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=59s) Android XR is a unified platform designed for a wide range of devices. \[01:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=64s) Android XR devices power different types of experiences. \[01:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=68s) We have augmented experiences for audio and Display Glasses, and then we have immersive experiences for XR headsets and wired XR glasses. \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=78s) Today, we'll be discussing building immersive experiences for wired XR glasses and XR headsets. \[01:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=84s) Creating immersive experiences can be done via our Jetpack XR SDK or using \`OpenXR\` with an with a real-time engine. \[01:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=94s) We support Unity, Godot, and Unreal so you can build your immersive experiences for Android no matter what tool you use. \[01:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=102s) In this talk, I'm going to explain how you can leverage Jetpack's \`SceneCore\` API, alongside Godot and a new \`OpenXR\` extension, to make this possible. \[01:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=114s) Here you can see Godot running side-by-side with Jetpack's spatial panels running at the same time. \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=120s) Notice how Godot is rendered as a spatial content, providing a 3D volume alongside 2D Compose UI within a spatial container. \[02:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=130s) This approach enables developers to run physics simulations, custom shaders using their real-time engine of choice, whilst applying native Android development practices to the rest of your application. \[02:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=147s) With Android XR and XREAL AURA, you too can create experiences like this. \[02:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=151s) And in this talk, we'll teach you how to build this experience using Godot and Android Studio, and then you hear from our partners at NBA and Beyond Sports on how they built it using Unity as a library. ### Spatial containers \[02:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=163s) Historically, building an XR experience with \`OpenXR\` has meant building an experience that renders every single pixel. \[02:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=170s) This means if a developer needs to display a second activity, they could not have both at once. \[02:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=176s) To solve this, Khronos, the OpenXR working group, in collaboration with several industry leaders, have released \`OpenXR\` Spatial Containers extension. \[03:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=185s) Think of Spatial Containers as \`OpenXR\` in a box. \[03:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=188s) Instead of your engine owning the whole skybox, it is granted a system-managed 3D volume that can live side-by-side with Jetpack's XR spatial panels, other Spatial Containers, and standard Android activities. \[03:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=202s) Let's say you want to make use of Android XR by displaying two spatial panels at once, whilst running an immersive game. \[03:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=208s) You render everything in the engine, and it makes it possible in these use cases to have the Godot editor and a spatial container running at the same time. \[03:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=218s) As of Spatial API level 4, Google has implemented Spatial Containers into Android XR. \[03:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=224s) Spatial Containers support two crucial display modes. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=228s) First is bounded mode. \[03:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=230s) This provides a defined 3D volume with several built-in avoidances. \[03:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=233s) A user can grab your spatial container, they can rotate it, position it, grab it, minimize it, and it supports stereo depth projection, giving you that magic window or that 3D pop-out effect that you have whilst clipping the container's edges too. \[04:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=250s) The second is unbounded mode. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=252s) If the user decides they want full immersion, your app can request a seamless transition from its bounded mode into full space mode, and then you can also drop back into bounded mode. \[04:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=264s) With the addition of Spatial Containers, Android Android XR opens the door for new and expansive ideas. \[04:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=270s) Let's say you want to bring your Android UI into your game, or maybe you want to create a custom shader for displaying 3D content in your application. \[04:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=278s) Before the introduction of Spatial Containers, it's impossible to have both Compose and a game engine running at the same time. \[04:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=285s) And when looking at application development in real-time engines, we've effectively lived in two different paradigms as well. \[04:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=292s) For native Android developers, your application runtime is a built around Jetpack Compose. \[04:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=296s) It's designed for rapid, reactive UI, battery efficiency, dynamic layouts, system accessibility, and seamless text input. \[05:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=305s) It idles when nothing happens, and it's predictable. \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=309s) For game engine developers, the domain is real-time rendering, where tools like Godot and Unity shine. \[05:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=315s) They don't just wait around for user interaction. \[05:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=318s) They run a continuous tick and render loop. \[05:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=320s) So this can be at 60, 90, 100 frame rates per second. \[05:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=324s) They do physics calculations, complex shader shaders, skeletal animations, spatial audio, and all of this with incredible performance. ### Approaches for integrating 3D engines \[05:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=333s) So what happens if you want the best of both worlds? \[05:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=335s) Previously developers had to implement one of these two approaches. \[05:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=339s) Option A is rewriting your entire application inside a real engine like Godot or Unity. \[05:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=346s) Throwing away your existing codebase means losing a lot of your native Compose UI, reimplementing basic text and navigation, and writing wrappers around Android APIs such as text-to-speech. \[05:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=357s) Option B is building a low level 3D graphics rendering pipeline from scratch inside your native app using raw Vulkan and \`OpenXR\` APIs. \[06:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=367s) Instead of delivering product features, you're essentially building your own proprietary engine. \[06:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=373s) So today I can show you how you can make the most of Godot as a library and Unity as a library. \[06:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=378s) And with this, the addition of spatial containers, you can now have the best of both worlds. \[06:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=384s) We can achieve this by embedding a real-time engine directly inside a library inside your Jetpack application. \[06:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=390s) You retain the production Android app structure, the business logic, and seamless rendering of 3D spatial content inside your application. \[06:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=400s) This also means you can have one APK for all form factors. \[06:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=402s) Where you don't just want to show 3D content, you can choose not to load the library into the activity or the fragment and keep your codebase clear, and allows you to support many devices. \[06:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=414s) The philosophy is straightforward, decouple the application and make the real-time engine a library. \[07:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=420s) Instead of choosing between an Android app or an engine, you treat the engine as an embedded software library, also known as an AAR dependency. \[07:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=428s) You pull this directly into your Gradle build, just like any other library. \[07:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=432s) Your native Android code remains the absolute brain of the application hosting the 3D components. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=438s) Jetpack Compose XR handles what it does best, rendering native accessible fluid UI and managing app state. \[07:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=446s) And when a 3D element is needed, the app hosts an embedded rendering view that's rendered by the game engine itself. \[07:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=452s) Today, we're going to deep dive exactly how this works under the hood for Godot. \[07:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=456s) And I'll start by the mechanics of embedding and establishing bidirectional communication between Kotlin and GDScript. \[07:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=463s) And then we'll look at the new \`OpenXR\` extension, Spatial Container, that will really unlock the new generation of multitasking and spatial layout. \[07:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=471s) Let's take a quick look at the demo I showed before. \[07:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=474s) I made this using Godot and Android Studio. \[07:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=475s) And this clip shows the Jetpack Compose for XR rendering native 2D UI spatial panels for our scoreboard and notifications and highlights. \[08:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=485s) And on top of this, Godot is rendering a simulation of a soccer match. ### Communication between Kotlin and Godot \[08:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=495s) Here you can see a breakdown of how we communicate from Kotlin to GDScript. \[08:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=500s) To do this, Godot provides a plug-in architecture. \[08:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=503s) You write a lightweight Kotlin class that extends a \`GodotPlugin\`. \[08:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=507s) This class serves as an interface between the JVM and Godot's C++ runtime. \[08:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=513s) Because of this, interactions between your app and Godot are very very lightweight. \[08:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=518s) Godot's architecture supports two-way communication between Godot and Kotlin. \[08:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=523s) When a game event occurs in Godot, such as a goal or foul, Godot can directly invoke Kotlin functions and update Compose UI in real time. \[08:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=534s) Then when the user interacts with the media player, let's say, to pause or select different highlights, Kotlin emits a signal back to Godot, and the corresponding game engine actions happen. \[09:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=544s) Once the Godot plug-in is crossed, performance and management simply falls along the domain lines. \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=549s) Apply the best standard practices for Android apps and the best standard practices for Godot projects. \[09:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=556s) Now we'll look at the architecture. \[09:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=558s) Let's look at how we wire this into Godot into an Android app. \[09:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=561s) The Godot engine runtime is distributed via Maven as an AAR. \[09:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=566s) Integrating into your build just follows standard Android practices. \[09:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=570s) There is one important step to be aware of straight away, and that is what I call the asset trap. \`\`\`kts androidResources { ignoreAssetsPattern = "!.svn:!.git:!.gitignore:!.ds_store:!\*.scc:_\*:!CVS:!\*\~:!android:!export_presets.cfg" } \`\`\` \[09:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=575s) In a Godot project, your scenes and project config- configuration files live together. \[09:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=580s) And when embedding Godot, the Godot project is added directly inside your assets folder. \[09:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=585s) So this means all the imported 3D meshes, compressed textures, and compiled textures, it all stores as a runtime artifact inside a hidden file called .godot. \[09:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=595s) By default, Android will strip out these strip out this folder when doing the build, so it ignores any directory with a dot period. \[10:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=604s) So if you sync and build your app normally, APK will build, but it will crash and load because those things have not been compiled into the APK. \[10:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=612s) So, to fix this, you can just explicitly override the AAPT options inside your build.gradle and allow for the leading dots to happen from Godot. \[10:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=620s) And once you do that, you can run your Godot scene once in the Godot editor, and from there you can build everything else from Android Studio. \[10:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=627s) In order to support spatial containers and the latest \`OpenXR\`, I recommend using Godot 4.8 and above, Godot vendor extensions 5.2, and the Khronos \`OpenXR\` loader 1.1.63. \`\`\`kts dependencies { // Godot 4.8 Android Library + Godot OpenXR Vendors plugin + Khronos OpenXR Loader implementation("org.godotengine:godot:4.8.0.dev-SNAPSHOT") implementation("org.godotengine:godot-openxr-vendors-androidxr:5.1.0-stable") implementation("org.khronos.openxr:openxr_loader_for_android:1.1.63") // Jetpack XR SDK (Compose for XR, SceneCore, Runtime) implementation("androidx.xr.compose:compose:1.0.0-beta02") implementation("androidx.xr.scenecore:scenecore:1.0.0") implementation("androidx.xr.runtime:runtime:1.0.0") \`\`\` ### Rendering Godot in Jetpack Compose \[10:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=643s) Once the assets are packaged, how does Godot and Compose actually render? \[10:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=648s) The Godot library provides a factory method called \`onInitRenderView\`. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun GodotView(godotHost: GodotHost, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) { // 1. Initialize Godot's native render surface val renderView = remember(godotHost) { godotHost.godot!!.onInitRenderView(godotHost) } // 2. Host the SurfaceView inside Jetpack Compose AndroidView( modifier = modifier, factory = { renderView } ) } \`\`\` \[10:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=652s) This returns a \`SurfaceView\` that Godot just renders to. \[10:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=655s) So, you wrap this in a Composable function, and Godot can now be sized, padded, and placed any- anywhere inside an entity panel. \`\`\`kotlin Subspace { SpatialPanel( modifier = SubspaceModifier .width(960.dp) .height(540.dp) .offset(z = (-200).dp) .movable() , ) { GodotView( godotHost = godotHost, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(), ) } } \`\`\` \[11:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=665s) The engine itself cannot manage the life cycle. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun GodotView( godotHost: GodotHost, modifier: Modifier = Modifier, lifecycleOwner: LifecycleOwner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current, ) { DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner, godotHost) { val observer = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event -\> val engine = godotHost.godot ?: return@LifecycleEventObserver when (event) { Lifecycle.Event.ON_START -\> engine.onStart(godotHost) .... implementation("androidx.xr.runtime:runtime:1.0.0") implementation("androidx.xr.scenecore:scenecore:1.0.0") implementation("androidx.xr.compose:compose:1.0.0-beta02") } \`\`\` \[24:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1450s) Next, let's see how we render Court View in Jetpack Compose. \`\`\`kotlin // Step 1: Request Full Space LocalSession.current?.scene?.requestFullSpace() // Step 2: A shared Subspace for NBA app content and embedded Unity Activity. override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?){ setContent { Subspace { SpatialPanel { AppContent() } // Court View val intent = courtViewFeature.intent val controller = rememberSpatialActivityPanelController(intent) SpatialActivityPanel(controller) } } } \`\`\` \[24:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1454s) Before we launch Court View, we bring you into full space. \[24:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1456s) This is required in order to display the spatial panel holding Unity. \[24:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1461s) Next, we send game information over AIDL to launch Court View for a specific game. \[24:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1466s) Unity itself is then started. \[24:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1468s) Our Android archive sends this as an intent to a Unity activity, and we wrap this in a SpatialActivityPanelController. \[24:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1476s) From there, we just pass that controller to a \`SpatialActivityPanel\`. \[24:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1481s) This panel is what holds Court View, and it's shared in our subspace with our main spatial panel. \[24:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1488s) This allows us to both control both of them at once without any issues. \[24:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1495s) And that's it. \[24:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1495s) I'll send it back to Luke. ### Conclusion and resources \[25:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1503s) Thank you very much. \[25:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1504s) As you can see, NBA was able to accelerate Court View by splitting the Unity and Jetpack Compose development. \[25:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1511s) To learn more on getting started with spatial containers and using it within your own Android XR apps, check out developer documentation on developer.android.com/develop/xr. \[25:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8dsUtPvOlY\&t=1522s) Thank you very much for joining us today, and we can't wait to see what you build.</a>

entries.title: Elevate your apps with the latest graphics features in Jetpack Compose and Android
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript focusing on the latest graphics features in Jetpack Compose and Android, helping developers understand how to enhance their app's visual performance.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-your-apps-with-the-latest-graphics-features-in-jetpack-compose-and-android.txt" target="_blank">Elevate your apps with the latest graphics features in Jetpack Compose and Android - Speakers: Rebecca Franks (Developer Relations Engineer), Aayush Chaudhary (Software Engineer), Rahul Ray (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevate-your-apps-with-the-latest-graphics-features-in-jetpack-compose-and-android ## About the talk Ready to take your Android UI from "it works" to "it's a work of art"? Join us for a tour of the latest graphics capabilities in Jetpack Compose. We'll show you how to build new visual effects, from delightful mesh gradients to progressive blurs, and using the powerful new graphics features in Android. We will also show you how to improve the performance of your graphics features, without sacrificing battery life or frame rates. ## Summary - Compose 1.12 introduces mesh gradients for rich multicolor blends across a 2D grid of vertices. On Android 14 and above, you can use the native drawMesh API to build custom geometry-driven visual effects. - Compose supports wide color gamuts to provide smoother gradient blending on supported hardware. Enable wide color gamut mode on your activity or window only when displaying rich media. - Compose 1.13 introduces native \`PolygonShape\` and \`MorphPolygonShape\` APIs for custom geometries. \`MorphPolygonShape\` reads progress during the outline resolution phase, updating shapes frame by frame without triggering recomposition. - Compose 1.13 adds progressive blur, while API level 37.2 introduces \`RenderNode.setBackdropRenderEffect\` for sampling background content. Developers can chain backdrop effects together to create frosted-glass or magnifying effects. - Optimize graphics performance by avoiding unnecessary work across frames. Decode only needed image pixels off the main thread and wrap animating effects in a \`graphicsLayer\`. ## Resources - \[Mesh Gradients Documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-mesh) - \[Understanding Color Guide\](https://goo.gle/understanding-color) - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[JetChat Sample App\](https://goo.gle/compose-jetchat) ## Topics jetpack-compose, android-graphics, mesh-gradients, shaders, blurring, color-gamut, performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to graphics features in Jetpack Compose \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=6s) Hi, everyone, and welcome to our session, Elevating Your Apps with the Latest Graphics Features in Compose and Android. \[00:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=12s) My name is Rebecca Franks, and joining me on stage today is-- \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=16s) I am Aayush Chaudhary. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=17s) Hey, I am Rahul Ray. \[00:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=20s) We are seeing an emerging trend in how you are all pushing the boundaries of what's possible on Android and Compose, using AI to really bring your incredible ideas to life. \[00:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=30s) And we love seeing apps that feel premium, native, and delightful. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=36s) We know that apps that feel good and consistently get great ratings from users are ones that generally take advantage of the latest system-level API changes, have continuity between surfaces with shared elements and blurring, they adapt delightfully across form factors, and are performant, and don't leave users guessing, and push the boundaries of what's possible with your device. \[01:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=62s) In this talk today, we're going to show you some of the latest features that help you take advantage of Android, from delighting users with mesh gradients, enabling wide color gamut support, delightful transitions with polygon shapes, what's new in blurring, and, finally, we'll cover how you can think about performance when adding new graphics features into your apps. \[01:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=82s) But throughout the talk today, we'll be covering some of the new APIs at different levels of the stack. \[01:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=87s) While the legacy view UI toolkit is in maintenance mode now, we continue to invest in the underlying Android graphics hardware rendering engines that power Jetpack Compose. \[01:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=99s) You can think of graphics in Android in three different layers: the Compose APIs at the first layer, and this is where all high-level, new UI graphics APIs, like mesh gradient painters, polygon shapes, and progressive blur APIs live. \[01:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=115s) And then we have the intermediate layer, where Compose's DrawScope, draw modifier nodes, and AGSL let you build custom effects. \[02:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=123s) But, finally, we have the Android platform, and Compose can always access a native Canvas and use brand-new OS rendering primitives right inside your Compose modifiers. \[02:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=134s) And we'll show you some of the examples of doing this today. \[02:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=137s) So let's get into it. ### Mesh gradients and custom mesh rendering \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=143s) So first, let's look at mesh gradients, a new API introduced in Compose 1.12. \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=148s) Previously, we have had linear gradients, previously, we have had linear, sweep, and radial gradients, which are great for simple transitions, but if you want rich multicolor blends like ambient backgrounds or floodlighting effects, you need 2D grid of system where, positions and colors can blend across space. \[02:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=167s) Now, to create a mesh gradient like this, first, specify how many rows and columns of patches you want. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { } } \`\`\` \[02:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=175s) And then inside the trailing lambda, call \`setVertex\` and assign a normalized offset ranging from 0F to 1F, along with a color for each grid intersection. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0f, 0.0f), indigo) } } \`\`\` \[03:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=185s) And then to animate those vertices, add animated offsets for eight ver-- vertices. \`\`\`kotlin val gradientPainter = remember { MeshGradientPainter(rows = 3, columns = 3) { setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0f, 0.0f), indigo) // .... setVertex(1, 1, Offset(0.2f, 0.4f) + Offset(animatedOffset, animatedOffset), coral) // .... setVertex(3, 0, Offset(0.0f, 1.0f), sunshine) // .... } } Box( modifier = modifier.padding(32.dp) .safeContentPadding() .aspectRatio(16 / 9f) .fillMaxWidth() .paint(gradientPainter) ) \`\`\` \[03:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=192s) Once your painter is defined, simply call it with any composable via a paint modifier. \[03:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=199s) Now, in the JetChat app, we added a feature to like a message when you double-tap on it. \[03:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=204s) To build this, we set up a 2 by 3 mesh and place our color stops across the component. \`\`\`kotlin MeshGradientPainter( rows = 2, columns = 3, hasBicubicColor = true, ) { // Row 0 (top edge, y = 0.0f) setVertex(0, 0, Offset(0.0000f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFFF6B6B)) setVertex(0, 1, Offset(0.3300f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFFFD6D6)) setVertex(0, 2, Offset(0.6700f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFE8C3FF)) setVertex(0, 3, Offset(1.0000f, 0.0000f), Color(0xFFE396FF)) // ... remaining vertices for Rows 0, 1, and 2 } \`\`\` \[03:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=211s) Notice that we set \`hasBicubicColor\` to true over here. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=214s) By default, colors interpolate linearly across triangles, which can sometimes leave visible patches. \[03:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=220s) Turning this on switches the shader to smooth bicubic interpolation so that colors can melt seamlessly into one another. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=228s) Now, what if you want to build an animated ambient glow like this behind the input box? \[03:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=235s) To approach an effect like this with mesh gradient, you need two things. \[03:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=239s) First, a smooth organic motion for the interior vertices and a way to soften the outer edges so that you don't end up getting a hard rectangle around the card. \[04:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=249s) So we start by setting up a \`rememberInfiniteTransition\` with two phase angles running slightly at different durations so that the motion feels organic rather than mechanical. \`\`\`kotlin val transition = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "userInputGlowMesh") val phase1 by transition.animateFloat( initialValue = 0f, targetValue = (2 \* PI).toFloat(), animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable( animation = tween(durationMillis = 2800, easing = LinearEasing), repeatMode = RepeatMode.Restart, ), label = "glowPhase1", ) val phase2 by transition.animateFloat( initialValue = 0f, targetValue = (2 \* PI).toFloat(), animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable( animation = tween(durationMillis = 4200, easing = LinearEasing), repeatMode = RepeatMode.Restart, ), label = "glowPhase2", ) \`\`\` \[04:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=260s) Here, we animate the interior vertices and we pin the outer rings, outer ring of the vertices with edges with 0 alpha. \[04:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=268s) Because the outer boundary is stationary and transparent, the glow naturally feathers out. \[04:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=273s) And, finally, we feed those animated offsets to our \`MeshGradientPainter\`. \`\`\`kotlin MeshGradientPainter( rows = 6, columns = 5, hasBicubicColor = true, ) { for (r in 0..6) { for (c in 0..5) { val offset = if (r in 1..5 \&\& c in 1..4) { val ampX = when (r) { 1, 2 -\> 0.048f 3 -\> 0.042f 4 -\> 0.028f else -\> 0.036f } val ampY = when (r) { 1, 2 -\> 0.028f 3 -\> 0.020f 4 -\> 0.022f else -\> 0.016f } val d = orbit(c, r, ampX, ampY) Offset( x = (baseU + d.x).coerceIn(0.04f, 0.96f), y = (baseV + d.y).coerceIn(0.05f, 0.95f), ) } else { Offset(baseU, baseV) } setVertex(r, c, offset, gridColors\[r\]\[c\]) } } } \`\`\` \[04:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=282s) The mesh gradient you just saw is drawn using \`drawMesh\` API on Android 14 and above. \[04:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=287s) So let's take a closer look at this API by building an effect from scratch. \[04:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=292s) For JetChat welcome screen, we want to draw a path that looks like a ribbon. \[04:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=296s) Notice two things here: the stroke width is not constant and the color runs along each stroke of the path. \[05:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=303s) Let's break this down and understand what we actually need to build this effect. \[05:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=308s) For each pixel, we need to decide whether to draw it or not and which color to use. \[05:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=313s) To figure that out, we need two distances. \[05:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=317s) The first value is how far a pixel is from center of the stroke. \[05:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=321s) The second distance is how far along the path a pixel is, from start to end. \[05:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=326s) This tells us which color to pick from the gradient and mixing in a little of the first value makes the color curve across the width. \[05:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=334s) So can we draw a gradient along a path using just path and paint? \[05:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=338s) So, yeah, we can. \[05:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=340s) That requires flattening a path into a list of short straight lines, which also gives distance along the path. \`\`\`kotlin val lines = remember { path.asAndroidPath().flatten(0.5f) } //... inside draw scope lines.forEach { line -\> //... drawLine( brush = Brush.linearGradient(...), start = Offset(line.start.x, line.start.y), end = Offset(line.end.x, line.end.y), strokeWidth = 30f, ) //... } \`\`\` \[05:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=347s) Then we draw each line with its own gradient. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=350s) It works, but each line requires a separate draw call and a paint object and the whole path still have a single width. \[05:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=358s) The other option is a runtime shader, but it only gets the pixels's position within the container bound. \[06:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=364s) It doesn't tell us what we need to draw this ribbon. \[06:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=367s) And like, we can't easily calculate it from pixels's position either. \[06:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=371s) Draw mesh gives us vertex shader for that. \[06:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=376s) So, what is a mesh? \[06:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=377s) A mesh is made of triangles with data at each corner and each corner is called a vertex. \[06:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=384s) Each vertex carries a small record of data. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=386s) Usually that record is it holds a position, but it doesn't have to. \[06:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=391s) The vertex shader read that record and computes the position from it. \[06:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=396s) Here, here's the path one triangle takes: The vertex shader runs for each corner, it calculates the corners' position, and any value we want to pass for pass along for each pixels. \[06:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=409s) Then the rasterizer find every pixel covered by that triangle and interpolates values from those three corners for each pixel. \[06:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=417s) Finally, the fragment shader runs for those pixels, use those interpolated values and calculated the calculate pixels's color. \[07:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=423s) That Let's see how we can write vertex and fragment shader with a simpler example, a straight line up with a pulse moving along it. \`\`\`text LineShaders.VERTEX uniform float2 uStart; uniform float2 uEnd; uniform float uHalfWidth; uniform float uTime; Varyings main(const Attributes a) { Varyings v; float2 dir = uEnd - uStart; float2 normal = normalize(float2(-dir.y, dir.x)); float along = a.corner.x \* length(dir); float pulse = (a.corner.x - uTime) / 0.18; float radius = uHalfWidth \* (1.0 + 0.6 \* exp(-pulse \* pulse)); float across = a.corner.y \* (radius + 1.0); v.position = uStart + dir \* a.corner.x + normal \* across; v.stroke = float3(along, across, radius); return v; } \`\`\` \[07:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=433s) The vertex shader takes a attribute as input and out returns a varyings. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=438s) Attributes are the data for single corner. \[07:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=440s) Here is just two numbers: its progress along the line, and which side of the line it is. \[07:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=446s) The varyings are then interpolated and passed to fragment shader. \[07:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=451s) We calculate the pixel distance from the start, and for stroke width, we use time to create a pulse pulse on the radius. \[07:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=460s) Then we multiply that radius by corner side, that gives us sign distance across the stroke. \[07:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=467s) As the GPU interpolate between those signs, the center lines become zero. \[07:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=473s) Finally, we calculate the corners' position, and we store all this value into a stroke varyings and pass them to the fragment shader. \[08:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=481s) Unlike runtime shader, a mesh fragment shader output a color via a parameter, and returns a position for sampling the paint if one is set. \`\`\`text LineShaders.FRAGMENT uniform float uLength; layout(color) uniform float4 uStartColor; layout(color) uniform float4 uEndColor; float2 main(const Varyings v, out float4 color) { float distance = abs(v.stroke.y); float coverage = 1.0 - smoothstep( v.stroke.z - 0.5, v.stroke.z + 0.5, distance); float side = distance / v.stroke.z; float4 ink = mix(uStartColor, uEndColor, clamp(v.stroke.x / uLength + 0.4 \* side \* side, 0.0, 1.0)); color = ink \* coverage; return v.position; } \`\`\` \[08:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=491s) Taking the absolute value of our across coordinate gives us pixel for pixel distance from center line. \[08:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=499s) We compare that distance to radius to get coverage, and for the color, we blend along the path of the line, and bend the gradient slightly towards the edge. \[08:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=509s) Multiply that coverage by multiply by that by a coverage, that's our final color. \[08:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=517s) On Compose side, we tie our shaders and data layout together with MeshSpecification object. \`\`\`kotlin val spec = remember { MeshSpecification.make( arrayOf(Attribute(TYPE_FLOAT2, 0, "corner")), vertexStride = 8, arrayOf(Varying(TYPE_FLOAT3, "stroke")), LineShaders.VERTEX, LineShaders.FRAGMENT) } \`\`\` \[08:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=523s) First, we declare our corner attribute as two floats starting at byte 0. \[08:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=528s) Since two float take 8 bytes, each corner stride in the buffer is 8. \[08:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=534s) Next, we declare our stroke stroke varyings as three floats, and we pass in the vertex and fragment shader we just wrote. \[09:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=546s) We build the ver- vertex buffer. \`\`\`kotlin fun lineCorners(segments: Int): ByteBuffer { val buffer = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((segments + 1) \* 2 \* 8) .order(ByteOrder.nativeOrder()) for (i in 0..segments) { val t = i / segments.toFloat() buffer.putFloat(t).putFloat(-1f) // one side buffer.putFloat(t).putFloat(1f) // the other side } return buffer.rewind() as ByteBuffer } \`\`\` \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=549s) At each step along the line, we complete the progress, we compute the progress from 0 to 1, and write two corners into the buffer. \[09:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=558s) Finally, we combine the spec and buffer into a mesh object. \`\`\`kotlin val mesh = Mesh( spec, mode = Mesh.TRIANGLE_STRIP, vertexBuffer = corners, vertexCount = (segments + 1) \* 2, bounds = RectF(0f, 0f, size.width, size.height) ) \`\`\` \[09:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=564s) Compose canvas does not expose \`drawMesh\` yet, so we drop down to \`nativeCanvas\` and draw the mesh.
