spec.blurRadiusPx.coerceAtLeast(0f) } surfaceView.setBlurRegions(listOf(region)) surfaceView.setBlurRegions(emptyList()) // Clear \`\`\` \[20:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1257s) This takes the list of areas of bounds, blur radius, alpha, and a list of corner radii on it. \[21:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1263s) When passing in these bounds, they must be relative to the SurfaceView on the screen. \[21:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1266s) So, you would want to keep track of the SurfaceView's coordinates and the area that you want to blur. ### RuntimeColorFilter \[21:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1273s) Another new piece from Android 16 and above is \`RuntimeColorFilter\`. \[21:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1277s) Previously, with images, you could only set a static matrix color filter and do effects like saturation. \[21:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1283s) However, with Android 16 and above, you can now pass in a shader that takes an in color, the input pixel for that particular content, and produces a new color. \[21:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1293s) For example, if we wanted to apply a cyberpunk filter for a for to a photo, we could define a small shader that's used as input into the \`RuntimeColorFilter\`. \`\`\`kotlin @Language("AGSL") private const val CYBERPUNK_SHADER = """ vec4 main(half4 in_color) { float lum = dot(in_color.rgb, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)); vec3 shadow = vec3(0.06, 0.04, 0.25); vec3 mid = vec3(0.92, 0.12, 0.58); vec3 high = vec3(0.18, 0.94, 0.98); vec3 col = lum \< 0.5 ? mix(shadow, mid, lum \* 2.0) : mix(mid, high, (lum - 0.5) \* 2.0); return vec4(mix(in_color.rgb, col, 0.7), in_color.a); } """ \`\`\` \[21:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1302s) This shader produces a cyberpunk theme, but you can do any other different effect that you want. \[21:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1308s) So, to use the shader itself, we apply the \`RuntimeColorFilter\` and convert it to a Compose color filter. \`\`\`kotlin AsyncImage( model = imageUri, contentDescription = filter.displayName, colorFilter = RuntimeColorFilter(CYBERPUNK_SHADER) .asComposeColorFilter(), contentScale = ContentScale.Crop, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize(), ) \`\`\` \[21:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1314s) As you can see in this example, we can now create more dynamic effects than before without needing to dive deeper into OpenGL, SurfaceView setups, or anything of that sort. \[22:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1322s) And this can also be applied to any composable, so not just images, as well. ### Graphics performance optimization \[22:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1329s) Thank you. \[22:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1330s) So, we have built some really nice effect, but let's make sure our app still feel fast and smooth. \[22:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1337s) When we scroll through the conversation, all of our effects are running together. \[22:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1341s) Let's start by measuring this scroll. \`\`\`kotlin @Test fun scrollFling() = measureScroll(swipeSteps = 5) private fun measureScroll(swipeSteps: Int) = rule.measureRepeated( packageName = TARGET_PACKAGE, metrics = defaultComposeScrollingMetrics(), compilationMode = CompilationMode.Full(), iterations = 5, setupBlock = { killProcess() } //... \`\`\` \[22:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1344s) We use a macro benchmark that launches an app in a fresh process and run the scroll through the conversation. \[22:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1352s) Then, we query the trace to count the frames that miss their deadlines. \`\`\`sql select count(\*) as late_frames from actual_frame_timeline_slice where upid = (select upid from process where name = 'com.example.compose.jetchat.perf') and jank_type like '%App Deadline Missed%' \`\`\` \[22:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1357s) That gives us six late frame. \[22:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1359s) Let's open one of the late frame. \[22:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1362s) So, right before this frame, Compose is prefetching next message before it scrolls up into the view. \[22:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1368s) Prefetch is supposed to fit into the short gap between frames, but preparing this message also decodes its image right onto the main thread, running long without yielding. \[22:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1379s) Because the main thread is stuck decoding this image, no new frames can start. \[23:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1385s) Then, when that message actually scrolls into the view, RenderThread has to allocate memory and upload all those pixels to GPU, so the same exact same image delays a second frame. \[23:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1398s) Now, we see where our time went, but do we even need all this work to draw this frame? \[23:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1403s) And how can we tell? \[23:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1405s) The trace tells us. \[23:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1407s) Whenever a large bitmap is drawn into a much smaller area on screen, Android logs a marker right into the trace. \[23:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1414s) It shows two numbers in pixel: the full bitmap dimension, and the area it actually covers on the screen. \[23:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1421s) Divide that by screen density and you got that value in DP. \[23:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1426s) Then, we search our code with that DP value to find that image. \[23:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1433s) This is what we find. \[23:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1434s) The image is loaded with \`painterResource\`, which doesn't know how big the container is, so it decodes the whole image at full resolution. \`\`\`kotlin Image( painter = painterResource(it), contentScale = ContentScale.Fit, modifier = Modifier.size(160.dp), contentDescription = stringResource(id = R.string.attached_image), ) \`\`\` \[24:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1442s) So, we replace it with \`AsyncImage\` from coil. \`\`\`kotlin AsyncImage( model = it, contentScale = ContentScale.Fit, modifier = Modifier.size(160.dp), contentDescription = stringResource(id = R.string.attached_image), ) \`\`\` \[24:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1445s) It measures the container first, so it only decodes the pixel it needs, and it does that work on a different thread. \[24:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1453s) Running the same benchmark again, image decoding on main thread dropped to 0, and late frame dropped to 2. \[24:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1459s) We won't be debugging those two frames here, but the takeaway is simple: try not to compute pixel that will never reach the frame. \[24:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1468s) So, image decoding was big enough to make frames late, but not every cost shows up as a dropped frame, and there are still smaller costs which we can avoid while writing the code. \[24:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1479s) So, let's see two of those. \[24:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1482s) Whenever we use a \`RuntimeShader\`, we should create it once because while it only compiles and get cached, it still parses its source string every time we create one. \[24:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1495s) And whenever an effect animates every frame, we can wrap it in a \`graphicsLayer\`, so the only animating element gets re-recorded, and instead of redrawing the UI around it. \[25:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1509s) For Jump to bottom button, it appears whenever we scroll. \[25:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1514s) This uses two \`RuntimeShader\` to show that effect, and every time the button appears, we recreate both, both of these shaders from its, their source string. \`\`\`kotlin val lensShader = RuntimeShader(MAGNIFIER_LENS_SHADER).apply { setFloatUniform("size", size.width, size.height) setFloatUniform("zoom", zoom) // ... val lensEffect = RenderEffect.createRuntimeShaderEffect(lensShader, "content") // ... val glassShader = RuntimeShader(GLASS_FINISH_SHADER).apply { \`\`\` \[25:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1524s) Parsing those two shader and building the effect takes hundreds of microsecond on main thread every time the button shows up. \[25:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1532s) Instead, we create the shader once for whole process, or we can remember it, and then updates its uniform. \`\`\`kotlin val lensShader = MagnifierShaders.lens.apply { setFloatUniform("size", size.width, size.height) setFloatUniform("zoom", zoom) // ... private object MagnifierShaders { val lens: RuntimeShader by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { RuntimeShader(MAGNIFIER_LENS_SHADER) } val glassFinish: RuntimeShader by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { RuntimeShader(GLASS_FINISH_SHADER) } \`\`\` \[25:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1539s) With that change, building that effect is nearly 40 times faster, and the cost when button appears drop by 20 times. \[25:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1549s) In the mesh gradient glow we saw earlier, the glow animates every frame inside the \`drawBehind\`. \`\`\`kotlin Box( modifier = Modifier .matchParentSize() .drawBehind { // Behind the card, scaled past its bounds. translate(top = -58.dp.toPx()) { scale(scaleX = 1.38f, scaleY = 2.85f) { with(glowMeshPainter) { draw(size, alpha = glowAlpha) } \`\`\` \[25:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1554s) So reading state in draw phase keeps composition and layout, but the display list cannot update a single draw command in place. \[26:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1564s) So Compose walks up the tree to find the nearest node with graphics layer, which here, is the red outline, which is whole screen, and re-records that entire layer every frame. \[26:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1575s) By putting a \`graphicsLayer\` right onto the box, the travel stops at the green outline, so the, so only glow box is re-recorded, and main thread drawing slice dropped by two-tenth of a millisecond. \`\`\`kotlin Box( modifier = Modifier .matchParentSize() .graphicsLayer() .drawBehind { // Behind the card, scaled past its bounds. translate(top = -58.dp.toPx()) { scale(scaleX = 1.38f, scaleY = 2.85f) { with(glowMeshPainter) { draw(size, alpha = glowAlpha) } \`\`\` \[26:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1589s) With Perfetto, analyzing what goes wrong in trace can be difficult, so you can use trace analysis skill to help you gather some insights. \[26:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1597s) And if you'd like more assistant in writing performant Compose code, be sure to install Android CLI and use Compose performance skill to get started. \`\`\`shell android skills add perfetto-trace-analysis android skills add jetpack-compose-performance \`\`\` ### Summary and resources \[26:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TirZPDPV8Dw\&t=1607s) If you'd like to see the examples we have demonstrated today, take a look at the JetChat app, available at this link.</a>

entries.title: Elevating camera experiences across devices with CameraX and on-device intelligence
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk session and interactive transcript about elevating camera experiences across devices using CameraX and on-device intelligence. It matters because it provides developers with key insights and resources from the talk to help build consistent, intelligent camera features on Android.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevating-camera-experiences-across-devices-with-camerax-and-on-device-intelligence.txt" target="_blank">Elevating camera experiences across devices with CameraX and on-device intelligence - Speakers: Aman Choudhary (Developer Relations Engineer), Scott Nien (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/elevating-camera-experiences-across-devices-with-camerax-and-on-device-intelligence ## About the talk Users expect third-party apps to capture photos and videos with the same high fidelity as their device's native camera, regardless of lighting conditions or hardware tier. Delivering this consistency across the expanding Android ecosystem comes with key architectural considerations. This session demonstrates how to construct robust, professional capture pipelines that maximize device capabilities while remaining reliable across all form factors. We will explore the latest advancements in CameraX, showing you how to integrate cutting-edge capabilities like Motion Photos and on-device AI enhancements through Google Play services, alongside spatial experiences using the Jetpack XR SDK. We will also look at our CameraX skill, which allows the coding agent of your choice to automatically implement the concepts in this talk, and more! ## Summary - Jetpack CameraX is the recommended camera library for Android apps as Camera1 is deprecated. Play policy enforcements will begin disabling Camera1 next year in Android 18. - \`CameraXViewfinder\` adapts camera previews across different form factors such as foldables. In CameraX 1.7, it adds gesture controls and Screen Flash support. - Audio \& Display Glasses run apps on a host phone while exposing cameras on both devices. Passing \`ProjectedDeviceContext\` allows CameraX to capture images directly from the glasses. - The Feature Group API helps apps select supported combinations of camera capabilities. Starting with CameraX 1.6, it supports combining 4K recording with Video Stabilization. - On-device machine learning analyzes camera previews and captured media through ML Kit and MediaPipe. Developers can run tasks ranging from real-time gesture detection to generative image descriptions. ## Resources - \[Camera talk resources and migration guide\](https://goo.gle/ads-26-camera-talk-res) ## Topics camerax, android-camera, on-device-ml, gemini-nano, mediapipe, ml-kit, android-xr ## Transcript ### Introduction and CameraX overview Run inference on-device and get the description val response = generativeModel.generateContent(request) val description = response.candidates.first().text \`\`\` \[18:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1102s) Yes, the next on-device ML library we have is MediaPipe. \[18:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1108s) MediaPipe offers a wide range of machine learning solutions for your applications. \[18:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1113s) You can quickly visit the MediaPipe website to try out different samples such as face detection, object detection, image segmentation, and much more. \[18:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1122s) All of these use cases sound very similar to ML Kit, so which library should you use? \[18:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1128s) While MediaPipe and ML Kit solve similar problems, there are few key differences. \[18:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1133s) First is platform support. \[18:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1135s) MediaPipe works across Android, iOS, Web, and Python, whereas ML Kit focuses only on Android and iOS. \[19:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1144s) Next, MediaPipe offers model customization, whereas ML Kit provides ready-to-use APIs. \[19:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1150s) And finally, while MediaPipe is open source, ML Kit is a Google SDK. \[19:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1156s) Here is an example of gesture recognition using the MediaPipe Vision APIs. \[19:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1161s) This API detects the hand gestures in real time from camera input. \[19:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1167s) This could be used, for example, to start or stop the camera recording using simple hand gestures while standing at a distance from the phone. \[19:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1177s) Let's look at the code. \[19:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1178s) So first, you need to build the \`GestureRecognizerOptions\` object, providing the model path, live streaming mode, and a result listener. \`\`\`kotlin // 1. Build GestureRecognizerOptions val options = GestureRecognizerOptions.builder().setBaseOptions( BaseOptions.builder().setModelAssetPath(MP_RECOGNIZER_TASK).build()) .setRunningMode(RunningMode.LIVE_STREAM) .setResultListener { result, image -\> /\* Handle detected gesture \*/ } .build() // 2. Create the GestureRecognizer val gestureRecognizer = GestureRecognizer.createFromOptions(context, options) // 3. Convert CameraX ImageProxy to MediaPipe MPImage val bitmap = rotateBitmap(imageProxy.toBitmap(), imageProxy.imageInfo.rotationDegrees) val mpImage = BitmapImageBuilder(bitmap).build() // 4. Run gesture recognition on the image gestureRecognizer.recognizeAsync(mpImage, frameTime) \`\`\` \[19:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1189s) Then create a gesture recognizer object from the options. \[19:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1194s) Next, get the CameraX \`ImageProxy\` and convert it into a bitmap, and use the bitmap to generate a MediaPipe \`mpImage\` object. \[20:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1204s) Finally, you need to supply the MediaPipe \`mpImage\` object to the \`recognizeAsync\` call to detect gestures in real-time. ### Image and video enhancement \[20:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1213s) Next up, we have On-Device Image and Video Enhance available through the Google Play services API. \[20:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1222s) This model provides capabilities like tonemapping, deblurring, and Super Resolution on most premium devices. \[20:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1231s) Here is an example of an image tone mapped and upscaled using this model. \[20:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1236s) You can clearly see the richer colors in the sky and the sea and improved sharpness in the enhanced image. \[20:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1244s) Let's look at the code for Image Enhancement. \`\`\`kotlin // Step 1: Verify device support \& install module val enhancementClient = Enhancement.getClient(context) suspend fun prepare(): Boolean { if (!enhancementClient.isDeviceSupported().await()) return false if (!enhancementClient.isModuleInstalled().await()) { check(enhancementClient.installModule().await()) { "Enhancement module install failed" } } return true } \`\`\` \[20:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1247s) First, you need to query whether the underlying device supports it or not, and if necessary, you need to install the enhancement module on your device. \[20:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1257s) Next, create the \`EnhancementOptions\` object by specifying the bitmap and the enhancements that you want to opt for. \`\`\`kotlin // Step 2: Select Enhancement options \& create session val options = EnhancementOptions( width = bitmap.width, height = bitmap.height, enhancementMode = EnhancementMode.BITMAP, isTonemappingEnabled = true, isDeblurAndDenoisePhotoEnabled = true, isDeblurAndDenoiseVideoEnabled = false, isUpscalePhotoEnabled = false, isUpscaleVideoEnabled = false ) val enhancementSession = enhancementClient .createSessionAsync(options, enhancementExecutor) \`\`\` \[21:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1265s) Next, create a client session with Google Play services API, then define a callback to handle your resultant bitmap, and finally call the process function with the bitmap and the options to enhance your image. \`\`\`kotlin // Step 3: Process Enhancement val enhancedBitmap = suspendCancellableCoroutine { continuation -\> val enhancementCallback = object : EnhancementCallback { override fun onBitmapProcessed(result: Bitmap) { if (continuation.isActive) continuation.resume(result) } override fun onError(statusCode: Int) { if (continuation.isActive) { continuation.resumeWithException( Exception("Bitmap processing failed: $statusCode") ) } } override fun onSurfaceProcessed(timestamp: Long) {} } enhancementSession.process(bitmap, options, enhancementCallback) } \`\`\` \[21:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1280s) We have recently integrated the Video Enhancement APIs into Jetpack Media3. \[21:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1285s) You can check out our media talk to learn more about the Image and Video Enhancement APIs. \[21:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1293s) The last On-Device ML feature that we're going to cover is Low Light Boost. \[21:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1299s) Capturing in low light is a common problem for smartphone users. \[21:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1303s) Think of users capturing image or taking video calls in dimly lit surroundings. \[21:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1307s) Low Light Boost solves this problem by brightening up your camera preview in real-time. \[21:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1315s) There are two variants of Low Light Boost: hardware and software. \[21:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1319s) The hardware version uses the OEM hardware to enhance the dimly lit frames without using machine learning. \[22:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1326s) Whereas, in contrast, the software version uses a On-Device ML model to enhance the frames. \[22:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1335s) Let's quickly take a look at how we can integrate CameraX with Software Low Light Boost, which is also known as Google Low Light Boost. \[22:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1344s) Google Low Light Boost requires two key surfaces: first, you need an in-- input surface for the raw camera frames and an output target surface for the enhanced output frames. \[22:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1357s) To integrate with CameraX, simply wrap the Google Low Light Boost pipeline inside a CameraEffect. \[22:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1363s) CameraX automatically handles the surface lifecycle and routing seamlessly for you. \[22:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1371s) Finally, we're launching the Low Light Boost Effect in CameraX in Q4 2026. \`\`\`kotlin // Integrates SW Low Light Boost val lowLightBoostEffect = LowLightBoostEffect( CameraEffect.PREVIEW or CameraEffect.VIDEO_CAPTURE or CameraEffect.IMAGE_CAPTURE ) val sessionConfig = SessionConfig( useCases = listOf(preview, imageCapture), effects = lowLightBoostEffect ) cameraProvider.bindToLifecycle(.. sessionConfig) \`\`\` \[22:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1377s) With this, you'd be able to create a Low Light Boost object and up- add it to your session config, then bind the session config to your camera lifecycle, and it just works on supported devices. ### Summary and migration \[23:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1392s) That brings us to the end of both the sections. \[23:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1395s) Let's quickly summarize what all we covered today. \[23:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1399s) Today we talked about how you can elevate your camera experiences across devices with CameraX and on-device machine learning. \[23:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1407s) First, with \`CameraXViewfinder\`, you can enable your camera previews to adapt to different form factors. \[23:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1414s) Next, we saw that CameraX enables you to capture on XR devices as well. \[23:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1420s) Then the Feature Group API helps you to find the optimal combination of hardware features. \[23:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1426s) We also explored upgrades to the Image Capture and learnt about High-Speed Video Recording for slow motion videos. \[23:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1434s) Finally, we learned how to enhance the Concurrent Camera preview dy-- dynamically. \[24:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1440s) Next, we looked at some of the on-device machine learning solutions such as ML Kit and MediaPipe for building intelligent vision experiences. \[24:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1450s) Finally, we saw on-device Image and Video Enhancement along with Low Light Boost for brightening up your camera preview in real-time. \[24:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1459s) As mentioned earlier, we are planning to disable Camera1, hence we highly encourage you to migrate to CameraX. \[24:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1466s) To support this migration, we recently launched the CameraX skill. \[24:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1470s) We also have a migration guide and the camera samples repo to guide you. \[24:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1476s) You can visit this link to access more resources about the features we covered today. \[24:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1480s) It includes link to documentation, blog, migration resources, all in one place. \[24:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1487s) I'll take a second, pause. \[24:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1489s) Okay. \[24:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1490s) Thank you, everyone. \[24:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-9hwgo10Q\&t=1491s) This brings us to the end of our talk.</a>
entries.summary: This new documentation page covers best practices for building robust and consistent camera pipelines across diverse form factors using Jetpack CameraX and on-device machine learning. It details recent architectural updates, including CameraX 1.7 viewfinder features, Android XR integration, and the upcoming deprecation of the legacy Camera1 API.

entries.title: Enabling seamless cross-device interactions
entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds the talk session and interactive transcript for enabling seamless cross-device interactions from the Android Dev Summit, helping developers learn how to build connected experiences across multiple form factors.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/enabling-seamless-cross-device-interactions.txt" target="_blank">Enabling seamless cross-device interactions - Speakers: Yacine Rezgui (Developer Relations Engineer), Hanrui Gao (Developer Relations Engineer), Nataraj K R (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/enabling-seamless-cross-device-interactions ## About the talk As users move between phones, wearables, and audio peripherals, delivering fluid cross-device experiences has become essential for engagement. However, relying on standard networking approaches often leads to battery drain, latency spikes, and fragmented user sessions. This deep dive introduces specialized Android APIs built for multi-device communication, offering memory- and power-efficient patterns to keep transitions between devices instant, reliable, and intuitive. ## Summary - Companion Device Manager replaces foreground services for Bluetooth peripherals by waking apps based on presence and managing connections without draining battery. Android 17 adds new profiles specifically for medical devices and fitness trackers. - Jetpack Telecom acts as a system call coordinator for VoIP apps across connected devices like watches and cars, working back to Android 8. It also synchronizes mute and hangup actions via CallControlScope. - Upcoming Jetpack Telecom 1.1.0 features include unified call histories in the system dialer (SDK 36.1+) and automatic 5G network slicing on supported carrier networks. - Quick Share SDK is launching next year so developers can embed local, end-to-end encrypted file sharing directly into Android and iOS apps. Tap to share (launched with Pixel 11) can even automatically wake a closed receiving app. ## Resources - \[Devices per person in 2023 chart\](https://www.statista.com/chart/32691/average-number-of-devices-and-connections-per-capita/) ## Topics cross-device, companion-device-manager, jetpack-telecom, quick-share, bluetooth, voip, peer-to-peer ## Transcript ### Introduction to cross-device interactions \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=5s) Hi, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=6s) Welcome to Enabling Seamless Cross-Device Interactions. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=11s) I'm Hanrui, and today I'm joined by my colleagues, Yacine and Nataraj. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=17s) When we talk about connectivity, what often comes to mind is a basic network link or Bluetooth headsets. \[00:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=24s) On Android, connectivity is much broader than that. \[00:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=28s) It's really about making devices work better together. \[00:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=33s) Today, we will walk through common cross-device scenarios and show you which API is right for each one. \[00:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=41s) For quite a long time, we used to build apps for a single device, phone only. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=48s) Then wearables took off. \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=50s) Soon it became very common to have a smartwatch paired with a phone, syncing data in the background or taking calls directly. \[01:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=60s) Add ear-- add wireless earbuds. \[01:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=63s) Now, users switch audio device mid-call, from watch to phone to earbuds or over to their cars. \[01:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=71s) More recently, many users also carry a second big screen device, like a foldable or tablet. \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=78s) They expect the app to work smoothly across these devices. \[01:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=84s) And that extends to laptops and Chromebooks, where user can run Android apps and stay connected right from their desk. \[01:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=94s) Even back in 2023, an average user owned between three to four devices. \[01:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=100s) Users expect more than just standalone functionality on these devices. \[01:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=106s) They look for an extraordinarily better-together experience. \[01:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=110s) That better-together experience is especially clear when people are in the same room like us today and want an easy way to share photos, links, or apps to the people next to them. \[02:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=126s) Looking at the numbers, the ecosystem is huge and growing fast. \[02:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=132s) In this year, there are around 22 billion IoT devices worldwide, growing 14% year-over-year. \[02:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=139s) And among all these end points, Wi-Fi makes up a third and Bluetooth makes up a quarter. \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=148s) Cross-device connectivity is no longer an edge case. \[02:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=152s) It's part of our everyday life. \[02:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=155s) Yet today, most apps still build their cross-device features on low-level network and Bluetooth APIs, which creates three challenges. \[02:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=165s) First, battery and memory. \[02:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=168s) Keeping background scans and services running drains battery and memory. \[02:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=173s) Second, latency. \[02:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=175s) Unpredictable delays disrupt real-time calls and data sync. \[03:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=180s) And third, connection friction. \[03:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=182s) Managing discovery, pairing, and reconnection across all devices is complex and easily leads to broken user experience. \[03:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=192s) To get rid of those headaches, we've built purpose-built APIs across three major areas to make cross-device features really simple. \[03:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=202s) I'll start with companion apps, and then Nataraj will cover VoIP apps, and later Yacine will talk about P2P sharing. ### Overview of companion apps \[03:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=212s) Let's take a look at companion apps first. \[03:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=215s) A companion app is an app you install on your phone so that a companion device, like a smartwatch or glucose sensor, can work well with it. \[03:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=226s) In this section, we will focus on Bluetooth-connected devices. \[03:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=231s) There are typically four categories of companion devices. \[03:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=235s) First, medical devices, like glucose sensors and vital signs monitors. \[04:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=242s) And wearables, like smartwatch and fitness bands. \[04:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=248s) Headsets, with Fast Pairing and smart controls. \[04:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=251s) And car kits, for things like digital car keys and hands-free calling. \[04:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=258s) Each category has its own key user journeys, but for all of them, they all depend on a reliable connection between the device and the phone. \[04:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=268s) For medical devices, that connection can even be life-critical. \[04:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=273s) Let's walk through four common needs we see across these categories. \[04:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=278s) First, device management. \[04:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=281s) The app needs to find the right device among everything nearby, like the watch here, not the earbud or the speaker, and then start the pairing flow to connect. \[04:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=294s) Second, presence checking. \[04:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=296s) The app needs to know when the device is nearby and when it's gone. \[05:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=300s) And when the device shows up, the app needs a way to be woken up so it can do its job even the user hasn't opened it. \[05:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=311s) Third, connection maintenance. \[05:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=313s) Once connected, apps want the connection to be reliable and persistent. \[05:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=320s) If the connection drops, say the user walks out of range and then comes back, the app needs to reconnect automatically, even it is not running at that time. \[05:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=333s) And fourth, data sync and transfer. \[05:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=337s) This is where the real value is. \[05:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=340s) Syncing sensor readings, pushing firmware updates, or sending settings to the device. \[05:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=346s) For medical devices, this can be critical. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=350s) A missed reading can mean a missed alert. \[05:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=354s) All of these need the app process to be alive and connected at the right time. \[06:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=362s) So, how have apps met all these needs? \[06:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=365s) Traditionally, apps relied heavily on foreground service. \[06:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=370s) Here is a typical implementation. \[06:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=372s) If you have ever built a companion app before, this may look familiar. \[06:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=377s) You declare Bluetooth scan and connect permissions, foreground service permissions, and foreground service type of connected device, and then notification permission because a foreground service has to show a persistent notification. \`\`\`xml \`\`\` \[06:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2-EfHHa_NxE\&t=394s) Then you run a sticky entries.title: Evolving Tiles to Wear Widgets using Jetpack Glance and Remote Compose
entries.summary: Added a new developer summit talk document detailing how to evolve Wear OS tiles into widgets using Jetpack Glance and Remote Compose. This provides developers with essential insights and modern tooling strategies for building watch face UI components.

entries.title: Evolving Tiles to Wear Widgets using Jetpack Glance and Remote Compose - Speakers: François Deschênes (Product Manager), Yuri Schimke (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/evolving-tiles-to-wear-widgets-using-jetpack-glance-and-remote-compose ## About the talk In this session, we will take a technical deep dive into the evolution from full-screen Tiles to dynamic, partial-height Wear Widgets. We will explore the technical benefits of the unified Jetpack Glance API and the new Remote Compose engine, detailing how they seamlessly align with Modern Android Development. Finally, we will share the latest UX guidance and walk through practical migration strategies to help you build the next generation of glanceable UI. ## Summary - Wear OS is evolving full-screen Tiles into Wear Widgets built with Jetpack Glance and powered by Remote Compose. - Remote Compose shares the same compiler and runtime as Jetpack Compose UI while safely decoupling your UI from the app process. - Small and large container sizes align with mobile grid formats, while Jetpack Glance Wear APIs maintain backward compatibility down to Wear 4. - Migrating existing Tiles to widgets can use either a recommended dual-service strategy or a single compatibility service. ## Skills - \[Tiles to widgets migration skill\](https://goo.gle/skills-repo) ## Resources - \[Tile to widget service migration\](https://goo.gle/wearos-tiles-widgets-migration) - \[Horologist media sample app\](https://goo.gle/media-sample) - \[Wear Widgets getting started guide\](https://goo.gle/wear-widgets) ## \[04:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=270s) With dual service, which we recommend, you'll keep your existing TileService for older Wear OS devices and add a new GlanceWearWidgetService for Wear OS 7+. \[04:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=283s) In contrast, with the single service, you create a new, single GlanceWearWidgetService that handle both protocols, running in a compatibility mode to translate your widget into a Tile on older devices. \[04:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=297s) Either way, you'll continue to reach your users. \[05:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=300s) It just affects what code you maintain going forward. \[05:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=306s) And we've just published comprehensive documentation on the Android developer site detailing exactly how and when to use both these patterns. \[05:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=315s) Check it out to learn more about which strategy is best for your app. ### Building UI with Remote Compose \[05:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=322s) Now let's talk about the UI layer. \[05:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=325s) When migrating, your mental model shifts. \[05:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=327s) Previously, tiles use ProtoLayout, a library built exclusively for Wear tiles. \[05:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=333s) Wear Widgets, on the other hand, builds on Remote Compose. \[05:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=337s) Remote Compose shares exact the same foundation as Jetpack Compose UI, using the same core compiler and runtime. \[05:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=345s) And it's designed to feel familiar, closely matching Compose UI libraries like foundation and Material 3. \[05:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=353s) But instead of a box, column, or text, you'll simply swap them for \`RemoteBox\`, \`RemoteColumn\`, or \`RemoteText\`. \[06:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=362s) You'll get familiar with writing "remote" a lot in this case. \[06:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=368s) Plus to speed up your workflow, we've included a full set of ready-to-use Remote Compose components designed specifically for widgets. \[06:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=377s) This means your existing Wear Material 3 designs, including what you've got in Figma, can be easily adapted to widgets, making this familiar to both engineers and designers. \[06:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=391s) To see just how aligned these frameworks are, let's look at a concrete example. \[06:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=395s) We're going to build our own app component on top of Material 3 switch button. \[06:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=400s) On the left, we have the standard Wear Compose component you'd write inside your app, and on the right is the Remote Compose version. \`\`\`kotlin // Wear Compose @Composable fun HistoryEraserButton( onClick: () -\> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier, checked: Boolean = true, onCheckedChange: (Boolean) -\> Unit = {}, ) \`\`\` \`\`\`kotlin // Wear RemoteCompose @RemoteComposable @Composable fun RemoteHistoryEraserButton( onClick: Action, modifier: RemoteModifier = RemoteModifier, checked: RemoteBoolean = true.rb, onCheckedChange: Action = Action.Empty, ) \`\`\` \[06:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=412s) Notice how similar the patterns are. \[06:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=415s) When writing Remote Compose code, however, you'll use the \`RemoteComposable\` annotation. \[07:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=422s) And where you use familiar params like modifier and boolean, they have equivalent Remote Compose types like \`RemoteModifier\` and \`RemoteBoolean\`. \[07:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=435s) And you use actions instead of lambdas. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=438s) Instead of defining the execute to the code to execute inside the lambda, you'll need to declare an action such as launching a pending intent, calling a service, or updating a value. \[07:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=452s) Let's jump to the body of our component. \[07:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=455s) You'll notice even the theming is aligned. \[07:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=459s) You can apply your Material 3 color scheme to the Remote Compose component exactly as you would in standard Compose, which lets your widget exactly match your app's branding. \`\`\`kotlin // Wear Compose val colors = MaterialTheme.colorScheme SplitSwitchButton( checked = checked, onCheckedChange = onCheckedChange, toggleContentDescription = "Arm Eraser", onContainerClick = onClick, modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth(), colors = SwitchButtonDefaults.splitSwitchButtonColors( checkedContainerColor = colors.errorContainer, ... ), label = { Text("History Eraser") }, secondaryLabel = { Text("Don't touch it!") }, ) \`\`\` \`\`\`kotlin // Wear RemoteCompose val colors = RemoteMaterialTheme.colorScheme RemoteSplitSwitchButton( checked = checked, onCheckedChange = onCheckedChange, toggleContentDescription = "Arm Eraser".rs, onContainerClick = onClick, modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth(), colors = RemoteSplitSwitchButtonDefaults.splitSwitchButtonColors( checkedContainerColor = colors.errorContainer, ... ), label = { RemoteText("History Eraser".rs) }, secondaryLabel = { RemoteText("Don't touch it!".rs) }, ) \`\`\` \[07:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=473s) And finally, let's see the result. The resulting UI is exactly what you'd expect, a clean, responsive, animated toggle button. ### Compose preview support for widgets \[08:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=484s) It's hard to tell the difference. \[08:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=488s) To help you design, iterate, and verify your widget layouts without always running on a device or emulator, we've added Compose preview support for Wear Widgets. \[08:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=500s) Because widgets depend on OEM specific container constraints, such as size, shape, padding, corner radius, we build on the standard preview annotation, but with an additional parameter provider to inject these configurations. \`\`\`kotlin @Preview(name = "Squircle Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetSquirclePreview( @PreviewParameter(SquircleAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) @Preview(name = "Round Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetRoundPreview( @PreviewParameter(RoundAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) \`\`\` \[08:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=518s) The library provides preconfigured \`PreviewParameter\` provider implementations that match real-world Wear OS devices. \[08:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=530s) These preview annotations let you easily verify your layout across very various different hardware shapes. \[08:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=538s) Beyond testing your layouts, you can use these previews to generate the static images required for the on-device widget picker. \`\`\`kotlin @Preview(name = "Widget Picker Preview", device = "spec:width=1000dp,height=1000dp,dpi=320") @Composable fun WeatherWidgetRectangularPreview( @PreviewParameter(RectangularAllWidgetPreviewParams::class) params: WearWidgetParams ) = WearWidgetPreview(MockWeatherWidget(65, WeatherCondition.CLOUDY), params) \`\`\` \[09:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=545s) The library provides a parameter for rectangular preview shape which emulates the full uncropped rectangular containers. ### Sample implementation and migration tools \[09:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=557s) And if you want to see how exactly this works in practice, we've refreshed our Horologist media sample app to include a new widget that showcases this API. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=567s) We show how to add both the small and large versions of the media widget. \[09:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=575s) Check it out on GitHub to see side-by-side the comparison of the legacy ProtoLayout code and the new Remote Compose implementation. \[09:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=583s) We're sure you'll like it. \[09:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=587s) Finally, this wouldn't be a, you know, a talk without mentioning AI. \[09:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=592s) To speed up your migration, we've published a new tiles to widgets migration skill on GitHub. \[09:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=598s) You can use it with your agent of choice, or you can add it directly to Android Studio using the Android CLI. \`\`\`shell android skills add wear-widgets android skills add --all \`\`\` \[10:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=604s) Now I'll hand you back to François to wrap things up. ### Summary and wrap-up \[10:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=612s) Thank you. \[10:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=612s) Thank you, Yuri. \[10:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=613s) So as you can see, evolving your tiles into Wear Widgets is a very straightforward process. \[10:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=619s) To recap, by migrating to Jetpack Glance Wear and Remote Compose, you are not simply updating your UI, you are joining a more unified Android widgets ecosystem. \[10:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=631s) You can now build beautiful, backward compatible widgets using a modern, declarative framework fully aligned with Jetpack Compose. \[10:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=640s) You can start migrating your tiles today by heading over to the Getting Started guide on Android Developers site for more-- for all the details. \[10:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=650s) We look forward to seeing all the expressive, glanceable experiences you build for the wrist. \[10:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=655s) Thank you very much for joining us today, this morning, and we hope you enjoy the rest of the conference. \[11:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5--1viVciq4\&t=661s) Thank you.
entries.summary: This document introduces the evolution of full-screen Wear OS Tiles into partial-height Wear Widgets powered by Jetpack Glance and Remote Compose, providing developers with familiar declarative APIs, migration strategies, and backward compatibility guidelines.

entries.title: Extend your app to Gemini and Search with the Connected Apps Platform
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript explaining how developers can extend their apps to Gemini and search using the Connected Apps platform.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/extend-your-app-to-gemini-and-search-with-the-connected-apps-platform.txt" target="_blank">Extend your app to Gemini and Search with the Connected Apps Platform - Speakers: Kateryna Semenova (Staff Developer Relations Engineer), Mai Lowe (Group Product Manager) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-4G-4w9FKDw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/extend-your-app-to-gemini-and-search-with-the-connected-apps-platform ## About the talk The new Connected Apps Platform lets you integrate your app's services directly into Gemini, AI Mode in Search, and the Android intelligence system. This session provides a practical guide to getting started. Using code examples and learning from real-life case studies, we'll walk through the development lifecycle: building, testing, and publishing your first connected app to reach users within their AI-powered workflows. By the end of this session, you'll be able to: - Integrate your service with the Connected Apps Platform. - Test your integration across different AI surfaces. - Publish your app's features into users' AI workflows. ## Summary - The Connected Apps Platform provides a single entry point to launch app capabilities across Gemini and Search using declarative schemas. It will open in phases, starting with a preview for US developers. - Integrations use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard through either remote servers or local on-device servers via the AppFunctions Jetpack library. Remote servers can also return custom UI rendered inside an iframe. - Confirmations scale with risk to protect user trust. Developers mark tools as read-only or with \`destructiveHint\`, helping Gemini ask for explicit confirmation when actions modify or delete data. - Gemini Developer Mode lets you inspect tool calls and latency against public endpoints. It is available now to developers in the US. - Google Connected Console handles the production rollout for approved developers. You configure endpoints, manage testers across selected surfaces, and submit your app for review. ## Resources - \[Connected Apps preview sign-up\](https://developers.google.com/connected-apps) - \[AppFunctions integration guide\](https://developer.android.com/ai/appfunctions) ## Topics gemini, search, connected-apps, mcp, appfunctions, android ## Transcript ### Introduction entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-gemini-nano-and-gemma-4-powering-on-device-intelligence.txt" target="_blank">Inside Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 powering on-device intelligence - Speakers: Sara Smoot (Engineering Lead Gemma) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ekS4_gV6Ojc - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-gemini-nano-and-gemma-4-powering-on-device-intelligence ## About the talk Gemma 4 brings capable, multimodal AI directly to Android devices. In this session, we'll trace how Gemma evolved into a model family built for efficiency and explore what the edge-optimized E2B and E4B models can do on-device, from vision and audio understanding to agentic function calling. We'll cover the architecture behind that efficiency, including Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), and show how Gemma and Gemini Nano work together through AICore. You'll learn how Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) preserves model capability within 1.1--3.5 GB RAM footprints, while Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) accelerates decoding speeds 1.5x--3x for responsive, real-time experiences. ## Summary - Gemma 4 models expand on-device multimodal capabilities with 128K-token context on E2B/E4B under an Apache 2 license. - Multi-token prediction drafter models cut decode latency by 40% and save 30% to 40% energy. They share the base model's KV cache to avoid regenerating prefills. - Quantization-aware training compresses the custom mobile quantization checkpoint to under 1 GB using targeted 2-bit quantization. - Android applications can integrate the models hands-off through AICore as Gemini Nano 4, or bundle them with LiteRT for custom fine-tunes. ## Resources - \[Gemma 4 model card\](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/model_card_4) - \[Gemini Nano on Android\](https://developer.android.com/ai/gemini-nano) - \[Gemma 4 on Hugging Face\](https://huggingface.co/collections/google/gemma-4) - \[Gemma 4 on Kaggle\](https://kaggle.com/models/google/gemma-4) ## Topics gemini-nano, gemma-4, on-device-ai, mobile-ml, aicore, litert, entries.title: Inside the first wave on Googlebook with Notability and Logitech
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk session detailing the first wave of app optimization on Google tablets and foldables with Notability and Logitech. It matters because it provides developers with real-world insights and strategies for adapting Android apps to large screens and stylus inputs.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-the-first-wave-on-googlebook-with-notability-and-logitech.txt" target="_blank">Inside the first wave on Googlebook with Notability and Logitech - Speakers: Emilie Roberts (Developer Relations Engineer), Ryan Shea (Head of Android), Joe Yezhou Wang (Engineering manager at Logitech) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aZjbDY3UXws - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/inside-the-first-wave-on-googlebook-with-notability-and-logitech ## About the talk The launch of Googlebook opens up a new frontier for high-fidelity, desktop-grade experiences. In this session, we go behind the scenes with two pioneering partners who built for this platform from the ground up. Notability will share their journey creating a desktop-class Android app using Jetpack Compose. Learn about their journey moving from other app platforms with desktop top-of-mind. Second, Logitech will dive into the hardware side, discussing how they are building and customizing peripherals to integrate seamlessly with Googlebook. Join the session to get practical, real-world insights on optimizing inputs, leveraging large-screen APIs, and delivering a premium, cohesive user experience across hardware and software. ## Summary - Jetpack Compose and Navigation 3 make it easy to adapt layouts across devices based on available window size rather than device form factors. - Desktop-class experiences require supporting multi-input models such as keyboards and trackpads. Features like Continue On in Android 17 also let users hand off tasks between devices. - Jetpack Ink gives developers a low-latency drawing pipeline without having to manage custom rendering threads or complex layer handoffs. - The allowlisted Peripheral Customization API lets developers map peripheral hardware triggers to OS actions using vendor and product IDs. ## Topics googlebook, entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/insights-into-agent-code-generation-from-android-bench.txt" target="_blank">Insights into agent code generation from Android Bench - Speakers: Tomáš Mlynarič (Android DevRel) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/insights-into-agent-code-generation-from-android-bench ## About the talk AI models can generate entire features in minutes, but is the code correct? We built Android Bench, our AI evaluation benchmark, to answer this question after analyzing thousands of generated code changes. This talk shares insights from our journey, including all the ways we saw models cheats, how prompt specificity leads to higher code quality and how different agents approach the same task. ## Summary - Android Bench 2.0 uses closed-source tasks to prevent contamination and evaluate AI coding agents on complex Android development work. - Evaluation relies on implementation-agnostic UI tests and a Multimodal LLM Judge instead of brittle unit tests or strict pixel-diffing. - Built-in cheating detectors catch agent shortcuts such as test tampering or fake background drawables. Any detected shortcut results in an immediate failing grade. - Cost per task varies widely from advertised token prices because talkative models burn more tokens by repeatedly rebuilding and rerunning. - Frontier models achieve around 80% completion rates but pass only 20% to 40% of tasks due to subtle flaws. ## Resources - \[Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities\](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified) - \[Android Bench leaderboard and benchmarks\](https://d.android.com/bench) ## Topics android-bench, benchmarking, llm-evaluation, code-generation, ai-agents ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android Bench \*\*Tomáš Mlynarič\*\* \[00:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=4s) Morning, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=6s) Let's get this started. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=7s) In March, we launched Android Bench, our data set and leader board on measuring LLMs on Android development tasks. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=16s) Since then, we've run it against many new models. \[00:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=19s) And just last month, we released Android Bench 2.0. \[00:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=23s) While it's only been a couple of months, in the world of AI, that feels like eternity. \[00:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=28s) My name is Tomáš, and I'm going to share our journey of Android Bench and how we got where we are now. \[00:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=35s) Let's start with 1.0. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=36s) In 1.0, we took real-world problems from open-source repositories. \[00:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=42s) We filtered the GitHub projects with GitHub issues, pull requests solving those issues and tests verifying the solutions. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=52s) We split the pull requests into task buckets for AI models. \[00:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=56s) The GitHub issue became the instructions for the, or the prompt for the model, and we planted them in the state before the PR. \[01:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=65s) And once the model created some work, we took the tests and applied them to the output, which gave us either passed or failed outcome. \[01:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=74s) This one attempt of AI trying to solve it, we call a trial. \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=78s) And we could also compare it based on the human crafted solution from that PR, or we call it the golden solution. \[01:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=86s) This methodology is similar to quite known SWE-bench benchmark. \[01:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=92s) We started with over 10,000 potential tasks, and not all of them were good fit. \[01:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=97s) Some had incomplete instructions or overspecified instructions. \[01:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=103s) The tests fair tasks. \[01:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=116s) During those reviews, we used the state-of-the-art models to get some results. \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=120s) And we started with around 30% tasks solved, which we call a pass rate. \[02:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=128s) And then, when we locked the data set for the official release, the top models were already at around 70%. \[02:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=136s) But that's like a month later. \[02:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=139s) And then we had a plan to evaluate new models every month, and then we watched how they are getting better. \[02:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=149s) And in August release, 92% pass rate was for the best model. \[02:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=155s) And we knew that our bar is too low, and this data set is saturated. ### Introducing Android Bench 2.0 \*\*Tomáš Mlynarič\*\* \[02:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=160s) But we anticipated that, and we're already hard at work on 2.0, which we released last month. \[02:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=168s) The goal is, and was, to raise the bar with complex, real-world Android tasks and provide guidance and transparency on LLM performance for you, developers, but also to push model makers to prioritize Android by giving them good benchmark to, hill climb against. \[03:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=187s) And also providing analysis and results serving both you and the model makers. \[03:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=207s) OpenAI published an article. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=209s) They found that the models were able to production open-source apps that we kept closed, with modern libraries and architectures. \[04:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIIAwylLb5Q\&t=279s) For example, Nav 2 to Nav 3, XML views to entries.summary: This document introduces Android Bench 2.0, an AI evaluation benchmark designed to measure LLM performance on complex Android development tasks while preventing training data contamination. It highlights key testing strategies like implementation-agnostic UI checks and a Multimodal LLM Judge to accurately grade AI-generated code.

entries.title: Integrate your app with the Android intelligence system
entries.summary: This new documentation page provides an embedded talk session and interactive transcript from the Android Dev Summit focusing on how to integrate apps with the Android intelligence system.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/integrate-your-app-with-the-android-intelligence-system.txt" target="_blank">Integrate your app with the Android intelligence system - Speakers: Sarah Shamsie (Product Manager at Google), Dan Galpin (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UsqDEfyOH2E - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/integrate-your-app-with-the-android-intelligence-system ## About the talk Android is evolving into an intelligence system where agents like Gemini orchestrate tasks across apps. To unlock new user experiences and participate in these agentic workflows, your app must expose its core capabilities. This session is a practical guide to integrating your app with Android's intelligence layer. We'll survey key integration paths - including on-device Android MCP, server-side MCP, and Task Automation - and provide a decision framework for choosing the right path for your use case. We'll also explore proactive experiences with Personal Context. You will learn how to: - Select the optimal integration path for your app's needs. - Implement both reactive and proactive intelligence features. - Balance performance and security in agentic integrations. ## Summary - Android MCP is a unified on-device tool calling framework powered by the Jetpack AppFunctions library. It maps MCP primitives to Kotlin constructs and runs on Android Binder IPC. - On-device tools excel when accessing encrypted data or device sensors. Alternatively, platform-driven Task Automation lets pre-loaded agents simulate touch events without code changes. - Your app acts as an Android MCP server while agents discover and call tools. Declare tools with \`AppFunctionDeclaration\`, provide KDoc descriptions, and avoid relying on Kotlin default values. - The Connected Apps Platform, currently in preview, lets you test your AppFunctions with Gemini. Set up your connected app in Google Connected Console, then upload your bundle in Play Console. ## Resources - \[Jetpacker travel sample app\](https://goo.gle/jetpacker) - \[Sample agent source entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces the Android intelligence system and guides developers on how to integrate their apps with agentic workflows using the Jetpack AppFunctions library (Android MCP). It explains key integration paths, such as on-device tool calling and proactive assistance, to help apps participate seamlessly in AI-driven experiences like Gemini.

entries.title: Lessons from WhatsApp's Wear OS journey
entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds a Dev Summit talk session and interactive transcript regarding WhatsApp's development journey on Wear OS. It matters because it provides developers with real-world insights, best practices, and lessons learned from building a major messaging app for smartwatches.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/lessons-from-whatsapps-wear-os-journey.txt" target="_blank">Lessons from WhatsApp's Wear OS journey - Speakers: Martin Pelant (Software Engineer, Meta), Subhag Bhatia (Software Engineer, Meta) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/lessons-from-whatsapps-wear-os-journey ## About the talk Hear directly from WhatsApp engineers on how they upgraded their Wear OS app at scale. This session covers the architectural and UX decisions behind integrating Material 3 and adopting Wear Widgets. Gain direct insight into the lessons, patterns and tools the team used to update their app and deliver a cohesive user experience. ## Summary - Sharing Android phone code with Wear OS cuts duplicate work but requires dependency injection and manifest overrides. Tests should compare multibinding sets so modularized features do not silently disappear. - Runtime notification bridging management prevents duplicate alerts while letting the watch operate independently. Turning bridging off at login and back on at logout stops phone mirrors from double-buzzing. - Material 3 migrations on round displays require managing behavioral changes alongside visual styling. Using \`TransformingLazyColumn\` properly means applying transformations at only one level and avoiding caching positions with Compose's \`remember\`. - App expiry limits can trigger sudden active user drops if watches fail to update promptly. Scheduled update reminders direct users to Google Play before their ninety-day build expires. ## Topics wear-os, material-3, jetpack-compose, modularization, notifications, tiles-and-widgets ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=4s) Hi everyone. \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=5s) My name is Martin. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=6s) And I'm Subhag. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=7s) We are engineers at Meta on the team behind WhatsApp on Wear OS. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=11s) And we recently modernized our app. \[00:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=13s) So today, we are going to share the lessons we learned from migrating to shared codebase and then building new experiences on top of it. \[00:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=20s) What makes WhatsApp on Wear OS interesting is that it works without your phone. \[00:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Mi3zullvIYY\&t=24s) Once it's linked, it acts as its own WhatsApp device, end-to-end encrypted just like your
