entries.summary: This document summarizes key architectural, modularization, and UX lessons learned during WhatsApp's migration of its Wear OS app to a shared Android codebase. It details strategies for handling dependency injection, manifest merging, runtime notification bridging, and Material 3 UI adaptations.

entries.title: Let agents generate UI in your Android apps with A2UI
entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring a talk session and interactive transcript about letting AI agents generate UI in Android apps using A2UI. This provides developers with insights into emerging AI-driven UI paradigms showcased at the Android Dev Summit.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/let-agents-generate-ui-in-your-android-apps-with-a2ui.txt" target="_blank">Let agents generate UI in your Android apps with A2UI - Speakers: Anton Beloglazov (Software Engineer), Nick Butcher (Product Manager) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/let-agents-generate-ui-in-your-android-apps-with-a2ui ## About the talk A2UI is transitioning from web-centric components to native Android. The new Jetpack Compose renderer for A2UI v0.9 enables developers to render dynamic, LLM-generated UI natively. Instead of webviews, it leverages a Coroutine-driven actor framework, sealed-class lifecycles, and native Material 3 integration. This session walks through the new architecture, explaining how server-driven component trees translate into reactive Compose nodes, and how built-in layout transitions handle structural updates smoothly without blocking the UI. ## Summary - A2UI provides a declarative, open JSON protocol for agentic back ends to describe dynamic user interfaces instead of text responses. - The protocol revolves around catalogs that define allowed components and functions, along with surfaces that represent agent-controlled UI pieces. - Jetpack Compose's A2UI library renders streamed surface models natively using Material 3 components with built-in accessibility and progressive rendering. - In-memory data models update bound UI elements instantly without contacting the agent, while outbound events route user actions back. - Developers can customize existing catalog items or create custom components to strictly control what the agent can display. ## Resources - \[A2UI Compose documentation\](https://goo.gle/a2ui-compose-docs) - \[Material 3 A2UI demo\](https://goo.gle/material3-a2ui-demo) - \[JetPacker sample app\](https://github.com/android/ai-samples) - \[A2UI specification\](https://a2ui.org) ## Topics a2ui, generative-ui, jetpack-compose, android, ai-agents, material-design ## Transcript ### Introduction to generative UI and A2UI \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=6s) Hi, everyone, and welcome to this talk where we're going to be talking about how to generate UI in your Android apps using our brand new A2UI library. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=14s) My name is Nick Butcher, I'm a product manager working on Jetpack Compose. \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=17s) Hey everyone, I'm Anton, I'm an engineer on the Compose team. \[00:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=21s) I'm working on this new Jetpack Compose A2UI renderer that we're very excited to tell you about today. \[00:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=27s) Yes, now with the rise of AI capabilities, many apps are looking at how AI can help you to improve or build new experiences for their users. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=36s) One of the exciting experiences that some people are looking at is generative UI, which is how, at runtime, agentic back ends can create brand new UIs for your users, which we think is very interesting. \[00:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=48s) But unfortunately right now, many agentic back ends' responses are trapped in walls of text, like this. \[00:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=55s) So, here's an example where I've asked an a- agent to generate me a new feature for booking a trip. \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=61s) So, here's the prompt. \[01:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=62s) And as you can see, it's given actually quite a decent answer, but it's trapped in this wall of text which I can't really easily interact with and it looks nothing like the rest of my application. \[01:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=73s) Generative UI allows you to create an experience like this instead, where you can generate a new UI on the fly in response to dynamic input, opening up possibilities for more customization, or more new experiences. \[01:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=86s) So, here's an example of a UI that's created using like standard, native components. \[01:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=92s) So, you can absolutely build this kind of experience today yourself, but you'd have to define your own like format for interchange with the back end, your own kind of event stream, and functions, and so on. \[01:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=102s) A2UI, which stands for Agent-to-UI, is an open protocol which is a JSON format for defining all of these things. \[01:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=113s) So, one of the things I really like about A2UI is it's a declarative format. \[01:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=117s) The agent is just returning a JSON representation of the UI to render. \[02:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=121s) It's not returning any code that your client then needs to execute, which can open you up to certain security vulnerabilities. \[02:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=128s) It's just declarative. \[02:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=130s) So, what other concepts do we need to know about A2UI? ### Core concepts: Catalogs and surfaces \[02:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=133s) Just two main concepts: catalogs and surfaces. \[02:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=136s) Catalog has components like text, button, row, and column that the agent can use to build the UI. \[02:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=141s) A catalog also has functions that the agent can use for formatting text, validating user input, or opening URLs. \[02:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=149s) A catalog is a contract that defines what components and functions your app supports, and the agent can only build with those. \[02:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=156s) This means, as Nick mentioned, the agent never executes arbitrary code in your app. \[02:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=160s) It composes a UI from the building blocks that you design and trust. \[02:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=164s) One more important concept is a surface. \[02:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=166s) A surface is one piece of UI that the agent controls, like this trip planner example on the slide. \[02:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=172s) The agent describes the UI for a surface in JSON using the A2UI protocol messages, like \`createSurface\`, \`updateComponents\`, and using the components and functions defined in your catalog. \[03:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=184s) So speaking of catalog, catalog is a very fundamental concept in A2UI, cuz it controls what components that the agent can use to construct an interface. \[03:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=193s) The A2UI spec defines something called the basic catalog, which is a set of common components you can use for constructing most UIs. \[03:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=201s) The Jetpack Compose A2UI renderer provides an implementation of the basic catalog using Material 3 components. \[03:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=207s) Most of the catalog components are ready to use out of the box. \[03:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=210s) There are three media components: image, video, and audio player, where you need to plug in your library of choice. \[03:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=216s) For example, you may choose Coil for image loading and Media3 for the video and audio player. \[03:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=222s) But the real power of A2UI and our new renderer library is that you can create your own, completely custom components and catalogs, and fully control what the agent can use to build the UI. \[03:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=232s) We'll come back to catalogs later. \[03:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=234s) Okay, so let's take a look at what this looks like. \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=237s) So, if we can switch to the demo machine, please. \[04:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qIvsFGvlHdo\&t=240s) This is our demo app, which we're going to use, and we're going to build up the A2UI renderer to show you entries.summary: This new documentation page explains how to use the A2UI (Agent-to-UI) protocol and Jetpack Compose renderer to allow LLM-backed AI agents to dynamically generate native Material 3 user interfaces within Android applications.

entries.title: Mastering on-device intelligence with ML Kit and LiteRT in Google Play services
entries.summary: Added a new developer summit talk document covering on-device intelligence with ML Kit and LiteRT in Google Play Services. This documentation provides developers with insights and resources on building efficient machine learning features directly on Android devices.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/mastering-on-device-intelligence-with-ml-kit-and-litert-in-google-play-services.txt" target="_blank">Mastering on-device intelligence with ML Kit and LiteRT in Google Play services - Speakers: Chintan Parikh (Lead Product Manager), Fergus Henderson (Staff Software Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LiBWWJ9IKag - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/mastering-on-device-intelligence-with-ml-kit-and-litert-in-google-play-services ## About the talk Stop choosing between plug-and-play AI convenience and custom model flexibility---you can deploy both in a single, ultra-lean app without adding megabytes of binary bloat. In this session, we'll demonstrate how to build this exact dual-stack architecture in a single Android app. You'll see how to leverage ML Kit for ready-to-use classical ML tasks (like doc scan) alongside LiteRT standalone in Play services for your custom computer vision or audio workloads. We'll dive deep into how both implementation paths unite under the hood to utilize the modern LiteRT runtime, giving your app seamless, hardware-accelerated performance on CPU and GPUs with a virtually zero-byte download footprint. Key takeaways for developers: -Uncompromised performance: Both turnkey and custom models are hardware-accelerated automatically using the unified CompiledModel API. -Micro-APKs: Dramatically reduce your app's download size by offloading both the ML Kit and LiteRT runtimes to Play services. -Hybrid integration: Master running multiple ML workflows side-by-side in production without resource conflicts. ## Summary - LiteRT in Google Play services shares one maintained runtime across apps to reduce APK sizes by about 8 MB. - Turnkey ML Kit features and custom LiteRT models can run together in a single application on the same runtime. - The CompiledModel API simplifies GPU acceleration and delivers up to 1.4x faster performance than legacy TFLite GPU inference. - Platform availability extends beyond phones to Wear OS 4 or later and Android Automotive OS on Android 11 or later. - Adopting LiteRT in Google Play services involves updating Maven dependencies to \`play-services-litert\`, calling \`LiteRt.initialize\` to obtain an environment, and passing it to \`CompiledModel.create\`. - Migrating to the 2.x CompiledModel API is recommended because 1.x is in maintenance mode and NNAPI is going away. ## Skills - \[Android LiteRT skill\](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/device-ai/litert/) ## Resources - \[Docs \& samples\](https://developers.google.com/edge/litert/android) ## Topics on-device-ai, ml-kit, litert, google-play-services, gpu-acceleration, machine-learning ## Transcript ### Introduction and entries.summary: This new documentation page provides a technical overview and architectural guide on building dual-stack on-device AI applications using ML Kit for turnkey classical machine learning and LiteRT in Google Play services for custom models. It details how developers can achieve hardware-accelerated performance with a reduced binary footprint and minimal APK size bloat.

entries.title: Memory troubleshooting with Firebase Crashlytics
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript covering memory troubleshooting techniques using Firebase Crashlytics. It helps developers diagnose and resolve memory-related issues in their Android apps.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/memory-troubleshooting-with-firebase-crashlytics.txt" target="_blank">Memory troubleshooting with Firebase Crashlytics - Speakers: Polina Govorkova (Senior Software Developer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2ruqmicLr08 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/memory-troubleshooting-with-firebase-crashlytics ## About the talk Keep your app's memory footprint lean-and-mean and non-segfaulty with Firebase Crashlytics. This session explores our comprehensive suite of memory troubleshooting tools available in the Firebase console and in Android Studio. We'll start by covering how to leverage ANR insights and GWP-ASan reports to diagnose elusive memory bugs and then dive into our latest tooling for Out-Of-Memory (OOM) and Memory Limiter Kill (MLK) events, designed specifically to help you navigate and adapt to the new memory limits introduced in Android 17. ## Summary - Application Not Responding errors often trace back to background bottlenecks or memory exhaustion rather than active CPU load. Firebase Crashlytics queries \`ApplicationExitInfo\` to surface multithread traces and identify root blocking threads. - Out of memory crashes occur when apps exceed runtime Java heap limits. Crashlytics integrates with Android 17's \`ProfilingManager\` to collect de-obfuscated heap snapshots that can be inspected in Perfetto or through the Android CLI. - Android 17's Memory Limiter terminates individual processes that consume excessive total RAM, including native allocations. Crashlytics groups these terminations on the dashboard alongside heap dumps to help separate C++ memory leaks from managed heap allocations. - Native memory corruption frequently surfaces on system threads rather than in app code. Crashlytics supports GWP-ASan and Arm MTE, and GWP-ASan reports pinpoint exact allocation and deallocation sites for bugs such as use-after-free. ## Resources - \[ApplicationExitInfo API reference\](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/app/ApplicationExitInfo) - \[ProfilingManager API reference\](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/os/ProfilingManager) - \[Memory Limiter documentation\](https://source.android.com/docs/core/perf/memory-limiter) - \[GWP-ASan guide\](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/gwp-asan) - \[ARM MTE guide\](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/arm-mte) - \[Heap dump early access signup\](https://goo.gle/crashlytics-memory) ## Topics firebase-crashlytics, android-memory, anr, out-of-memory, entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces memory troubleshooting techniques and tooling using Firebase Crashlytics and Android Studio. It explains how to diagnose ANRs, Out-Of-Memory (OOM) events, and memory leaks to help developers adapt to new memory limits in Android 17.

entries.title: Migrating two decades of the Google Play app to Jetpack Compose
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript about migrating the Google Play app to Jetpack Compose, showcasing modern Android UI adoption strategies for large-scale codebases.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/migrating-two-decades-of-the-google-play-app-to-jetpack-compose.txt" target="_blank">Migrating two decades of the Google Play app to Jetpack Compose - Speakers: Kirill Grouchnikov (Software engineer), Jon Boekenoogen (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/migrating-two-decades-of-the-google-play-app-to-jetpack-compose ## About the talk This year, Android officially became Compose-first for building all UI, placing legacy Views into maintenance mode. For Google Play, that journey began back in 2020. Across an engineering footprint spanning nearly two decades and billions of users, migrating to Jetpack Compose was achieved through proven best practices, close collaboration with the core Compose team and continuous tooling evolution. Discover how modernizing Google Play with Compose delivered measurable improvements in velocity and long-term stability. The session walks through connecting agentic Figma design workflows with Compose implementation, automating quality to prevent unnecessary recompositions and crafting expressive interfaces with dynamic color, rich typography and layered shapes. You will leave with tested strategies to triage bugs faster and scale your own Compose migration with confidence. ## Summary - Google Play moved 97% of user impressions to Compose-only screens over six years. Major pages also saw a 30% improvement in jank rate over the past 14 months. - Incremental adoption mitigates business risks across large codebases. Teams can build familiarity on low-traffic screens first, then advance toward hosting \`ComposeView\` directly at the Activity root. - Dynamic theming works entirely in code using \`MaterialTheme\` overlays and the Material Color Utilities library. This avoids Activity teardowns, though generating color schemes at build time helps limit runtime latency. - Unidirectional data flow and declarative UI simplify architecture and remove several types of race conditions. Running data sources and UI transforms in parallel improved Google Play's load latency by dozens of milliseconds. - Automated Lint checks enforce code quality and design system rules. Play uses them to block hardcoded colors and flag potential performance pitfalls such as \`BoxWithConstraints\`. ## Topics jetpack-compose, migration, performance, theming, unidirectional-data-flow, product area, and from those initial design explorations, maybe slides, maybe Figma spec, you can feed that into that agent, and the agent helps quickly identify which components already exist so that they don't need to be redesigned and respec'd, so they don't need to be reimplemented from scratch. \[21:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1301s) And that cuts down quite significantly on the design costs and on the implementation costs. \[21:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1308s) On the implementation side of things, we lean very heavily on core and custom Lint rules. \[21:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1312s) A couple of core Lint rules that I want to call out are FrequentlyChangingValueDetector that helps identify sources of unnecessary recompositions, which can lead to latency and jank, and the other one is ScaffoldPaddingDetector for flagging cases where we use the Material Compose Scaffold composable, but ignore the incoming paddings. \[22:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1336s) It's not a source of latency and jank, but, in some cases, it can lead to very difficult-to-debug, kind of like, layout misalignments in certain cases where, like, it's edge-to-edge, or folding, unfolding. \[22:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1349s) And, finally, BoxWithConstraints, it comes with certain performance considerations. \[22:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1353s) It might take two frames to properly lay out everything. \[22:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1356s) We don't block it outright, but we do flag it as a Lint warning so that the developer that is working on that particular screen knows that they are making a specific choice to use BoxWithConstraints, or maybe they can choose to use something else for that specific layout. \[22:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1373s) For the theming automation, again, color tokens, typography tokens, shape tokens. \[22:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1379s) We have a Lint rule that blocks the usage of hardcoded colors and hardcoded typography. \[23:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1385s) We have a Lint rule that flags usage of Material 2 components. \[23:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1389s) We only want to use Material 3, the latest and greatest, including the new expressive components that were introduced last year and this year. \[23:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1398s) We want We have a custom Lint rule that prevents people from reading colors from, let's say, legacy XML files. \[23:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1405s) We want to be Compose-first and Compose-only for new screens. \[23:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1410s) And, Text composables, specifically in the Material design system, they have fallbacks for style and color. \[23:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1418s) They read it from local content color and local typography, but we don't want to rely on that. \[23:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1424s) We want every single text to be intentionally using the specific style, typography style, and the specific color from the design spec. \[23:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1432s) So, that's a Lint rule that we have. \[23:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1433s) And the last one, along the lines of that ScaffoldPaddingDetector, we have a custom Lint rule that enforces that every single Composable function that we have uses its input modifier. \[24:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1446s) Again, to prevent like, you know, new usages from being like incorrectly placed, or not respecting the incoming background, or whatever it might be. ### Conclusion \[24:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1457s) And these are the three main points that we would like you to take out of this presentation. \[24:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1465s) First one is that today, at the end of 2026, in our opinion, Compose is a mature UI toolkit, proven at scale. \[24:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1473s) Android itself is Compose-first. \[24:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1476s) Earlier this year at Google I/O, we announced that all the UI libraries and all the agentic flows are Compose-first. \[24:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1484s) And, as Jon mentioned earlier in the presentation, crawl, walk, jog, and run, we suggest that you migrate incrementally, especially large codebases, to accelerate your velocity for developer flows and for the agentic flows. \[25:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1501s) And, with that, we thank you for sharing your time with us today, and in a few minutes, myself and Jon will be outside to take any questions that you have. \[25:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7h_kcpNGKnw\&t=1511s) And, again, thank you for your time.</a>
entries.summary: This document outlines the Google Play team's multi-year journey of migrating a massive, legacy codebase to Jetpack Compose, detailing phased adoption strategies, performance wins, and architectural best practices.

entries.title: Moving beyond 2D with custom 3D geometry in the Jetpack XR SDK
entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring a talk session and interactive transcript on moving beyond 2D with custom 3D geometry using the Jetpack XR SDK. This matters as it provides developers with resources for building immersive spatial experiences on Android.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/moving-beyond-2d-with-custom-3d-geometry-in-the-jetpack-xr-sdk.txt" target="_blank">Moving beyond 2D with custom 3D geometry in the Jetpack XR SDK - Speakers: Egor Yusov (Software Engineer), Jay Abi-Saad (Software Engineer) - Track: Android XR - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/moving-beyond-2d-with-custom-3d-geometry-in-the-jetpack-xr-sdk ## About the talk Transitioning your Android applications from traditional 2D screens into spatial environments requires a new approach to constructing shapes. In this session, we will explore the Custom Mesh API in the Jetpack XR SDK, which allows you to programmatically generate procedural 3D geometry directly at runtime. We will walk through the core workflow, from defining vertex layouts to rendering dynamic objects seamlessly within the user's physical space. By the end of this talk, you will have the practical skills to build interactive, custom 3D geometry completely from code. ## Summary - The glTF introspection API in Jetpack SceneCore exposes model metadata at run time. You can play embedded animations, transform subnodes, or override meshes with materials and textures. - Jetpack SceneCore includes mesh APIs to generate custom 3D geometry in Kotlin. Four building blocks such as VertexLayout and \`MeshBuffer\` construct models triangle by triangle without 3D tools. - Dynamic meshes support real-time updates as users draw paths or animate surfaces. Updating only the changed vertex data streams modifications straight to the GPU without recreating the mesh or entity. - Gemini in Android Studio can write complex vertex animation and lighting math for the mesh APIs. One prompt generates working code that animates vertex grids and recalculates normals every frame. ## Resources - \[Android XR Emulator\](https://goo.gle/xr-tools) - \[Jetpack XR SDK\](https://goo.gle/jetpack-xr-sdk) ## Topics jetpack-xr, jetpack-scenecore, android-xr, 3d-geometry, mesh-api, gltf ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android XR and SceneCore \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=5s) Hey, folks. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=6s) I'm Jay. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=6s) And I'm Egor. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=7s) And we're software engineers working on Jetpack XR at Google. \[00:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=11s) With XREAL Aura right around the corner, we want to make sure you have all the tools you need to build great spatial experiences on the platform. \[00:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=19s) But best of all, you don't even need XR hardware to get started. \[00:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=24s) All the features we'll show are available today in the Android XR Emulator in Android Studio. \[00:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=29s) Our goal is to show you that with the Jetpack SceneCore library, you don't need deep 3D knowledge to build rich spatial experiences on the platform. \[00:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=38s) Everything you'll see is running in an Android app, written in idiomatic Kotlin right inside Android Studio. \[00:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=43s) We recently promoted Jetpack SceneCore to stable, and today we'll cover some cool advancements of our 3D model APIs, as well as our brand-new mesh APIs, which allow you to build custom 3D geometry on the fly. ### Working with glTF 3D models \[00:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=58s) But let's start with 3D models. \[01:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=60s) When it comes to 3D models, the first thing we need is a file format. \[01:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=65s) Open standards are a core part of the Android XR DNA. \[01:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=69s) So, naturally, we went all in with the glTF format from the Khronos Group. \[01:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=74s) Now, if you're not from the 3D world, you might be asking, "What's a glTF?" \[01:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=78s) You can think of it as a JPEG, but for 3D models. \[01:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=82s) The glTF asset structure provides data for things like animations, subnodes, and meshes. \`\`\`json { "asset" : {...}, "nodes" : \[ { "name" : "Right_Arm", "rotation" : \[...\], "scale" : \[...\], "translation" : \[...\], }, \], "animations" : \[ { "name" : "Wave", }, \], "meshes" : \[ { "name" : "Torso", "primitives" : \[ ... \], }, \], // Way way more! } \`\`\` \[01:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=88s) But for the purpose of this talk, you can think of subnodes as parts of a model, each with their own position and rotation. \[01:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=96s) Meshes are the surfaces you see, and the animations are movements of those subnodes and meshes that the asset's author baked in ahead of time. \[01:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=104s) Cool. \[01:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=105s) Now, at this point, you might be asking, "Where can I get a glTF model in the first place?" \[01:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=110s) Well, on top of the many models that are out there, you can also create your own. \[01:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=114s) Now that we've covered the basics of the glTF format, let's go ahead and use it in our app. \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=120s) We start with a basic Android XR project using Jetpack SceneCore. \[02:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=124s) You can see a spatial panel with an activity floating in the user's space. \[02:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=129s) You can grab it, move it, and resize it to your liking. \[02:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=133s) And although this talk is all about 3D, definitely check out the rest of the Jetpack XR SDK as well. \[02:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=140s) All right, spatial panels are fun, but we want more magic. \[02:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=144s) And what better way to add some magic than throwing in a 3D model? \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=148s) Well, it just so happens that our designer made this glTF model of a car. \`\`\`kotlin // Load assets/models/car.glb val carModel = GltfModel.create( session, Paths.get("models", "car.glb") ) // Create an entity in the scene val carEntity = GltfModelEntity.create( session, carModel, parent = session.scene.activitySpace ) \`\`\` \[02:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=153s) They even embedded animations in it, which we'll use later on. \[02:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=157s) Using SceneCore, I can use our 3D model APIs to load it right into our scene. ### Model animations and subnode manipulation \[02:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=163s) But let's make the car feel a bit more alive. \[02:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=167s) Remember all that rich metadata inside a glTF? \[02:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=170s) With a new glTF introspection API, you can now access it, starting with animations. \`\`\`kotlin // Access every animation in car.glb val animations = carEntity.getAnimations() .associateBy { it.name } // Open the doors... animations\["lf_door_open"\]?.start() animations\["rt_door_open"\]?.start() // ...and close them again animations\["lf_door_close"\]?.start() animations\["rt_door_close"\]?.start() // Same for the hood and trunk animations\["hood_open"\]?.start() animations\["trunk_open"\]?.start() \`\`\` \[02:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=176s) In just a few lines of code, I can individually play any glTF animations built into the car model, like opening and closing the doors, the hood, or the trunk. \[03:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=187s) But animations are not the only piece of metadata that you can access. \[03:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=192s) The glTF introspection API also exposes subnodes in the model as \`GltfModelNode\`, allowing you to move, rotate, and scale them to your liking. \`\`\`kotlin // Wheel sub nodes, named by our designer val nodes = carEntity.nodes.associateBy { it.name } val front = listOf("lf_frontWheel_geo", "rt_fontWheel_geo").map { nodes\[it\]!! } val rear = listOf("lf_RearWheel_geo", "rt_RearWheel_geo").map { nodes\[it\]!! } // Update a sub node's transform at runtime fun GltfModelNode.rotate(q: Quaternion) { localPose = localPose.copy(rotation = q) } // Each frame: steer front, spin all four fun drive(steerDeg: Float, spinDeg: Float) { val steer = Quaternion.fromAxisAngle( Vector3.Up, steerDeg) val spin = Quaternion.fromAxisAngle( Vector3.Right, spinDeg) front.forEach { it.rotate(steer \* spin) } rear.forEach { it.rotate(spin) } } \`\`\` \[03:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=203s) For example, here, I can individually update the position and the rotation of the wheels as the car drives. \[03:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=209s) And to be clear, what you're seeing is not an embedded glTF animation. \[03:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=214s) Here, I'm individually spinning and steering the wheels all at run time. ### Applying materials and textures \[03:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=220s) One last piece of metadata that you can access is any mesh in the glTF model. \[03:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=225s) Now, Egor will dive deeper into meshes in a moment. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=228s) But for now, let's style up our car. \[03:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=231s) Using our texture API, we can load a PNG image texture, say of a metal pattern. \`\`\`kotlin // Load a PNG with the Texture API val metal = Texture.create( session, Paths.get("textures", "metal.png")) // Create KhronosPbrMaterials val (body, doors, hood) = List(3) { KhronosPbrMaterial .create(session, AlphaMode.OPAQUE) } body.setBaseColorFactor(CYAN) doors.setBaseColorFactor(PINK) hood.setBaseColorTexture(metal) // Override meshes by sub node name val nodes = carEntity.nodes.associateBy { it.name } nodes\["mainBody_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(body) nodes\["lf_door_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(doors) nodes\["rt_door_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(doors) nodes\["hood_geo"\]?.setMaterialOverride(hood) \`\`\` \[03:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=237s) Then, with our material API, we can plug it right into a \`KhronosPbrMaterial\`. \[04:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=242s) Now, if you're new to 3D, you can think of a mesh as a tabletop, a material as a tablecloth, and a texture as a pattern printed on that cloth. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=252s) But here, instead of a tabletop, we use the material objects we created to override the meshes associated with the car's hood and doors subnodes. \[04:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=261s) In just a few lines of code, we've transformed the look and feel of our car, again, all at run time. \[04:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=267s) That's some cool stuff, but here's an even better idea. \[04:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=271s) How awesome would it be to draw a race track for the car to drive on? \[04:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=275s) Here, a pre-made glTF model is not the right fit. \[04:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=279s) Instead, we need the ability to generate 3D geometry on the fly. \[04:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=283s) So, I'll hand it over to Egor to tell you all about our brand-new Jetpack SceneCore mesh APIs. ### Introduction to mesh APIs \[04:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=290s) Thanks, Jay. \[04:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=291s) Let's make it so that the user can draw their race track in the-- with their finger in their living room. \[04:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=297s) The track does not exist until it's drawn, so nobody can model it ahead of time. \[05:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=301s) We will build it in code, one triangle at a time. \[05:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=305s) A mesh starts with vertices, points in space. \`\`\`kotlin // 4 vertices: x, y, z val positions = floatArrayOf( 0f, 0f, 0f, // v0 1f, 0f, 0f, // v1 0f, 1f, 0f, // v2 1f, 1f, 0f // v3 ) // 2 triangles = 6 indices val indices = intArrayOf( 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3 ) \`\`\` \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=309s) Each one carries attributes like a position, a normal for lighting, color, texture coordinates. \[05:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=315s) Indices connect the dots. \[05:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=317s) Every three make a triangle. \[05:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=319s) Two triangles make a square, six indices, but only four vertices, because they share two. \[05:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=326s) Keep going and you get a cube. \[05:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=328s) Every 3D model, including Jay's car, is built the same way, just with more triangles. ### Building blocks of the mesh API \[05:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=335s) Mesh API maps onto that with four building blocks: \`VertexLayout\`, \`MeshBuffer\`, \`CustomMesh\`, and \`MeshEntity\`. \[05:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=342s) Let's take them one at a time. \[05:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=345s) First, VertexLayout. \`\`\`kotlin // How to read each vertex from bytes val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) // 12 B .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) // 12 B .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) // 8 B .build() // stride: 32 B // Offsets and stride are computed, // or set them explicitly. // Attributes can live in separate buffers val split = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .startNextBuffer() .addAttribute(COLOR, UBYTE4_NORM) .build() \`\`\` \[05:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=347s) Your vertex data is just bytes in a ByteBuffer, and every mesh packs them differently. \[05:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=350s) VertexLayout says how to read yours: which attributes, what type, and where each one sits. \[05:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=358s) Here, it's a position, a normal, and UVs, the texture coordinates, 32 bytes total. \[06:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=364s) Attributes can also live in separate buffers, so that you can update only the ones that change. \[06:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=370s) Second, \`MeshBuffer\`, a container for raw data. \`\`\`kotlin // Vertex bytes + 32-bit indices val meshBuffer = MeshBuffer.create( session, layout, vertexData = listOf(ByteBufferRegion( vertexBytes, 0, vertexBytes.capacity())), indexData = ByteBufferRegion( indexBytes, 0, indexBytes.capacity())) // Copied to the GPU: reuse your // ByteBuffers right away // Need updates at runtime? val dynamic = MeshBuffer.createDynamic( session, layout, vertexCount = 1000, indexCount = 3000) \`\`\` \[06:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=374s) You give it the layout, the vertex bytes, and 32-bit indices. \[06:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=378s) The data is copied to the GPU right away, so that you can reuse or release your ByteBuffers. \[06:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=384s) By default, the \`MeshBuffer\` is static. \[06:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=386s) It's set once and optimized for fast rendering. \[06:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=389s) And if you need to change it at runtime, \`createDynamic\` allocates a fixed capacity that you may update later. \[06:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=397s) Third, \`CustomMesh\`, a view into a \`MeshBuffer\`. \`\`\`kotlin // A view: which indices to draw, and how val road = CustomMesh .BuilderFromMeshBuffer(session, meshBuffer) // subset 0: asphalt .addSubset(TRIANGLES, indexOffset = 0, indexCount = roadCount) // subset 1: lane markings .addSubset(TRIANGLES, indexOffset = roadCount, indexCount = lineCount) .build() // Shortcut: builds MeshBuffer + CustomMesh CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData(session, layout) \`\`\` \[06:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=401s) It doesn't copy any data. \[06:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=403s) It says which range of indices to draw and how, triangles or triangle strips. \[06:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=409s) Here, the asphalt and the lane markings live in the same \`MeshBuffer\`. \[06:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=414s) Multiple custom meshes may share the same \`MeshBuffer\`, and when you don't need sharing, \`BuilderFromMeshData\` creates the mesh and the buffer in one step. \[07:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=424s) Finally, MeshEntity places the mesh in the scene. \`\`\`kotlin // Place the mesh in the scene graph val roadEntity = MeshEntity.create( session, mesh = road, // one material per subset materials = listOf(asphalt, paint), pose = Pose(Vector3(0f, 0f, -1f)), parent = session.scene.activitySpace) // It's an Entity: move it, re-parent it roadEntity.setPose(Pose(Vector3(0f, -0.5f, -1f))) roadEntity.parent = tableAnchor // Same mesh, another entity val ghost = MeshEntity.create( session, road, listOf(glass, glass)) \`\`\` \[07:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=428s) The mesh is the what. \[07:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=430s) The entity is the where. \[07:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=432s) Like the panel and Jay's car, it's an entity, so it has a position and a parent, the thing it is attached to. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=438s) Move the parent, and the road moves with it. \[07:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=441s) You also provide one material per subset, so that the same mesh may appear with different material in different entities. ### Building custom and dynamic meshes \[07:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=451s) So, now let's put it all together and build the mesh, the road mesh. \`\`\`kotlin // Describe a vertex val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) .build() // Path points -\> ribbon of triangles val (vertices, indices) = buildRoad(path) // Build the mesh... val roadMesh = CustomMesh .BuilderFromMeshData(session, layout) .addVertexData(vertices) .setIndexData(indices) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) .build() // ...and put it in the scene val road = MeshEntity.create( session, roadMesh, listOf(asphalt), parent = session.scene.activitySpace) \`\`\` \[07:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=455s) We define the vertex: the position, the normal, and UVs, the texture coordinates. \[07:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=460s) A small helper function turns user path into a ribbon. \[07:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=465s) For each point on the path, it adds two vertices on each side and two triangles that connect them to the next pair. \[07:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=472s) It's plain Kotlin, writing bytes into a ByteBuffer. \[07:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=474s) You don't need any kind of 3D tool. \[08:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=480s) \`BuilderFromMeshData\`, the shortcut we just saw, creates the mesh and the \`MeshBuffer\`, and computes the bounds for us. \[08:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=488s) Finally, \`MeshEntity.create\` places the \`roadMesh\` in the scene with the asphalt material. \[08:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=494s) But we want our track to grow live as the user draws that. \[08:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=498s) For that, we use a dynamic mesh. \`\`\`kotlin // Fixed GPU capacity, allocated once val track = CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData( session, layout, maxVertices = 2 \* MAX_POINTS, maxIndices = 6 \* MAX_POINTS) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) // Covers everything the track can become .setBounds(playArea) .build() // Hand moved: upload only the new segment val buffer = track.meshBuffer buffer.updateVertexData( bufferIndex = 0, vertexData = segmentVertices, offsetInBytes = n \* VERTEX_BYTES) buffer.updateIndexData( segmentIndices, offsetInBytes = n \* INDEX_BYTES) \`\`\` \[08:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=501s) The only difference, we give the builder the maximum capacity up front, so that the GPU buffers can be allocated. \[08:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=508s) Then, as the user draws, \`updateVertexData\` and \`updateIndexData\` upload only the new segments, not the entire mesh. \[08:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=517s) One gotcha: the renderer uses bounds to skip anything off-screen, so set the bounds to cover everything the track may become, like the play area here. \[08:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=528s) You may notice that the API is not the difficult part here. \[08:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=531s) The difficult part is the vertex math, the normals, texture coordinates, triangle order. \[08:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=537s) That's exactly the kind of code that AI is great at writing. \[09:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=541s) But let's say we want to put things one step farther. \[09:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=543s) Now Now, I want a checkered flag waving at the wind at the destination. ### Generating animated meshes with Gemini \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=549s) Vertex animation math is the tricky part, so I asked Gemini. \[09:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=553s) In Android Studio, I gave it one prompt: "Using the Jetpack SceneCore Mesh API, build a 20x12 flag grid with checkerboard UVs, animate a wind wave every frame with updateVertexData, and recompute normals so that the lighting follows the folds." \[09:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=568s) A few seconds later, I got working code. \[09:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=571s) Let's look at what it did. \[09:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=574s) It built a flag mesh as the grid of 20 by 12 cells, two triangles per cell, and it made a smart choice with the layout. \`\`\`kotlin // 20 x 12 cells = 273 vertices val layout = VertexLayout.Builder() // buffer 0: updated every frame .addAttribute(POSITION, FLOAT3) .addAttribute(NORMAL, FLOAT3) .startNextBuffer() // buffer 1: never changes .addAttribute(UV0, FLOAT2) .build() val flagMesh = CustomMesh.BuilderFromMeshData( session, layout, maxVertices = 273, maxIndices = 1440) .addVertexData(restPose) // buffer 0 .addVertexData(checkerUVs) // buffer 1 .setIndexData(gridIndices) .setTopology(TRIANGLES) .setBounds(swingBounds) .build() \`\`\` \[09:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=581s) Positions and normals are placed in Buffer 0, and they updated every frame. \[09:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=586s) Texture coordinates are placed in Buffer 1, and they never change. \[09:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=590s) The mesh is dynamic, and the bounds are set to cover the full swing of the flag. \[09:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=596s) Every frame, each vertex gets a sine wave that grows towards the free edge, so that the pole side stays put. \`\`\`kotlin // Gemini wrote the math fun wave(t: Float) { for (i in 0 until 273) { val u = (i % 21) / 20f // 0 at the pole setZ(i, 0.06f \* u \* sin(6f \* u - 4f \* t)) } recomputeNormals() // from neighbors } // Every frame: one upload (\~6.5 KB) while (isActive) withFrameNanos { ns -\> wave(ns / 1e9f) flagMesh.meshBuffer.updateVertexData( bufferIndex = 0, vertexData = ByteBufferRegion( posNormals, 0, 273 \* 24)) } \`\`\` \[10:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=605s) The normals are recomputed from the neighboring positions, which is what makes the folds catch the light. \[10:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=610s) \`updateVertexData\` uploads about 6.5 KB of data to the GPU each frame. \[10:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=616s) We do not recreate the mesh or the entity. \[10:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=619s) Now let's see it all together. \[10:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=621s) We place the car model on the table, then we use ARCore to draw the track. \[10:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=627s) The mesh flag we just-- the flag mesh we just built appears at the destination. \[10:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=632s) The car drives along the track, and we use glTF Introspection API to steer and spin the wheels of the car. \[10:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=639s) The mesh appears with the asphalt material, but we can also use mesh API together with the material API to change the look and feel of the road, like you can see on the video. \[10:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=648s) That is like that is some powerful stuff right at your finger fingertips. ### Summary and getting started \[10:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=654s) Today, we've covered a lot of ways to take your apps from 2D to spatial. \[10:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=659s) With the glTF Introspection API, you can now tap directly into the inner metadata of a glTF model, triggering embedded animations, transforming individual subnodes, and even swapping materials to alter its look and feel all at runtime. \[11:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=673s) Then, we saw that when pre-made 3D models weren't enough, we could leverage our brand new Mesh API to build custom geometry. \[11:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=681s) Whether you need to build static shapes from scratch or stream dynamic shapes dynamic geometry in real time, you now have the tools to do so. \[11:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=689s) And like Egor just showed, pairing those building blocks with Gemini means you don't even need to do the math alone. \[11:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=695s) Now, I'll repeat something I said earlier: everything you saw was running in an Android app, written in idiomatic Kotlin, right inside Android Studio. \[11:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=704s) I see a lot of laptops in the audience today, and I hope that Egor and I excited you enough to open up Android Studio and spin up the Android XR Emulator today. \[11:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=713s) Let your imagination run loose, and use your existing Android skills, along with what we showed today, to build amazing XR experiences. \[12:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mssk4zPs0zU\&t=721s) On behalf of Egor and myself, thank you so much for joining us today, and enjoy the rest of the Android Dev Summit.</a>
entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces the custom 3D geometry and glTF introspection APIs in the Jetpack XR SDK, enabling developers to programmatically generate procedural meshes and manipulate 3D models at runtime using Kotlin.

entries.title: Navigating multi-device quality
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript focusing on navigating multi-device quality and publishing beyond mobile on Google Play. It matters because it helps developers understand how to optimize and distribute apps across various form factors.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/navigating-multi-device-quality-publishing-beyond-mobile-on-google-play.txt" target="_blank">Navigating multi-device quality \& publishing beyond mobile on Google Play - Speakers: Jan Kleinert (Developer Relations Engineer), Faustine Liao (DFX Operations Lead) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/navigating-multi-device-quality-publishing-beyond-mobile-on-google-play ## About the talk As the Android ecosystem expands across wrists, living rooms, vehicles, and XR, the opportunity to reach users on new screens is growing. However, distributing across Wear OS, Android TV, Android Auto, Android Automotive OS, or Android XR introduces distinct considerations for testing, store listings, and app reviews. This session explores how to effectively utilize Google Play Console for non-mobile form factors to help streamline a predictable multi-device launch. We will cover key distribution decisions, including how to structure track strategies and package names, configure targeted testing tracks, and tailor store listings. You'll get a practical walkthrough of form-factor App Quality guidelines to help avoid common review pitfalls and publish on Google Play with greater confidence. ## Summary - Modular app bundles isolate form-factor releases from your mobile app. If a form-factor review fails, only that specific bundle is blocked while your mobile release publishes as intended. - Play Console tracks offer flexible publishing paths, with exceptions for Wear OS and Android Auto. Wear OS requires a dedicated track, while Android Auto must use the standard mobile track. - Internal testing tracks distribute builds to up to 100 testers without triggering a Play review. Closed and open testing tracks do trigger reviews, helping you resolve hurdles before launch. - Form-factor review rejections often stem from missed device requirements, such as car app category limits or absent screenshots. Provide valid demo account credentials in Play Console whenever your app requires login. ## Resources - \[Android user experience guidelines\](https://developer.android.com/quality/user-experience) - \[Android TV app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/tv-app-quality) - \[Android XR app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/xr-app-quality) - \[Android for Cars app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/car-app-quality) - \[Wear OS app quality guidelines\](https://goo.gle/wear-app-quality) ## Topics google-play, multi-device, android-tv, android-auto, wear-os, android-xr, app-quality ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=5s) Welcome, everyone. \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=6s) Thank you so much for joining us for this session on navigating multi-device app quality and publishing on Google Play for form factors beyond mobile. \[00:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=14s) I'm Jan Kleinert, a Developer Relations Engineer on the Android for Cars team. \[00:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=18s) And I'm Faustine Liao, an Operations Lead on the Play Trust and Safety team. \[00:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=22s) We are so excited to have everyone here with us today. \[00:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=25s) So for years, when we said Android development, most of us really pictured just like a mobile device, but the Android ecosystem has expanded far beyond just smartphones. \[00:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=34s) So today, your users are interacting with apps in their living rooms on Android TV, maybe in the carpool line or while they're charging their cars on Android Auto or Automotive OS, on their wrists with Wear OS, and increasingly in immersive 3D spaces with Android XR. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=52s) This is a massive opportunity for growth, but expanding to these form factors means there are just a few marginal considerations to take into account for your publishing strategy. \[01:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=61s) The overall process from building your app to having it published and live on Google Play remains generally the same as you're used to for mobile releases. \[01:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=70s) Build and prepare your app, then create your listing in Play Console, test your app, upload and submit your production release, and then wait for review and approval. \[01:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=80s) However, there are some unique considerations for publishing apps for form factors beyond mobile. \[01:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=86s) And today, we're going to give you a clear framework to help you prepare for a smoother, more predictable multi-device release process. \[01:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=94s) Let's start with the foundation: how to architect and package your app. ### App architecture and packaging \[01:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=100s) So before you even touch Google Play Console, you have an important architectural decision to make. \[01:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=104s) Do you build a single, unified app bundle containing everything for all the form factors you support, or do you break your app into form factor-specific modules and generate Android App Bundles, or AABs, for each? \[01:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=117s) So when I'm saying modules or modularization, what I'm referring to is just a means of structuring your codebase in a way that improves maintainability. \[02:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=125s) There are many approaches to modularization, but, in general, what you're doing is, organizing your codebase into loosely coupled, self-contained parts, where each part is a module. \[02:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=136s) So while a unified Android app bundle approach might sound simpler to manage, we actually recommend the modular approach. \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=143s) So here's an example that demonstrates why we recommend this modular approach. \[02:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=148s) So let's imagine you have an app that supports both mobile and Android TV. \[02:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=153s) If you submit a single Android app bundle on the standard mobile release track and your Android TV app fails a review check, it halts the entire release. \[02:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=163s) So that's going to impact both the release of your Android TV app and your mobile app. \[02:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=167s) So even though there wasn't an issue with your mobile app specifically, you'll need to address the issues that caused that Android TV review to fail and resubmit your app for review before the release can be made available to your users. \[03:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=181s) Now on the other hand, modular Android app bundles for each form factor will give you more granular control and help you isolate those form factor releases from your mobile releases. \[03:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=192s) So instead, if you have separate app modules for your mobile app and your TV app, you can generate separate Android app bundles for each. \[03:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=200s) And then if there's an issue with the review for your TV app, then only that app's release is going to be blocked until you can resolve the issue. \[03:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=210s) The mobile app's release will be published as intended. \[03:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=215s) Now as I mentioned earlier, there are many approaches to modularization. \[03:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=219s) So here's just one example of an approach for modularizing an audiobook app that has a mobile experience and an Android Automotive OS experience. \[03:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=228s) So up at the top, in green, we have an app module for each form factor, and this helps separate out the platform-specific dependencies. \[03:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=236s) Then in yellow, we have feature modules, and those correspond to isolated parts of the app's functionality. \[04:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=242s) The data modules are in blue, and then at the bottom, we have core, or common, modules, which are usually used, to contain code that other modules use frequently. \[04:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=252s) And then in your project's Gradle settings files, you can include, set up this multi-module Gradle configuration to support this kind of modularization. \`\`\`kts ... rootProject.name = "MultiFormFactorApp" // Define modules for each form factor include(":app:automotive") include(":app:mobile") include(":core:network") include(":data:books") include(":data:reviews") include(":feature:home") include(":feature:player") include(":feature:reviews") \`\`\` \[04:20\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=260s) So you'll keep using the same package name or application ID for each app module and bundle. ### Track strategy in Google Play Console \[04:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=268s) That modular approach ties directly into your track strategy in Play Console. \[04:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=273s) When you publish, you have the standard mobile track, but we also offer dedicated form factor tracks. \[04:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=280s) For Android TV, Android XR, and Android Automotive OS, you have a choice. \[04:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=286s) You can publish alongside mobile or use their dedicated form factor tracks. \[04:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=291s) However, there are two exceptions. \[04:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=294s) For Wear OS, you must use the dedicated Wear OS track. \[04:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=298s) And for Android Auto, because it is fundamentally an extension of your mobile app projected onto the car screen, the only choice is the standard mobile track. \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=309s) If you're managing multiple tracks, versioning is critical. \[05:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=313s) One approach is to assign the first couple of digits of your version code to the form factor. \[05:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=318s) For example, 01 for mobile, 02 for Wear OS, 03 for Android Automotive OS, and so on. \[05:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=327s) We generally recommend you make the version codes at least seven digits in length, so those remaining digits can be used for the app version. \[05:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=337s) This helps prevent version code collisions in Play Console. \[05:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=342s) Once your app is packaged, it's now time to test. \[05:44\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=344s) Form-factor development requires thorough testing, and Google Play gives you three distinct channels to do this before releasing to production: internal testing, closed testing, and open testing. \[06:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=360s) If you're using dedicated form-factor tracks, you can also combine these testing tracks with your form factors, giving you even more granular control over the process. \[06:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=369s) For example, you could have a closed testing release for your mobile app on the standard track and a separate closed testing release for your Android TV app on the dedicated Android TV form-factor track with different sets of testers if you want to set it up that way. \[06:25\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=385s) So, internal testing is a great starting point. \[06:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=388s) It lets you quickly distribute your app to up to 100 testers, and, crucially, it does not trigger a Play review. \[06:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=394s) So, this means you and your testers can install your app on devices quickly and validate the experience on emulators or a real TV, watch, or other device. \[06:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=403s) And with internal tests, you'll get a unique URL that you can share with those testers. \[06:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=409s) Once you're happy with the results of your internal testing, you can move to closed testing and open testing. \[06:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=415s) You can expand beyond internal testing with a closed testing release, which lets you test pre-release versions of your app with a wider set of testers to get targeted feedback. \[07:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=427s) You can manage your closed testing groups either as lists of email addresses or through Google Groups. \[07:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=433s) Open testing, on the other hand, helps you run a test with a larger group on Google Play. \[07:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93NhXMuUDJo\&t=438s) You will be visible on Google Play, and anyone can join the open testing program. entries.summary: This document introduces best practices for publishing and maintaining multi-device Android applications across form factors like Wear OS, Android TV, Android Auto, and Android XR using the Google Play Console. It matters because modular packaging and targeted testing tracks help developers isolate form-factor updates, streamline reviews, and avoid blocking mobile production releases.

entries.title: On-device intelligence: Optimized performance and quality using Android ML Kit APIs
entries.summary: Added a new developer documentation page featuring a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript about optimizing performance and quality using Android ML Kit APIs for on-device intelligence.

Internal testing shows a 2x speedup compared to running models in the cloud. - Gemini Nano memory usage dropped from 3.6 GB to 1.1 GB. Key optimizations include 2-bit quantization and a shared KV cache. - Prefix caching and speculative decoding significantly accelerate inference. Reusing system prompts cuts processed tokens by 60%, while a smaller drafter model delivers an average 2x speedup. - New on-device capabilities expand app interactions through speech translation and function calling. Adding thinking mode raises tool-calling accuracy on Gemini Nano 4 by 13 points out of 100. - Multimodal embeddings combine with AppSearch to store and retrieve data through cosine similarity. Your app executes the search logic locally, protecting user privacy and data security. ## Resources - \[Prompt API Android documentation\](https://developers.google.com/ml-kit/genai/prompt/android) ## entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/optimize-media-playback-and-maximize-reach-with-jetpack-media3-apis.txt" target="_blank">Optimize media playback and maximize reach with Jetpack Media3 APIs - Speakers: Donovan McMurray (Developer Relations Engineer), Toni Heidenreich (Software Engineer), Kristina Simakova (Engineering Manager) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/optimize-media-playback-and-maximize-reach-with-jetpack-media3-apis ## About the talk Media consumption accounts for a large portion of user time spent on mobile devices, which requires the playback experience to be flawless, highly efficient and mindful of battery life. Furthermore, users expect these experiences to seamlessly transition across their devices, from phones to living room TVs and beyond. Explore how architectural updates in Media3 and ExoPlayer power seamless playback across form factors. The discussion centers on crafting responsive interfaces with the Media3 Compose UI toolkit, eliminating buffering in feeds using the new PreloadManager and extending your app to living room screens and Android XR with CastPlayer and spatial audio. ## Summary - Media3 UI Compose provides ready-made player composables and customizable building blocks. You can override specific control slots while letting the library manage player state and transitions. - A newly rewritten CastPlayer replaces the standalone Cast SDK. It implements the standard player interface and automatically delegates playback between local ExoPlayer instances and remote Cast devices. - The rebuilt editing pipeline decouples from OpenGL and manages hardware buffers directly. This zero-copy approach lowers memory overhead, and decoupling lets developers integrate modern graphic frameworks like WebGPU. - Media3 adds out-of-the-box support for Eclipsa Video and Eclipsa Audio on Android 17 and later. Prescriptive HDR metadata adapts highlights to ambient light, while spatial audio handles multiple mixed presentations. - Built-in optimizations like PCM audio offload reduce screen-off power consumption by up to 20%. The upcoming CodecDB uses benchmark metrics to select device-optimal encoder settings. ## Resources - \[Media3 GitHub repository\](https://github.com/androidx/media) - \[Media3 developer documentation\](https://goo.gle/media3) ## Topics jetpack-media3, exoplayer, jetpack-compose, google-cast, video-editing, audio, performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to Jetpack Media3 \[00:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=0s) Okay. \[00:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=5s) Welcome everyone. \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=7s) My name is Toni. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=8s) I'm an engineer on the Android media team. \[00:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=10s) And together with Kristina and Donovan, we're going to talk about how Jetpack Media3 can help you with all your media needs on Android. \[00:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=18s) Media3 is Android's support library for everything media-related, whether it's playback with ExoPlayer, sharing media with media session and Cast, or ed-- editing media with transformer, or inspecting media, like extracting frames or metadata. \[00:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=36s) Media3 covers this entire space in a single library group. \[00:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=42s) As a support library, it's bundled into your app. \[00:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=45s) That means we can ensure consistency, so the same code running on all OS versions and all devices. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=52s) It also helps with updatability. \[00:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFs0FLMGAeM\&t=54s) Every bug fix we do reaches down to API 24, and it's not tied to any OS release cycle. entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/outperform-yourself-in-compose.txt" target="_blank">Outperform yourself in Compose - Speakers: Andrei Shikov (Software Engineer), Andrew Bailey (Software Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t5ujT_o8qj0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/outperform-yourself-in-compose ## About the talk Jetpack Compose makes it easy to design high-quality user interfaces, but it can be difficult to track down issues that affect UI performance. These kinds of issues can lead to problems that your users notice, like startup latency, and dropped frames that appear as scroll jank or choppy animations. In this talk, we'll introduce tools to uncover what's impacting your UI's performance, focusing on Perfetto and (re-)composition tracing. We'll then explore specific anti-patterns you may be using that are secretly costing you, how you can find them in your code, and what positive patterns you can replace them with. By the end of this talk, you'll understand how to think in Compose with a performance mindset, and how to profile, analyze, and verify performance optimizations in your app. ## Summary - Perfetto traces record on-device activity and show Compose slices such as composition and layout along the main thread. Use them to inspect frame timelines and track phase durations. - Every operation inside composables has a cost, including launching and canceling coroutines. Audit side effect APIs and consider merging effects with identical keys to reduce composition overhead. - Composition tracing annotates composable functions, and recomposition tracing (1.13+) tracks state reads and writes causing recomposition. They help diagnose unexpected work directly within Perfetto traces. - ComputedState (Compose 1.13+) avoids unwanted invalidations and is typically faster than DerivedState during read-after-write invalidations. DerivedState remains useful when expensive calculations or allocations benefit from caching. - Skipping composables carries upkeep costs and parameter comparison overhead. Rely on strong skipping and object identity equality, or avoid invalidations entirely, rather than forcing stability. ## Skills - \[Android Skills repository\](https://github.com/android/skills) ## Resources - \[Perfetto Trace Viewer\](https://ui.perfetto.dev) - \[Composition and recomposition tracing guide\](https://goo.gle/composition-tracing) - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds a video talk and interactive transcript from the Android Dev Summit focusing on powering interactive surfaces with Remote Compose.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/powering-interactive-surfaces-with-remote-compose.txt" target="_blank">Powering interactive surfaces with Remote Compose - Speakers: Nicolas Roard (Sr Staff Software Engineer), John Hoford (Developer), John Zoeller (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=csh2Opo_wjE - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/powering-interactive-surfaces-with-remote-compose ## About the talk Remote Compose introduces a new way to project expressive and interactive UI onto remote surfaces like widgets. By serializing layouts into compact binary payloads, RemoteCompose decouples UI from host execution to deliver significant advantages. Key benefits include edge interactivity that enables high-performance rendering through local execution on the remote device, fluid scaling that allows UIs to reflow across diverse form factors via remote-side component evaluations, and a unified developer workflow that removes the need for platform-specific remote UI frameworks through familiar Jetpack Compose APIs. This session unpacks these benefits and provides live production examples, including modern Wear OS Widgets and the glanceable Wear Workout Tracker experience in Runkeeper. ## Summary - Remote Compose packages UI into a compact binary document instead of sending an app or screen copy across process boundaries. - Developers create documents using Compose APIs or JSON. Android Studio provides live previews while writing composables. - Loaded documents run by themselves directly on the player. They handle events such as resizing and touch without round trips to its creator. - Built-in optimizations such as component templates and document compression shrink payloads down to a few kilobytes. - Jetpack Glance emits Remote Compose documents for launcher widgets and Wear OS widgets. This decouples the UI from app execution to save battery. ## Resources - \[ASICS Runkeeper Wear OS open beta\](https://goo.gle/runkeeper-wearos) - \[Migrating Wear OS tiles to widgets\](https://goo.gle/wearos-tiles-widgets-migration) ## Topics remote-compose, jetpack-compose, android-widgets, wear-os, ui-framework ## Transcript ### Introduction and overview of Remote entries.summary: This new documentation page introduces Remote Compose, a feature that serializes Jetpack Compose UIs into compact binary payloads to project interactive content onto remote surfaces like widgets efficiently.
