entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scale-your-app-for-every-screen-with-compose.txt" target="_blank">Scale your app for every screen with Compose - Speakers: Francesco Romano (Senior Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scale-your-app-for-every-screen-with-compose ## About the talk The Android ecosystem is vast, with users shifting seamlessly across phones, tablets, foldables, and desktop environments. Now that we are Compose First, this session explores how to architect your app for resizable windows and diverse aspect ratios---where traditional layout assumptions break down, leading to stretched UIs and lost state. Explore how the latest capabilities in Jetpack Compose, Navigation 3, and WindowManager can help you build dynamic layouts that naturally scale from compact screens to dual-pane displays. Walk away with strategies to accelerate your development workflow using Gemini and our skills, like the adaptive skill, to automatically refactor legacy codebases for larger screens. ## Summary - Android platforms require adaptive apps because the system ignores orientation and aspect ratio locks on larger screens starting in Android 16, with manifest opt-outs removed in Android 17. - The experimental \`MediaQuery\` API declaratively tracks active UI capabilities such as window size and folding postures. It replaces stitching together multiple legacy platform managers into Compose state. - Stable \`Grid\` and \`FlexBox\` primitives provide adaptive layout building blocks. \`Grid\` enables parameterized multi-dimensional arrangements within a single composable, while \`FlexBox\` provides one-dimensional space distribution and wrapping. - Jetpack Navigation 3 structures app-level multi-pane flows around state and scenes. Custom scene strategies evaluate UI capabilities and window size classes to dynamically switch between single-pane and multi-pane presentations. - Compose Adaptive skills for Gemini automate app migrations to modern responsive components. The updated skill refactors layouts, resolves state loss bugs, and configures desktop inputs such as keyboard shortcuts and cursors. ## Resources - \[Install Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) ## Topics jetpack-compose, adaptive-layouts, mediaquery, grid-layout, flexbox, navigation-3, android-skills ## Transcript ### Introduction to scaling apps across screens \*\*Francesco Romano\*\* \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=6s) Hi everyone. \[00:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=8s) Today, we're going to have a deep technical dive on how to scale your app to every screen with Jetpack Compose. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=16s) Why scaling to every screen? \[00:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=17s) Because the Android ecosystem has expanded across so many different form factors. \[00:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=22s) Your APK can run on phones, foldables, tablets, Chromebooks and Googlebooks, TVs, automotive infotainment systems, XR devices, and so on. \[00:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=33s) So first thing, it's meet your users where they are. \[00:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=37s) And second, the shift of the Android platform towards adaptive apps, it's not transitory. \[00:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=46s) It's not like we're going back to a phone-only world, it's here to stay. \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=50s) And I have a quick timeline here. \[00:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=53s) In 2022, we started laying the foundation. \[00:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=57s) We had Android 12L, the first release of Jetpack WindowManager, we gave you APIs like window size classes, and we published the first version of the adaptive app quality guidelines. \[01:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=70s) Then, we also updated Google Play so that ratings are split by device type, and we started to include the adaptive app quality guidelines into ranking decisions. \[01:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=83s) In Android 15, we also had desktop windowing landed in AOSP, and Compose Material 3 Adaptive that hit stable. \[01:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=94s) And then starting from Android 16, SDK 36, the system simply ignores orientation locks, aspect ratio locks, resizability flags on bigger screens. \[01:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=106s) Together with the release of connected displays, now your APK can run in virtually any window size. \[01:54\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=114s) And SDK 36 gave you one temporary manifest flag to opt out from orientation and aspect ratio override. \[02:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=123s) In Android 17, that opt-out is gone. \[02:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=126s) So building adaptive, it's a baseline platform requirement. \[02:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=133s) Now, over the last decade, we worked closely with teams across the ecosystem, and we learned first-hand why building adaptive can feel hard. \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=143s) You have some state loss, fragmented window APIs, unclear signals on when to switch layout, and just some old assumptions baked deep down into the codebase. \[02:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=156s) So we took everything that we learned from this decade of developer challenges, and we built it directly into two places: first, into the UI toolkit itself. \[02:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=167s) Today, we will explore some major new capabilities in Jetpack Compose: media query, grid, \`FlexBox\`, and Navigation 3. \[02:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=176s) But also in agentic tools that write the code with you through the official Android skills for Gemini in Android Studio and the Android CLI. \[03:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=187s) For example, we will see the Compose adaptive skills that was released at the Google I/O earlier this year. \[03:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=193s) It was already capable of migrating phone layouts to bigger window sizes. \[03:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=199s) Now, it can also fix your state loss, it can implement foldable-unique experiences like tabletop, and improve input support by discovering and implementing keyboard shortcuts, custom cursors, tooltips, and so on. \[03:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=219s) Okay, let's start with Jetpack Compose, which is the foundation for all of this. \[03:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=227s) Jetpack Compose went stable in 2021, so that marks its fifth birthday. \[03:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=233s) And over those five years, we've seen across thousands of production apps how much easier and more reliable it is to build adaptive with Compose. \[04:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=245s) Android development is now officially Compose-first. \[04:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=248s) That means all the new modern adaptive layouts, styling, navigation components are built for Compose. \[04:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=257s) And from a system architecture perspective, the biggest advantage of Compose for adaptive apps over the legacy view system, it's how state and UI interact. \[04:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=270s) And to explain this, I want to do a quick comparison with the view system. \[04:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=275s) So, think about how the view system worked. \[04:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=279s) Your UI was a tree of mutable objects that you inflated once from static XML files. \[04:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=289s) You had different resource qualifiers, and let's start with the major issue here: duplication across different resource qualifiers. \[04:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=298s) When you build an adaptive UI in XML, you don't have any conditional logic inside the layout file. \[05:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=304s) Instead, you just duplicate the entire hierarchy across resource folders, like layout, layout smallest window 600 dp, layout land, and so on. \[05:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=317s) Okay, look at the \`EditText\` example on the right. \`\`\`xml \`\`\` \`\`\`xml \`\`\` \[05:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=321s) That's the exact same logical component that handles text input, and it's scattered across different XML files. \[05:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=332s) If you update an attribute like \`inputType\` or \`maxLength\` in the phone layout, nothing in the compiler forces you to update it also in the tablet layout. \[05:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=342s) And because the components are decoupled across different files, structural drift is almost guaranteed over time. \[05:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=353s) And that duplication is also linked to another issue, which is state loss during configuration changes. \[06:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=360s) Remember that the in the View system, UI components are stateful. \[06:05\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=365s) An \`EditText\` owns its internal Editable buffer, custom cursor position, focus state, some state. \[06:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=375s) So, when a user, let's say, unfolds the device or resizes the window across a certain threshold, Android destroys the entire view hierarchy and inflates the new XML files from scratch. \[06:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=389s) To save the user input, the framework relies on onSaveInstanceState, which will pack the state linked to the ID of that view. \[06:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=399s) But that creates three possible failure modes. \[06:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=403s) First, if someone accidentally named the ID \`text_input\` instead of \`text_msg\` in the other XML, the state restoration silently drops the user's input text with zero warnings. \[06:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=419s) Second, onRestoreInstanceState runs after onViewCreated, which can frequently clashes with the ViewModel observers, can cause callback loops. \[07:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=431s) And third, if you swap the widget type across qualifiers, let's say on a compact screen maybe you want a spinner, and on a wider screen you want a RadioGroup, if they share the same ID, that crashes at runtime with a ClassCastException. \[07:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=449s) In Jetpack Compose, instead, your UI is not an object that you construct once. \[07:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=455s) Your UI is a pure function of state. \[07:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=458s) And that change completely what a configuration change even is. \[07:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=465s) What is a configuration change in Compose? \[07:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=468s) I have a hint. ### Handling configuration changes and UI capabilities \*\*Francesco Romano\*\* \[07:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=472s) Yeah. \[07:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=472s) In Compose, a configuration change is just another recomposition, and recompositions happen all the time. \[07:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=479s) When the window gets wider, maybe because the user unfolded the devices, your composables read the new size, and the ones whose output depends on it just rerun. \[08:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=491s) That's That's the whole event. \[08:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=493s) But now, let's see what it means to write modern adaptive apps using the latest Compose tools and, components. \[08:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=503s) So, the XML world made you ask questions like, "Am I running on a phone, a tablet, or a desktop?", and then branching the UI based on the device category. \[08:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=515s) But there's a fundamental reason to avoid doing that. \[08:38\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=518s) Even when running on the exact same physical device, the application context and the UI capabilities can change dynamically at runtime. \[08:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=529s) So, The message that I want to leave is that UI decisions should be driven by the current active capabilities: current window size, posture, some hardware characteristics. \[09:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=543s) So, let's see a classic example, which is desktop windowing on an external monitor. \[09:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=549s) If you take your Pixel phone and plug it on an external monitor on your desk, the exact same app process that was just running on a 6-inch portrait screen is now running on a 32-inch wide monitor with physical keyboard and mouse attached. \[09:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=567s) So, checking what the device type the app is running on guarantees nothing about the screen it is actually being displayed on, or the input modalities. \[09:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=580s) And, on top of that, Android supports multi-windows, so windows can be resized. \[09:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=586s) Even if the screen of a Googlebook is bigger than the phone, your app may be running on a 400 dp wide window, together with other apps. \[09:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=599s) So, querying the static physical display metrics can also be meaningless. \[10:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=606s) So, to architect apps for Compose first, we need to understand how to query the environment. \[10:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=613s) And I want to start by try to formalize the concept of UI capabilities. \[10:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=619s) UI capabilities includes not only the window width and height or the foldable posture, but also input and output modalities that are currently active. \[10:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=629s) We have seen in the desktop environment users are not always using touch screen. \[10:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=636s) They can use keyboard and mouse. \[10:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=637s) In the automotive system, some cars have a rotary knob or different input, different way to input signals. \[10:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=646s) And also, beyond the screen size and input, how far the user is from the display, like the viewing distance, or whether a hardware camera or microphone is currently connected. \[11:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=661s) Those are all the UI capabilities. ### Detecting postures with the mediaQuery API \*\*Francesco Romano\*\* \[11:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=664s) Now, if you wanted to retrieve all of the signals, you had to stitch together 5, 6 different APIs from different sources. \[11:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=673s) You needed the configuration object, the WindowMetricsCalculator, the WindowInfoTracker, the InputManager, the PackageManager, and then, manually, converting each of them in a state, a Compose state. \[11:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=687s) Did you like doing that? \[11:29\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=689s) I did not. \[11:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=691s) To solve this, we introduced the MediaQuery API in \`androidx.compose.ui\`. \`\`\`kotlin mediaQuery { ... } derivedMediaQuery { ... } \`\`\` \[11:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=696s) It's inspired by the CSS media queries. \[11:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=699s) And the word media doesn't mean audio or video playback. \[11:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=703s) It refers to the medium, the environment on which your UI is being rendered. \[11:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=709s) And MediaQuery gives you a single declarative Compose-native way to query the UI capabilities. \[11:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=717s) Let's look at the properties exposed in the \`UiMediaScope\`. \`\`\`kotlin sealed interface UiMediaScope { @get:FrequentlyChangingValue val windowWidth: Dp @get:FrequentlyChangingValue val windowHeight: Dp val windowPosture: Posture // Flat, Tabletop, Book val pointerPrecision: PointerPrecision // Fine, Coarse, Blunt, None val keyboardKind: KeyboardKind // Physical, Virtual, None val hasCamera: Boolean val hasMicrophone: Boolean val viewingDistance: ViewingDistance // Near, Medium, Far } \`\`\` \[12:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=721s) \`windowWidth\` and \`windowHeight\` in Dp. \[12:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=723s) \`windowPosture\`, which is meant for foldables right now, and can be Flat, Tabletop, or Book. \[12:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=730s) \`pointerPrecision\` tells you the precision of the primary pointing device: Fine for mouse, Stylus, or Trackpad; Coarse for Touch; Blunt for joystick, controllers, or None. \[12:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=743s) \`keyboardKind\` can be physical, virtual, or none. \[12:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=747s) \`hasCamera\` and \`hasMicrophone\` dynamically track whether this hardware is available. \[12:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=752s) Think about external camera that can be plugged in. \[12:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=755s) And \`viewingDistance\` reports Near, Medium, or Far. \[12:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=761s) But I think it's easier if we look at a real example, which is detecting if the device is in Tabletop mode. \[12:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=768s) Tabletop mode is a posture that lets users half fold the device and usually set it on a surface. \[12:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=776s) And it's great for extended video playback, for a video call, time-lapse photography. \[13:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=784s) It's also super useful for, you know, following a recipe or watch a slideshow. \[13:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=791s) Now, if you wanted to detect Tabletop posture before MediaQuery, you had to write all of this code. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun currentVideoPlayerLayout(): VideoPlayerLayout { val context = LocalContext.current val windowLayoutInfo by WindowInfoTracker.getOrCreate(context).windowLayoutInfo(context) .collectAsStateWithLifecycle(null) val isTabletopPosture = windowLayoutInfo?.displayFeatures?.any { displayFeature -\> displayFeature is FoldingFeature \&\& displayFeature.state == FoldingFeature.State.HALF_OPENED \&\& displayFeature.orientation == FoldingFeature.Orientation.HORIZONTAL } ?: false return if (isTabletopPosture) { VideoPlayerLayout.Tabletop } else { VideoPlayerLayout.Default } } \`\`\` \[13:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=797s) You had to obtain the context, get an instance of WindowInfoTracker, collect the \`windowLayoutInfo\`, which is a flow, a lifecycle aware Compose state, and then iterate through the \`displayFeatures\` to check if there is one that is a \`FoldingFeature\`, is half opened, and is horizontal. \[13:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=816s) And that is just to detect the posture. \[13:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=819s) That is a lot of boilerplate. \[13:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=822s) With a new MediaQuery API, all of that shrinks down to just this few lines of code. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun currentVideoPlayerLayout(): VideoPlayerLayout { return mediaQuery { when(windowPosture) { UiMediaScope.Posture.Tabletop -\> VideoPlayerLayout.Tabletop else -\> VideoPlayerLayout.Default } } } \`\`\` \[13:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=827s) The \`mediaQuery\` function takes a single lambda parameter, and inside that lambda's receiver scope, it exposes the set of properties that we just saw. \[13:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=837s) In this example, by simply checking \`windowPosture\` in a when expression, we can immediately return the right composable. \[14:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=847s) And here are two other examples of how to use the API. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun AdaptiveChatControls( onStartVideoCall: () -\> Unit, onSendMessage: () -\> Unit, ) { // 1. Return a Dp value directly based on pointer precision val chipPadding = mediaQuery { if (pointerPrecision == PointerPrecision.Fine) 2.dp else 8.dp } // 2. Return a Boolean combining hardware capabilities val canVideoCall = mediaQuery { hasCamera \&\& hasMicrophone } val hasPhysicalKeyboard = mediaQuery { keyboardKind == KeyboardKind.Physical } Row(modifier = Modifier.padding(chipPadding)) { if (canVideoCall) { IconButton(onClick = onStartVideoCall) { Icon(Icons.Default.Videocam, contentDescription = "Video call") } } Button(onClick = onSendMessage) { Text(if (hasPhysicalKeyboard) "Send (Ctrl+Enter)" else "Send") } } } \`\`\` \[14:11\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=851s) First is information density. \[14:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=853s) So when a user is on a laptop, a desktop monitor with a mouse, and pointer precision is Fine, we can tighten the padding on our UI components from, in this example, 8 Dp to 2 Dp to show more content comfortably, since users are not using their fingers, the touch targets can be smaller. \[14:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=875s) Also, capability-driven actions. \[14:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=879s) Let's say we have a chat input bar, we can check \`hasCamera\` and \`hasMicrophone\` to dynamically show or hide the video call action button, or we can combine keyboard kind is physical to show, or not, some keyboard shortcut hints like press Ctrl+Enter to send. \[14:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=897s) Those are all retrieved at the run time. \[14:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=899s) And MediaQuery is also great for testing and preview generation. \`\`\`kotlin @Preview(name = "Tabletop + Fine Pointer", widthDp = 840, heightDp = 700) @Composable fun TabletopPlayerPreview() { val simulatedMediaScope = object : UiMediaScope { override val windowWidth = 840.dp override val windowHeight = 700.dp override val windowPosture = UiMediaScope.Posture.Tabletop override val pointerPrecision = UiMediaScope.PointerPrecision.Fine override val keyboardKind = UiMediaScope.KeyboardKind.Physical override val hasCamera = true override val hasMicrophone = true override val viewingDistance = UiMediaScope.ViewingDistance.Medium } CompositionLocalProvider(LocalUiMediaScope provides simulatedMediaScope) { VideoPlayerScreen() } } \`\`\` \[15:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=907s) So, basically, MediaQuery resolves its receiver through a composition local called \`LocalUiMediaScope\`. \[15:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGTkTKX7qq4\&t=914s) So, you can simply provide a fake \`UiMediaScope\` via \`CompositionLocalProvider\` in your preview, and you don't need to spin up foldable devices and put 90° or attach a mouse just to run a Compose UI test. ### Responsive screen layouts with Grid and FlexBox \*\*Francesco Romano\*\* entries.summary: This new documentation page provides a technical overview of building adaptive, resizable applications across diverse Android form factors using Jetpack Compose. It highlights recent platform requirements starting in Android 16, introduces new layout and navigation APIs like `MediaQuery`, `Grid`, `FlexBox`, and Navigation 3, and discusses leveraging Gemini-powered Android skills for automated migrations.

entries.title: Scaling input interactions beyond the touchscreen with Jetpack Compose
entries.summary: This new documentation page adds a Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript regarding scaling input interactions beyond the touchscreen using Jetpack Compose, helping developers build more adaptable UIs.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scaling-input-interactions-beyond-the-touchscreen-with-jetpack-compose.txt" target="_blank">Scaling input interactions beyond the touchscreen with Jetpack Compose - Speakers: Alex Vanyo (Software Engineer), Jeremy Walker (Compose Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iztM_PgoCjw - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/scaling-input-interactions-beyond-the-touchscreen-with-jetpack-compose ## About the talk As new form factors move beyond the touchscreen, Compose's input system has evolved to meet the challenge. Its layered architecture provides the foundation for supporting everything from advanced trackpad gestures to novel hardware inputs seamlessly. Through clear architectural breakdowns and hands-on code examples, follow the lifecycle of an input event all the way from the OS platform layer up to Compose gesture detectors and UI components. You will discover how to trace events across the entire stack, apply key architectural patterns for emerging input types, and confidently debug complex gesture interactions in your own apps. ## Summary - Jetpack Compose processes incoming Android pointer events through a six-phase pipeline. This pipeline maintains a hit path tree and dispatches events in three passes across UI nodes. - Trackpad inputs in Compose now map to mouse events instead of touch. Compose also converts platform fake finger events into dedicated pan and scale pointer events. - Intelligent eyewear trackpads introduce indirect input types rather than screen coordinate touches. They use a Primary Directional Motion Axis to map horizontal swipes into vertical next or previous navigation. - Testing support has expanded beyond touch with new methods such as \`performTrackpadInput\`. These APIs provide familiar testing surfaces to validate that apps handle non-touch devices correctly. ## Topics jetpack-compose, pointer-input, trackpads, gestures, intelligent-eyewear, accessibility entries.summary: This document outlines how Jetpack Compose's pointer input system has evolved to support diverse hardware inputs beyond touchscreens, such as trackpads, mice, and intelligent eyewear. It details the six-phase event pipeline, architectural patterns, and testing extensions like performTrackpadInput to ensure seamless cross-device compatibility.

entries.title: Take Compose state beyond the UI with Jetpack AppState
entries.summary: Added a new documentation page featuring the Android Dev Summit talk and interactive transcript on taking Jetpack Compose state beyond the UI using Jetpack AppState.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/take-compose-state-beyond-the-ui-with-jetpack-appstate.txt" target="_blank">Take Compose state beyond the UI with Jetpack AppState - Speakers: Ben Sagmoe (Developer Relations Engineer), Elif Bilgin Morris (Software Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/take-compose-state-beyond-the-ui-with-jetpack-appstate ## About the talk Compose's snapshot runtime, automatic dependency tracking, and atomic updates don't have to stop at the UI layer. Jetpack AppState lets you move Compose state upstream---streamlining what reaches your screens by hoisting and deriving state with the snapshot system before it ever hits the UI. In this session, you'll learn about AppState's two foundational libraries. We'll dive into StateStore for hoisting state, and Transform for using composition to derive state with plain Kotlin control flow---eliminating complex Flow combine chains and keeping your UI effortlessly in sync. ## Summary - Compose Runtime works as a general-purpose state management engine without Compose UI. Its snapshot system tracks reads dynamically and keeps concurrent updates consistent across properties. - Jetpack AppState Transform computes and exposes Compose State from headless composable blocks. It replaces complex Flow operator chains like \`combine\` while supporting early returns and nested state derivations. - Transform uses an eager headless frame clock to run transformations off the UI thread. The clock parks whenever watched states remain unchanged, avoiding wasted work. - Jetpack AppState StateStore shares Compose State across distinct components like activities and background services. Integrating it with DataStore lets individual keys survive process death without custom boilerplate. ## Resources - \[Molecule library on GitHub\](https://github.com/cashapp/molecule) - \[AppState documentation\](https://goo.gle/appstate-docs) - \[AppState Recipes repository on GitHub\](https://www.github.com/android/appstate-recipes) ## Topics jetpack-compose, jetpack-appstate, state-management, android-architecture, compose-runtime ## Transcript ### Introduction \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=6s) Hello, and welcome to Take Compose State Beyond the UI with Jetpack AppState. \[00:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=10s) My name is Ben, and I am a developer relations engineer working on that Jetpack architecture libraries. \[00:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=15s) And I'm Elif, and I'm one of the engineers who work on the app architecture libraries. \[00:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=19s) And today, we're here to talk to you about a future where Compose goes beyond the UI and into the data and domain layers of applications. \[00:27\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=27s) So, as I'm sure you're all well aware by now, Compose is the recommended toolkit for UI development on Android. \[00:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=33s) From tat-- phones and tablets to widgets, watches, TVs, and XR devices, Compose powers it all. \[00:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=39s) But as your app grows across these UI surfaces and background components, managing the state behind them gets harder, especially around two common pain points. \[00:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=50s) The first is deriving complex state. \[00:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=52s) Weaving together multiple data streams, local UI inputs, and ambient state, like network connectivity, that often turns into a tangle of operators like combine, flatMapLatest, and distinctUntilChanged. \[01:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=64s) And then the second is sharing state across components: keeping an activity, service, app widget, and more in sync, and making sure that that state can survive proc-ground-- process death when needed. \[01:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=76s) When we stepped back to look at these challenges, we came to look at how Compose itself is built. \[01:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=81s) Most people think of Compose as a UI toolkit, but it's actually two distinct layers: Compose UI on top and the Compose Runtime underneath. \[01:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=88s) While Compose UI handles layout, drawing, and input, the Compose Runtime is a general purpose engine for state management and recomposition. \[01:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=96s) It has no dependency on the UI. \[01:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=99s) And that's the realization that led us to build Jetpack AppState. \[01:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=103s) It's a family of libraries focused on making the most of Compose state beyond the UI. ### What is Compose State? \[01:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=109s) But before we dive into AppState, let's make sure we're on the same page when we talk about what we mean by Compose state. \[01:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=116s) And the answer is \`androidx.compose.runtime.State\`. \`\`\`kotlin /\*\* \* A value holder where reads to the \[value\] property during the execution of a \[Composable\] \* function, the current \[RecomposeScope\] will be subscribed to changes of that value. \*/ @Stable public interface State { public val value: T } \`\`\` \[02:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=120s) And the interface you're probably more familiar with, \`MutableState\`. \`\`\`kotlin /\*\* \* A mutable value holder where reads to the \[value\] property during the execution of a \[Composable\] \* function, the current \[RecomposeScope\] will be subscribed to changes of that value. When the \* \[value\] property is written to and changed, a recomposition of any subscribed \[RecomposeScope\]s \* will be scheduled. If \[value\] is written to with the same value, no recompositions will be \* scheduled. \*/ @Stable public interface MutableState : State { override var value: T public operator fun component1(): T public operator fun component2(): (T) -\> Unit } \`\`\` \[02:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=124s) Fundamentally, these are just bare-bones containers. \[02:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=127s) What makes them actually work is the Compose snapshot system. \[02:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=130s) So when we say Compose state, what we really mean is usually Snapshot State. \[02:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=136s) So, when you call \`mutableStateOf\`, you're making a container that routes reads and writes through the snapshot system. \[02:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=143s) And whenever your code runs inside of a snapshot observer, like a composition, you get two properties that a stream like a Flow doesn't give you. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } } \`\`\` \[02:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=152s) The first is automatic and dynamic read tracking. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Column { Text("Count: ${count.value}") AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } \`\`\` \[02:35\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=155s) So, automatic means that there's no subscribing or collecting. \[02:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=159s) Just reading \`.value\` is the subscription. \[02:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=162s) So, if we look at Counter here, reading \`count.value\` directly inside the composable reports to the that read to the composition, and it registers Counter in its list of readers. \[02:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=172s) And now look at \`AddButton\`. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Column { Text("Count: ${count.value}") AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } @Composable fun AddButton(onClick: () -\> Unit) { Button(onClick = onClick) { Text("Add") } } \`\`\` \[02:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=173s) It only writes to count on the click. \[02:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=175s) So, it isn't a reader. \[02:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=177s) When a user clicks \`AddButton\` and modifies count, the snapshot system tracks that write, which lets the composition know to invalidate Counter, but not \`AddButton\`. \[03:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=188s) And dynamic means that read tracking happens at runtime based on which code paths actually run. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val isVisible = remember { mutableStateOf(true) } val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Column { if (isVisible.value) { Text("Count: ${count.value}") } else { Text("Hidden") } AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } \`\`\` \[03:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=193s) So here, we're guarding the counter text behind an \`isVisible\` flag. \[03:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=197s) When \`isVisible\` is true, both \`isVisible\` and count are read. \[03:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=201s) So, Counter is registered as a reader of both of them. \[03:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=206s) And when \`isVisible\` is false, if the it-- the if branch doesn't run, count isn't read, so Counter is only registered as a reader of \`isVisible\`, not count. \`\`\`kotlin @Composable fun Counter() { val isVisible = remember { mutableStateOf(false) } val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Column { if (isVisible.value) { Text("Count: ${count.value}") } else { Text("Hidden") } AddButton(onClick = { count.value++ }) } } \`\`\` \[03:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=216s) So, when \`AddButton\` writes to count, there's nothing left to invalidate. \[03:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=221s) And now, the second property is not having to choose between consistency and granularity. \[03:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=226s) Consistency means that when you update multiple values in a snapshot, those changes stay isolated while your code runs, even if another thread is writing to them at the same time. \[03:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=235s) And those updates become visible all at once when the snapshot finishes. \[04:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=241s) Granularity means that separate properties can be dec-- declared and tracked individually, especially when they're unrelated. \[04:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=247s) So, updating one property only invalidates the readers that actually depend on it. \[04:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=253s) Let's take a look at this in some real code. \[04:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=255s) For example, we're going to look at a game that has three pieces of state: a level name, time survived, and score. \`\`\`kotlin val levelName: String = "Level 1 - Stay Alive!" val timeSurvived: Int = 0 val score: Double = 0.0 \`\`\` \[04:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=263s) So to start, let's look at a con-- a Flow implementation that chooses consistency at the expense of granularity by bundling everything into a \`GameUiState\` class. \`\`\`kotlin data class GameUiState( val levelName: String = "Level 1 - Stay Alive!", val timeSurvived: Int = 0, val score: Double = 0.0 ) \`\`\` \[04:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=273s) That means that every time \`updateScore\` runs, you copy the entire \`GameUiState\` so that both \`timeSurvived\` and score are able to update together in sync. \`\`\`kotlin data class GameUiState( val levelName: String = "Level 1 - Stay Alive!", val timeSurvived: Int = 0, val score: Double = 0.0 ) class GameViewModel : ViewModel() { val uiState = MutableStateFlow(GameUiState()) fun updateScore() = uiState.update { it.copy( timeSurvived = it.timeSurvived + 1, score = it.score + 10 + .01 \* it.timeSurvived ) } } \`\`\` \[04:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=282s) In the UI, \`GameScreen\` collects the UI state and reads from it to pass the properties that are relevant down to Header and \`ScoreBadge\`. \`\`\`kotlin data class GameUiState( val levelName: String = "Level 1 - Stay Alive!", val timeSurvived: Int = 0, val score: Double = 0.0 ) class GameViewModel : ViewModel() { val uiState = MutableStateFlow(GameUiState()) fun updateScore() = uiState.update { it.copy( timeSurvived = it.timeSurvived + 1, score = it.score + 10 + .01 \* it.timeSurvived ) } } @Composable fun GameScreen(viewModel: GameViewModel = viewModel()) { val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle() Column { Header(levelName = state.levelName) ScoreBadge( timeSurvived = state.timeSurvived, score = state.score ) } } \`\`\` \[04:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=290s) Because \`GameScreen\` reads every state, every call to \`updateScore\` invalidates \`GameScreen\` even though the header's data never changed. \[04:57\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=297s) Now, you could split every property into its own Flow to get granularity, but then you would lose consistency because another thread could update a value at while the other update block is running. \[05:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=309s) Now let's consider an alternate state-based implementation. \`\`\`kotlin @Stable class GameUiState { var levelName by mutableStateOf("Level 1 - Stay Alive!") var timeSurvived by mutableStateOf(0) var score by mutableStateOf(0.0) } \`\`\` \[05:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=313s) In this one, we use a \`GameUiState\` again. \[05:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=316s) But in this one, it's a little bit different because each property delegates to \`mutableStateOf\`. \[05:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=321s) Here, \`updateScore\` wraps its writes in \`withMutableSnapshot\`, and this is what gives us consistency across, writes. \`\`\`kotlin @Stable class GameUiState { var levelName by mutableStateOf("Level 1 - Stay Alive!") var timeSurvived by mutableStateOf(0) var score by mutableStateOf(0.0) } class GameViewModel : ViewModel() { val uiState = GameUiState() fun updateScore() = Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { uiState.timeSurvived += 1 uiState.score += 10 + .01 \* uiState.timeSurvived } } \`\`\` \[05:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=330s) And then in the UI, \`GameScreen\` passes State straight through to Header and \`ScoreBadge\`. \`\`\`kotlin @Stable class GameUiState { var levelName by mutableStateOf("Level 1 - Stay Alive!") var timeSurvived by mutableStateOf(0) var score by mutableStateOf(0.0) } class GameViewModel : ViewModel() { val uiState = GameUiState() fun updateScore() = Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { uiState.timeSurvived += 1 uiState.score += 10 + .01 \* uiState.timeSurvived } } @Composable fun GameScreen(viewModel: GameViewModel = viewModel()) { val state = viewModel.uiState Column { Header(state = state) ScoreBadge(state = state) } } \`\`\` \[05:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=334s) It doesn't read any of the properties, so when \`updateScore\` runs, \`GameScreen\` isn't a reader. \[05:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=340s) Only the actual component, in this case, \`ScoreBadge\`, is invalidated. \[05:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=346s) And lastly, notice that none of this is tied to the UI. \[05:49\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=349s) The UI just happens to be one place where these properties really shine. \[05:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=353s) And with that, thanks for coming to our talk. \[05:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=355s) Okay, jokes aside, I'll hand it over to Elif to take us through the first library, Transform. ### Introducing Transform \[06:01\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=361s) Okay. \[17:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1070s) All right. \[17:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1070s) All righty, thanks, Elif. \[17:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1076s) So, now that we've seen how Compose state is powerful and how Transform lets us derive it outside of the UI, one thing you might have noticed in the example so far is our inputs were Flows that we bridged using \`collectAsState\`. \[18:08\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1088s) But is that always necessary? \[18:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1090s) Why not use Compose state directly in our state holders? \[18:13\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1093s) So, to answer that question, I find it helpful to think about state within three broad categories. \[18:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1098s) The first is live state that's only ever stored in memory. \[18:21\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1101s) Think things like network or Bluetooth connection status. \[18:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1104s) You wouldn't want to use a persisted value. \[18:26\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1106s) And then, the second is transient state that should survive process death, but doesn't need to be stored indefinitely. \[18:31\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1111s) Think things like UI state, such as whether a card is expanded or not, and session state, like your navigation back stack or a form draft. \[18:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1119s) And then, the third is permanent state, which is stored indefinitely. \[18:43\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1123s) Think things like user preferences or a media library living in a database. \[18:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1128s) So, let's start with how you can use Compose state for both live and transient state. \[18:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1133s) Up until now, our architecture guidance kept Compose state in the UI layer, or at sometimes, in the ViewModels, and we told you to use Flow everywhere else. \[19:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1142s) But why was that? \[19:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1143s) And it's because as soon as you needed to combine a state property with a Flow, you had to convert it back using snapshotFlow. \[19:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1149s) But with Transform, that conversion isn't necessary. \[19:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1152s) So, let's look at what this looks or what this means, starting in a \`ViewModel\`. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class TaskListViewModel @Inject constructor( private val tasksRepository: TasksRepository, private val networkMonitor: NetworkMonitor, savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle, ) : ViewModel() { ... } \`\`\` \[19:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1157s) For local screen inputs, like \`selectedTaskIds\` here, you can declare plain \`mutableStateOf\` property instead of \`MutableStateFlow\`. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class TaskListViewModel @Inject constructor(...) : ViewModel() { var selectedTaskIds by mutableStateOf(emptySet()) private set } \`\`\` \[19:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1164s) And because this is something that you does don't necessarily want to persist across process death, it's okay that it's not like that it's just using \`mutableStateOf\`. \[19:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1173s) For things that you do want to survive process death, like the search query, you can back its mutable state directly with \`savedStateHandle.saveable\`. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class TaskListViewModel @Inject constructor(...) : ViewModel() { var selectedTaskIds by mutableStateOf(emptySet()) private set var searchQuery by savedStateHandle.saveable { mutableStateOf("") } private set } \`\`\` \[19:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1181s) And then, just like \`updateScore\` in the game example earlier, when a method updates multiple state values at once, wrapping the writes in \`withMutableSnapshot\` ensures consistency. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class TaskListViewModel @Inject constructor(...) : ViewModel() { var selectedTaskIds by mutableStateOf(emptySet()) private set var searchQuery by savedStateHandle.saveable { mutableStateOf("") } private set fun updateSearchQuery(query: String) { Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot { searchQuery = query selectedTaskIds = emptySet() } } } \`\`\` \[19:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1192s) Then, to combine \`searchQuery\` with a Room Flow, you just read it directly inside the Transform, while collecting the Flow. \`\`\`kotlin val tasksState: State = transform( initialValue = TaskListState.Loading, scope = viewModelScope, ) { val tasks = remember(searchQuery) { tasksRepository.getTasks(searchQuery) }.collectAsState(initial = null).value ?: return@transform TaskListState.Loading TaskListState.Success(tasks = tasks) } \`\`\` \[20:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1200s) So, what about live state like network connectivity? \`\`\`kotlin @Singleton class NetworkMonitor @Inject constructor( @ApplicationContext context: Context, ) { private val connectivityManager = context.getSystemService(ConnectivityManager::class.java) ... } \`\`\` \[20:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1203s) This usually lives in a Singleton that's because it's read across multiple screens or even by multiple app components, like services. \[20:10\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1210s) So, but that doesn't mean you can't use Compose State to store it. \[20:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1215s) In fact, it's often simpler than a flow-based version. \[20:17\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1217s) You don't need a callback flow or anything to do the adaption, you just update dot value directly in the callbacks. \`\`\`kotlin @Singleton class NetworkMonitor @Inject constructor(...) { ... private val _isOnline = mutableStateOf(checkCurrentConnectivity()) val isOnline: State = _isOnline } \`\`\` \[20:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1223s) And, if a consumer still needs a flow, you can use \`snapshotFlow\` to bridge back. \`\`\`kotlin @Singleton class NetworkMonitor @Inject constructor(...) { ... private val _isOnline = mutableStateOf(checkCurrentConnectivity()) val isOnline: State = _isOnline private val callback = object : ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback() { override fun onAvailable(network: Network) { _isOnline.value = true } override fun onLost(network: Network) { _isOnline.value = false } } init { connectivityManager.registerDefaultNetworkCallback(callback) } } \`\`\` \[20:28\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1228s) So, let's take a look what that looks like in the \`ViewModel\`. \[20:32\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1232s) You can read \`isOnline\` directly in a Transform, and it'll recompose when the value changes. \`\`\`kotlin val tasksState: State = transform( initialValue = TaskListState.Loading, scope = viewModelScope, ) { if (!networkMonitor.isOnline.value) { return@transform TaskListState.Offline } val tasks = remember(searchQuery) { tasksRepository.getTasks(searchQuery) }.collectAsState(initial = null).value ?: return@transform TaskListState.Loading TaskListState.Success(tasks = tasks) } \`\`\` \[20:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1237s) And, all this is just happening directly, there's no like, application scope, or, coroutine scope that you need to provide to update the state, it's just, you know, a direct, synchronous update. \[20:48\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1248s) So, with Transform, your \`ViewModel\` can combine State from Singleton managers, State in a \`ViewModel\`, and Flows from Repositories, all in a single Transform block. \[20:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1258s) And, now let's go back to transient State. \[21:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1260s) Earlier, I mentioned two types: UI state and session state. \[21:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1264s) For UI state, and even session state that lives inside of a single Activity, \`ViewModel\` and SavedState work great. \[21:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1269s) That's exactly what they were designed for. \[21:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1272s) But, when things start to break down is when that session state needs to be shared across a bunch of different UIs, and app components. \[21:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1278s) Once that state moves outside of a \`ViewModel\`, our existing APIs and guidance leave a bit of a gap. \[21:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1284s) So, first the SavedState APIs save into an Activity's Bundle, but that's not available in other app components, like a service. \[21:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1290s) Second, \`mutableStateOf\` in a Singleton, that only lives in memory, so it doesn't survive process death. ### Introducing StateStore \[21:36\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1296s) And, that's the gap that Jetpack AppState, \`StateStore\` fills. \[21:40\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1300s) It's a type-safe map of Compose State that can be shared across app components and backed by \`DataStore\` to provide, to survive process death. \[21:47\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1307s) You could wire \`DataStore\` into every Singleton yourself, but that means writing save and restore boilerplate for every property. \[21:53\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1313s) With the \`StateStore\` \`DataStore\` Integration, you hook up the \`DataStore\` once, and then you opt in each little bit of state that you want to persist. \[22:00\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1320s) So, let's build out that in our focus timer app. \[22:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1323s) We're going to start in-memory first, and then add \`DataStore\` persistence afterwards. \[22:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1327s) To set the stage, we're modeling a \`FocusSession\` as a sealed interface with idle, running, and paused states. \`\`\`kotlin sealed interface FocusSession { data object Idle : FocusSession data class Running(val taskId: String, val endTimeMillis: Long) : FocusSession data class Paused(val taskId: String, val remainingMillis: Long) : FocusSession } \`\`\` \[22:14\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1334s) And then, to store this state in \`StateStore\`, we defined a \`StateStoreKey\` with its type, \`FocusSession\`, and a default value, idle. \`\`\`kotlin sealed interface FocusSession { ... } object FocusSessionKey : StateStoreKey(defaultValue = FocusSession.Idle) \`\`\` \[22:23\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1343s) And then, we provide a Singleton \`StateStore\` in Hilt that we can inject into different components where we need it, such as Focus Session Manager. \`\`\`kotlin @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) object AppModule { @Provides @Singleton fun provideStateStore(): StateStore = StateStore() } @Singleton class FocusSessionManager @Inject constructor( private val stateStore: StateStore, ) { ... } \`\`\` \[22:30\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1350s) So, similar to how the \`ViewModel\` injects \`SavedStateHandle\`. \[22:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1354s) Okay. \[22:34\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1354s) So, now we've got a \`StateStore\`, but how do we use it? \[22:37\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1357s) Well, good thing, it's a small API. \[22:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1359s) It just has three methods, so we're going to go through them one by one. \[22:42\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1362s) The first is \`setState\`, which writes a new value for a key. \`\`\`kotlin fun startFocus(taskId: String, durationMinutes: Int = 25) { val endTime = System.currentTimeMillis() + durationMinutes \* 60_000L stateStore.setState( FocusSessionKey, FocusSession.Running(taskId = taskId, endTimeMillis = endTime), ) } fun endFocus() { stateStore.setState(FocusSessionKey, FocusSession.Idle) } \`\`\` \[22:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1366s) When a session starts, we set it to running, and when the session ends, we set it to idle. \[22:50\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1370s) That's it. \[22:52\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1372s) Second, we have, still have, \`updateState\`, which lets you compute a new value based off of the current value, such as calculating the time remaining when switching between running and paused. \`\`\`kotlin fun pauseFocus(nowMillis: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()) { stateStore.updateState(FocusSessionKey) { session -\> if (session !is FocusSession.Running) return@updateState session FocusSession.Paused(session.taskId, session.endTimeMillis - nowMillis) } } fun resumeFocus(nowMillis: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()) { stateStore.updateState(FocusSessionKey) { session -\> if (session !is FocusSession.Paused) return@updateState session FocusSession.Running(session.taskId, nowMillis + session.remainingMillis) } } \`\`\` \[23:03\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1383s) And lastly, there's \`getState\`, which returns a read-only State for a key, and it has the option to override the default value, if you want to change that up at a specific call site. \`\`\`kotlin @Singleton class FocusSessionManager @Inject constructor( private val stateStore: StateStore, ) { val session: State = stateStore.getState(FocusSessionKey) ... } \`\`\` \[23:12\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1392s) And, exposing the \`FocusSession\` State in this manager means that consumers never have to access \`StateStore\` or its keys directly. \[23:18\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1398s) You can in-- maintain write and read encapsulation. \[23:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1402s) And then, instead of consumers they just inject Focus Session Manager, which, well, they probably already have because they need to control the session, and then they can read the State. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class MiniTimerViewModel @Inject constructor( focusSessionManager: FocusSessionManager, ) : ViewModel() { ... } @EntryPoint @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) interface WidgetEntryPoint { fun focusSessionManager(): FocusSessionManager } \`\`\` \[23:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1413s) And then, those readers, they can either directly re-expose the State, or they can use Transform to make a new, updated State kind of like we saw with the Mini-Timer \`ViewModel\` example earlier. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class MiniTimerViewModel @Inject constructor( focusSessionManager: FocusSessionManager, ) : ViewModel() { val session: State = focusSessionManager.session } \`\`\` \[23:45\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1425s) And then, the UI Composables can read that State just like any other Compose State and recompose when necessary. \`\`\`kotlin @HiltViewModel class MiniTimerViewModel @Inject constructor( focusSessionManager: FocusSessionManager, ) : ViewModel() { val session: State = focusSessionManager.session } @Composable fun MiniTimerBar(viewModel: MiniTimerViewModel = hiltViewModel()) { val session by viewModel.session if (session !is FocusSession.Idle) { TimerReadout(session = session) } } \`\`\` \[23:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1431s) But so far, the \`FocusSession\` only ever lives in memory. \[23:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1435s) So, let's look at what it makes takes to survive process death. \[23:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1438s) So, first, we have to do some one-time setup by launching the \`syncToDataStore\` when we create the store. \`\`\`kotlin @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) object AppModule { @Provides @Singleton fun provideStateStore( @ApplicationContext context: Context, @ApplicationScope scope: CoroutineScope, ): StateStore = StateStore().apply { val path = context.dataStoreFile("app_state.json").absolutePath scope.launch { syncToDataStore(path = path, coroutineScope = scope) } } } \`\`\` \[24:04\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1444s) And then, after that, we opt in each key that we want to persist. \`\`\`kotlin @Serializable sealed interface FocusSession { @Serializable data object Idle : FocusSession @Serializable data class Running(val taskId: String, val endTimeMillis: Long) : FocusSession @Serializable data class Paused(val taskId: String, val remainingMillis: Long) : FocusSession } object FocusSessionKey : StateStoreKey(defaultValue = FocusSession.Idle), PersistToDataStore \`\`\` \[24:09\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1449s) All we have to do is make sure that the type is serializable and that the key implements \`PersistToDataStore\` interface. \[24:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1456s) And then, you might be wondering, okay, that seems easy. \[24:19\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1459s) So, what does it actually do to persist the key? \[24:22\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1462s) So, under the hood, \`syncToDataStore\` uses Transform's listener API, which is basically the exact same thing as Transform, except it doesn't return anything, it's just used for observation and side effects. \`\`\`kotlin suspend fun StateStore.syncToDataStore(dataStore: DataStore) { listener { ... } } \`\`\` \[24:33\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1473s) And then, within that listener, it reads every single key within the store, and it checks if one is a \`PersistToDataStore\` key. \`\`\`kotlin suspend fun StateStore.syncToDataStore(dataStore: DataStore) { listener { for (key in keys) { if (key is PersistToDataStore) { val value = getState(key).value LaunchedEffect(key) { // Restore saved value from dataStore on first access } LaunchedEffect(key, value) { // Flush updated value to dataStore on change } } } } } \`\`\` \[24:41\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1481s) When it is, it uses \`LaunchedEffect\` to sync those values back to \`DataStore\` whenever they change. \[24:46\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1486s) And, the thing I want to point out here is that having a standard container like \`StateStore\` is what lets us provide these drop-in integrations. \[24:51\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1491s) \`DataStore\` is just the first one we're looking at. ### Summary of Compose State categories \[24:56\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1496s) So, stepping back to our state categories, we now have a pretty clear picture of how you can use Compose State across your entire application. \[25:02\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1502s) From \`mutableStateOf\` for live state, to the SavedState APIs for screen-local presentation state, and \`StateStore\` for cross-component session state, and then lastly, we've got \`collectAsState\` for interop with Flows. \[25:15\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1515s) But really, interop isn't limited to any single category, you can just use those helpers like \`collectAsState\` whenever you need to bridge observable types into Compose State. \[25:24\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1524s) But for permanent state, one other thing we're looking at is ways to work with Compose or for \`DataStore\` and Room to directly expose Compose State, so you don't have to write your own like nicer syntax for doing that. \[25:39\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1539s) And with that, I'm happy to announce that Transform, \`StateStore\`, and the \`DataStore\` integration are all available in alpha today, and that we've also published all the documentation on developer.android.com, and we've got an AppState Recipes repo on GitHub that shows examples of using both \`StateStore\` and Transform. \`\`\`toml \[versions\] appstate = "1.0.0-alpha01" ... \[libraries\] ... transform = { module = "androidx.appstate.transform:transform", version.ref = "appstate" } transform-testing = { module = "androidx.appstate.transform:transform-testing", version.ref = "appstate" } statestore = { module = "androidx.appstate.statestore:statestore", version.ref = "appstate" } statestore-datastore = { module = "androidx.appstate.statestore:statestore-datastore", version.ref = "appstate" } \`\`\` \[25:55\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1555s) And, yeah, please give them a try in your app. \[25:58\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1558s) Give us feedback. \[25:59\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=69QYEXymfVo\&t=1559s) Like, we're in alpha, so this is when we can really iterate and make changes that'll make sure that they work for your use cases.</a>
entries.summary: Introduces Jetpack AppState, a set of libraries that leverages the Compose runtime and snapshot system beyond the UI layer to streamline state hoisting, derivation, and sharing across Android application components.

entries.title: The car is your canvas: Unlocking Android development for the road
entries.summary: Added a new developer summit talk page providing an embedded video and interactive transcript for 'The car is your canvas: Unlocking Android development for the road'. This enables developers to easily access sessions focused on building Android applications for automotive platforms.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/the-car-is-your-canvas-unlocking-android-development-for-the-road.txt" target="_blank">The car is your canvas: Unlocking Android development for the road - Speakers: Paul Lammertsma (Developer Relations Engineer), Thomas Weathers (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Apps foundation - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8YkU3aPbQYA - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/the-car-is-your-canvas-unlocking-android-development-for-the-road ## About the talk As in-car displays expand across Android Auto and Android Automotive OS vehicles, developers face a unique dual challenge: delivering rich, adaptive experiences while parked, and driver-safe, template-driven experiences while driving. In this comprehensive 30-minute technical session, we explore the end-to-end architecture and development approaches to adapting Android apps to cars. From the fundamentals of designing apps for use in cars, to the newest approaches for building media experiences that shift from audio to video as the car shifts from drive to park, you'll leave with everything you need to know to get your app on the road. ## Summary - Android for Cars targets two platforms: Android Auto and Android Automotive OS. One projects from a phone, while the other runs directly on the vehicle. - The Car App Library provides templates for driving-optimized interfaces that adapt to various car hardware configurations. - Parked car apps rely on standard Android activities for rich experiences like video streaming, games, and web browsers. - Car App Library 1.9 brings new UI components and brand customization tokens. It also expands media template support fully to Android Automotive OS. - Park-to-drive capabilities dynamically launch native video activities when parked, then switch back to media templates to maintain uninterrupted audio when driving. ## Resources - \[Android CLI\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[Android for Cars documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-cars) - \[Build games for cars guide\](https://goo.gle/games-in-cars) - \[What's new in Android for Cars\](https://d.android.com/training/cars/whats-new) ## Topics android-for-cars, android-auto, android-automotive-os, car-app-library, media3, parked-apps ## Transcript ### Introduction to Android for cars \[00:06\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8YkU3aPbQYA\&t=6s) All right. entries.title: Trace me if you can: Automated instrumentation and field profiling
entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds a talk session and interactive transcript from the Android Dev Summit focusing on automated instrumentation and field profiling. It matters because it provides developers with direct access to expert insights and discussions on advanced app performance tracing techniques.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/trace-me-if-you-can-automated-instrumentation-and-field-profiling.txt" target="_blank">Trace me if you can: Automated instrumentation and field profiling - Speakers: Rahul Ravikumar (Staff Software Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZtQgeIrmAo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/trace-me-if-you-can-automated-instrumentation-and-field-profiling ## About the talk Optimizing Android apps requires deep visibility into concurrent workflows and coroutine suspensions. While local profiling offers a useful snapshot, scaling these insights to production without overhead remains a challenge. This session delivers an architectural blueprint for a continuous performance feedback loop. androidx.tracing 2.0: Swap backends dynamically and propagate coroutine contexts (Perfetto flows) across threads. Smart Instrumentation: Use local ART tracing to find hotspots, then automate the injection of low-overhead trace points. Macrobenchmarking: Track regressions and verify performance gains on physical devices in CI. Field Tracing: Go beyond local and CI tracing, with ProfilingManager. ## Summary - Tracing 2.0 replaces older Android tracing APIs to remove label length limits and run seven times faster. It also lets you build custom sinks for backends such as OpenTelemetry. - Context propagation maps causal relationships across threads, coroutines, and processes. You can track asynchronous execution with \`traceCoroutine\` or pass propagation tokens into callback-based code. - Jetpack Compose 1.13 adds Recomposition Tracing, using custom metadata to show why recompositions occur. Traces record the modified state values and the exact call stacks that triggered them. - Android build tools use Tracing 2.0 to spot bottlenecks and speed up builds. Tracing guided optimizations that made R8 code shrinking 25% faster and cut Metalava post-submit times by 15%. ## Topics tracing, android-performance, perfetto, context-propagation, jetpack-compose, coroutines, profiling ## Transcript ### Introduction \& evolution of Android tracing \*\*Rahul Ravikumar\*\* \[00:07\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZtQgeIrmAo\&t=7s) Good afternoon, everyone. entries.summary: This new documentation details the features of Android's Tracing 2.0 library and automated profiling tools, which help developers achieve low-overhead performance feedback and granular execution tracking across threads, coroutines, and production devices.

entries.title: Type safe keep rules and DEX optimization
entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds a Dev Summit talk session and interactive transcript regarding type-safe keep rules and DEX optimization. It provides developers with direct access to modern Android build and optimization insights.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/type-safe-keep-rules-and-dex-optimization.txt" target="_blank">Type safe keep rules and DEX optimization - Speakers: Chris Craik (Android Performance Engineer), Breana Tate (Developer Relations Engineer) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/type-safe-keep-rules-and-dex-optimization ## About the talk Android apps often ship under-optimized due to overly conservative keep rules often from third-party libraries, leading to bloated APKs, slower cold starts, and degraded runtime performance. With Google Play's new performance thresholds for DEX optimization, app visibility now directly depends on staying ahead of the optimization curve. This talk introduces a modern R8 workflow to tackle rule bloat. You will learn to: - Use the R8 config analyzer and skill to identify legacy rule overhead. - Transition from broad wildcard keep rules to precise, type-safe, generated annotations. - Prevent optimization regressions with new Android CLI tools. ## Summary - Google Play enforces app-quality thresholds requiring more than 25% code optimization. Meeting them reduces memory usage while improving start-up speed and ANR rates. - The R8 Configuration Analyzer generates an HTML report showing which keep rules retain code. It highlights subsumed and unused rules and measures optimization potential before compilation. - Overly broad keep rules, often introduced to prevent reflection crashes or inherited from libraries, undermine app optimization. A single package-wide wildcard rule can keep dozens of unused classes. - Jetpack Keep uses lint to detect reflection and generate precise annotations and conditional keep rules directly from code. It exports standard consumer rules compatible with older R8 versions. - Android CLI inspects app bundles and AARs using Google Play's exact logic without an upload. It flags problematic rules and exports JSON reports for automated regression testing. ## Resources - \[App quality memory optimization blog post\](https://android-developers.googleblog.com/2026/08/app-quality-memory-optimization-secure-onboarding.html) - \[Google Play Console\](https://play.google.com/console) - \[R8 analyzer guide\](https://goo.gle/r8-analyzer) - \[Android CLI documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-cli) - \[R8 optimization documentation\](https://goo.gle/android-r8) - \[Jetpack Keep documentation\](https://goo.gle/jetpack-keep) ## Topics dex-optimization, r8, keep-rules, jetpack-keep, android-cli, app-performance ## Transcript ### Introduction to DEX optimization type-safe keep rules and DEX optimization. \[00:16\](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwlRxGJMzWs\&t=16s) Today, we're going to talk about what DEX optimization is, why you should care, and also, some entries.summary: Added a new documentation page for the Android Dev Summit talk on unlocking agentic capabilities in apps using ML Kit and generative AI, providing developers with session details and an interactive transcript.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/unlock-agentic-capabilities-in-your-app-with-ml-kit-genai.txt" target="_blank">Unlock agentic capabilities in your app with ML Kit GenAI - Speakers: Jolanda Verhoef (Developer Relations Engineer), Victoria Lestari (Software Engineer) - Track: Intelligent Apps - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tAy7IifZXG0 - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/unlock-agentic-capabilities-in-your-app-with-ml-kit-genai ## About the talk Take your Android AI features to the next level by building autonomous on-device agents. In this session, we dive into ML Kit's new agentic APIs, built directly on top of the direct model access APIs you already know. Using the open-source Jetpacker app, you'll learn how to chain multi-step actions across local data, manage stateful multi-turn sessions with isolated contexts, and wire up Android MCP to power both in-app assistants and Android system-level surfaces with a single codebase. ## Summary - Gemini Nano 4 natively supports Function Calling, letting on-device models translate natural language into actions and drive local APIs. - The Jetpack AppFunctions library defines tools through natural-language KDoc descriptions. Changing access levels can expose these functions to system agents such as Gemini. - The new agentic flows library (alpha) in ML Kit GenAI simplifies building agents by handling the execution loop and tool calls. - \`AgentRunner\` coordinates tool execution and provides session methods for multi-turn conversations without losing context. - Direct access via the Prompt API remains available for simple history control or complex setups like multi-agent and hybrid systems. ## Skills - \[Android Skills\](https://goo.gle/android-skills) ## Resources - \[Jetpacker sample code\](https://goo.gle/jetpacker) - \[AICore Developer Preview\](https://goo.gle/aicore-dev-preview) ## Topics ml-kit, on-device-ai, gemini-nano, ai-agents, function-calling, app-functions, aicore ## entries.title: What's new in Android dev tools
entries.summary: This new documentation page embeds the talk session and interactive transcript for 'What's new in Android dev tools' from the Android Dev Summit. It provides developers with direct access to the latest updates, tools, and improvements announced for Android development.

entries.title: <a href="https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/whats-new-in-android-dev-tools.txt" target="_blank">What's new in Android dev tools - Speakers: Esteban de la Canal (Software Engineer), Adarsh Fernando (Group Product Manager) - Track: Tools \& Performance - Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w-auFZP5gJo - Page: https://developer.android.com/events/dev-summit/talks/whats-new-in-android-dev-tools ## About the talk Discover what's next for Android development across Android Studio and the terminal with Android CLI. In this session, we unveil the latest in Android Studio Canary and Stable---from AI-assisted code migrations to Compose and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) support, to Lightbuild's declarative architecture. We'll also dive into the latest updates to the Android CLI toolchain. Learn how you can use it to automate your inner-loop workflows with improved access to devices, diagnostics tools for local and production issues, profiling workflows that let your agents test and validate optimizations and much more. ## Summary - Android CLI provides structured, predictable commands without interactive prompts, built specifically to help modern coding agents navigate developer workflows. - New Android CLI commands let agents render Compose previews without Android Studio and inspect production crashes from Crashlytics. They can also delta-push APK updates during installation. - Native Android x86 APK execution directly on Linux desktops runs apps as single processes with Logcat output and without nested virtualization. - Official Android plugins equip agents in Google Antigravity and Claude Code with Android CLI and architectural guidelines. Antigravity can view Compose previews and interact directly with devices. - Android Studio Rabbit 2 introduces Bring Your Own Agent and AI Change Review to inspect pull requests and fix issues. ## Resources - \[Android Studio download\](https://d.android.com/studio) - \[Android CLI feedback and downloads\](https://d.android.com/cli) ## Topics android-cli, ai-agents, android-studio,
